clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Harassment"
clauses.body: California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(b)(3) defines "harassment," for purposes of a civil harassment restraining order, as unlawful violence, a credible threat of violence, or a knowing and willful course of conduct directed at a specific person that seriously alarms, annoys, or harasses the person, and that serves no legitimate purpose. The course of conduct must be that which would cause a reasonable person to suffer substantial emotional distress, and must actually cause substantial emotional distress to the petitioner.
clauses.gap: California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(b)(3) states a four-part test for one form of statutory "harassment": (1) unlawful violence, a credible threat of violence, or a knowing and willful course of conduct directed at a specific person; (2) that seriously alarms, annoys, or harasses that person and serves no legitimate purpose; (3) that would cause a reasonable person to suffer substantial emotional distress; and (4) that actually caused the petitioner substantial emotional distress. This is California's codified definition; the elements, terminology, and burden of proof for a civil harassment restraining order vary by state, and this clause states only what California's statute provides, not a determination that it applies to a specific petitioner, respondent, or set of facts. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 527.6(b)(3)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: the four-part statutory definition of harassment
citations.quote: "Harassment" is unlawful violence, a credible threat of violence, or a knowing and willful course of conduct directed at a specific person that seriously alarms, annoys, or harasses the person, and that serves no legitimate purpose. The course of conduct must be that which would cause a reasonable person to suffer substantial emotional distress, and must actually cause substantial emotional distress to the petitioner.

clauses.title: "Course of Conduct" Defined
clauses.body: California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(b)(1) defines "course of conduct" as a pattern of conduct composed of a series of acts over a period of time, however short, evidencing a continuity of purpose, including following or stalking an individual, making harassing telephone calls to an individual, or sending harassing correspondence to an individual by any means. Constitutionally protected activity is excluded from the definition.
clauses.gap: California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(b)(1) defines "course of conduct" as requiring a series of acts over time — however short that period is — showing continuity of purpose, and lists following/stalking, harassing phone calls, and harassing correspondence as examples. The same subdivision expressly excludes constitutionally protected activity from the definition, meaning conduct otherwise falling within a "course of conduct" is not actionable under this statute if it is constitutionally protected. This definition is drawn from a single California statutory subdivision and applies only within the harassment definition discussed elsewhere in this document; course-of-conduct definitions and exclusions for restraining orders vary by state. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 527.6(b)(1)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: the statutory definition of course of conduct
citations.quote: "Course of conduct" is a pattern of conduct composed of a series of acts over a period of time, however short, evidencing a continuity of purpose, including following or stalking an individual, making harassing telephone calls to an individual, or sending harassing correspondence to an individual by any means, including, but not limited to, the use of public or private mails, interoffice mail, facsimile, or email. Constitutionally protected activity is not included within the meaning of "course of conduct."

clauses.title: Temporary Restraining Order Mechanism and Hearing Deadline
clauses.body: Under California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6, a petitioner may obtain a temporary restraining order with or without notice to the responding party, based on a declaration showing reasonable proof of harassment and that great or irreparable harm would result absent an order. A request for a TRO without notice is granted or denied the same day it is submitted (or the next judicial business day, if filed too late for review). A TRO issued under this section remains in effect for no more than 21 days, or up to 25 days if the hearing date is extended for good cause, and a full hearing on the petition must be held within that same 21-or-25-day period.
clauses.gap: California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6, subdivisions (d) through (g), authorizes a temporary restraining order issued with or without notice to the responding party, requires a same-day (or next judicial business day) ruling on a noticed-request TRO application, caps a TRO's duration at 21 days (25 days if the hearing date is extended for good cause), and requires the full hearing to be held within that same 21-or-25-day window. These are all provisions of one California statutory section (527.6); the TRO mechanism, notice rules, and hearing deadlines for civil harassment orders vary by state. This is a single statutory section (§ 527.6(d)-(g)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: the TRO mechanism, notice rules, duration, and hearing deadline
citations.quote: (d) Upon filing a petition for orders under this section, the petitioner may obtain a temporary restraining order in accordance with Section 527... A temporary restraining order may be issued with or without notice, based on a declaration that, to the satisfaction of the court, shows reasonable proof of harassment of the petitioner by the respondent, and that great or irreparable harm would result to the petitioner. (e) A request for the issuance of a temporary restraining order without notice under this section shall be granted or denied on the same day that the petition is submitted to the court... (f) A temporary restraining order issued under this section shall remain in effect, at the court's discretion, for a period not to exceed 21 days, or, if the court extends the time for hearing under subdivision (g), not to exceed 25 days, unless otherwise modified or terminated by the court. (g) Within 21 days, or, if good cause appears to the court, 25 days from the date that a petition for a temporary order is granted or denied, a hearing shall be held on the petition.

clauses.title: What a Civil Harassment Restraining Order May Include
clauses.body: California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(b)(6)(A) authorizes an order enjoining a party from harassing, intimidating, molesting, attacking, striking, stalking, threatening, contacting (directly or indirectly), or disturbing the peace of the petitioner, and from coming within a specified distance of the petitioner. Section 527.6(c) permits the court, on a showing of good cause, to extend an order to cover other named family or household members.
clauses.gap: California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(b)(6)(A) authorizes a personal-conduct order (prohibiting harassing, intimidating, molesting, attacking, striking, stalking, threatening, contacting, or disturbing the peace of the petitioner, among other listed acts) and an order for "coming within a specified distance of" the petitioner; subdivision (c) allows the court, on a showing of good cause, to extend an order to other named family or household members. Note: the text of section 527.6 itself does not itemize specific protected locations (such as home, workplace, or school) the way some other California statutes do — it authorizes a distance order generally, keyed to the petitioner. How any specific distance or location is expressed on a given order is a matter of the form and the court's order, not language appearing in this statutory subdivision. This is one California statutory section; what a civil harassment order may include varies by state. This is a single statutory section (§ 527.6(b)(6)(A), (c)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: the categories of relief a civil harassment order may include
citations.quote: An order enjoining a party from harassing, intimidating, molesting, attacking, striking, stalking, threatening, sexually assaulting, battering, abusing, telephoning, including, but not limited to, making annoying telephone calls, as described in Section 653m of the Penal Code, destroying personal property, contacting, either directly or indirectly, by mail or otherwise, or coming within a specified distance of, or disturbing the peace of, the petitioner. ... (c) In the discretion of the court, on a showing of good cause, a temporary restraining order or order after hearing issued under this section may include other named family or household members.

clauses.title: Duration and Renewal of a Permanent Order
clauses.body: California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(j)(1) allows an order issued after notice and hearing to last no more than five years, and permits one renewal, on request, for no more than five additional years without a showing of any further harassment since the original order issued. Section 527.6(j)(2) provides that if the order's expiration date is not stated on the form, the order's duration defaults to three years from issuance.
clauses.gap: California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(j) allows a restraining order issued after a full hearing to last up to five years, renewable once requested for up to five additional years without a further showing of harassment since the original order issued, and states that an order silent on its expiration date defaults to a three-year duration from issuance. This duration and renewal structure is set by one California statutory subdivision; maximum duration and renewal procedures for civil harassment orders vary by state. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 527.6(j)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: duration and renewal of an order issued after hearing
citations.quote: In the discretion of the court, an order issued after notice and hearing under this section may have a duration of no more than five years, subject to termination or modification by further order of the court either on written stipulation filed with the court or on the motion of a party. The order may be renewed, upon the request of a party, for a duration of no more than five additional years, without a showing of any further harassment since the issuance of the original order... (2) The failure to state the expiration date on the face of the form creates an order with a duration of three years from the date of issuance.

clauses.title: Criminal Consequences of Violating an Order
clauses.body: California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(t) states that willful disobedience of a temporary restraining order or order after hearing granted under section 527.6 is punishable pursuant to Penal Code section 273.6. Penal Code section 273.6(a) makes an intentional and knowing violation of such an order a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of not more than $1,000, imprisonment in county jail for not more than one year, or both. Section 273.6(b) increases the penalty where the violation results in physical injury: a fine of not more than $2,000, imprisonment in county jail for not less than 30 days nor more than one year, or both — though the court may, in the interest of justice and for stated reasons, reduce or eliminate the 30-day minimum if the person has served at least 48 hours.
clauses.gap: California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(t) cross-references Penal Code section 273.6 for the criminal consequence of willfully disobeying a section 527.6 restraining order. These are two independently enacted California statutory sections (Code of Civil Procedure and Penal Code). Whether violating a civil harassment order is a separate criminal offense, and what the penalty structure is, varies by state.

citations.cite: cross-reference to the Penal Code violation penalty
citations.quote: Willful disobedience of a temporary restraining order or order after hearing granted pursuant to this section is punishable pursuant to Section 273.6 of the Penal Code.

citations.cite: the misdemeanor penalty structure for violating a protective order
citations.quote: (a) Any intentional and knowing violation of a protective order, as defined in Section 6218 of the Family Code, or of an order issued pursuant to Section 527.6, 527.8, or 527.85 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or Section 15657.03 of the Welfare and Institutions Code, is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of not more than one thousand dollars ($1,000), or by imprisonment in a county jail for not more than one year, or by both that fine and imprisonment. (b) In the event of a violation of subdivision (a) that results in physical injury, the person shall be punished by a fine of not more than two thousand dollars ($2,000), or by imprisonment in a county jail for not less than 30 days nor more than one year, or by both that fine and imprisonment. However, if the person is imprisoned in a county jail for at least 48 hours, the court may, in the interest of justice and for reasons stated on the record, reduce or eliminate the 30-day minimum imprisonment required by this subdivision.

clauses.title: Distinction from the Domestic Violence Prevention Act
clauses.body: California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(w) states that section 527.6 does not apply to any action or proceeding covered by Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200) of the Family Code — California's Domestic Violence Prevention Act. Family Code section 6211 defines "domestic violence" as abuse committed against a spouse or former spouse, a cohabitant or former cohabitant, a person the respondent is or has been dating or engaged to, a co-parent, a child of a party, or a relative within the second degree.
clauses.gap: California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(w) expressly states that section 527.6 does not apply to actions or proceedings covered by Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200) of the Family Code — California's Domestic Violence Prevention Act (DVPA). Family Code section 6211 defines "domestic violence" by reference to specific relationships between the parties (spouse or former spouse; cohabitant or former cohabitant; a person the respondent is or was dating or engaged to; a co-parent; a child of a party; or a relative within the second degree). A civil harassment restraining order under Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6 and a domestic violence restraining order under Family Code section 6200 et seq. are governed by different statutes, use different Judicial Council forms, and involve different eligibility relationships between petitioner and respondent; a request that in fact involves one of the Family Code section 6211 relationships falls outside what section 527.6 covers. This document addresses only the Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6 civil harassment process and does not cover Domestic Violence Prevention Act proceedings. Both statutes are provisions of California law; which category of order applies, and whether an equivalent distinction exists, varies by state.

citations.cite: civil harassment does not cover DVPA proceedings
citations.quote: This section does not apply to any action or proceeding covered by Title 1.6C (commencing with Section 1788) of Part 4 of Division 3 of the Civil Code or by Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200) of the Family Code. This section does not preclude a petitioner from using other existing civil remedies.

citations.cite: the statutory definition of domestic violence by relationship category
citations.quote: "Domestic violence" is abuse perpetrated against any of the following persons: (a) A spouse or former spouse. (b) A cohabitant or former cohabitant, as defined in Section 6209. (c) A person with whom the respondent is having or has had a dating or engagement relationship. (d) A person with whom the respondent has had a child... (e) A child of a party or a child who is the subject of an action under the Uniform Parentage Act... (f) Any other person related by consanguinity or affinity within the second degree.

This declaration describes conduct alleged by the petitioner in connection with a request for a civil harassment restraining order under California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6.

clauses.title: Categories of Relief Authorized Under § 527.6
clauses.body: The following categories of relief are authorized under California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(b)(6)(A) and section 527.6(c): (1) a personal conduct order that {{respondentName}} not harass, intimidate, molest, attack, strike, stalk, threaten, batter, telephone, or contact {{petitionerName}}, directly or indirectly; (2) a stay-away order that {{respondentName}} remain a specified distance from {{petitionerName}}, with the specific distance and any specified locations set by the order; (3) an order addressing an animal owned, possessed, or kept by {{petitionerName}}, where applicable under section 527.6(b)(6)(A); and (4) inclusion of other named family or household members, on a showing of good cause under section 527.6(c). Which of these categories to request, and how to complete the corresponding portions of a court petition, is a decision left to the person preparing that petition.

clauses.title: PAGA Pre-Suit Notice: Content and Delivery Requirements
clauses.body: Before an aggrieved employee may bring a civil action under PAGA (Labor Code § 2699) for most Labor Code violations, Labor Code § 2699.3(a)(1)(A) requires the aggrieved employee or their representative to give written notice by online filing with the California Labor and Workforce Development Agency (LWDA), and by certified mail to the employer, {{companyName}}, of the specific provisions of the Labor Code alleged to have been violated, including the facts and theories to support the alleged violation. Under the current statute, a notice filed with the LWDA under this provision, and any employer response to it, must be accompanied by a $75 filing fee, which is subject to a fee waiver under Government Code §§ 68632 and 68633.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 2699.3) — used as evidence of what California's Private Attorneys General Act requires of a PAGA pre-suit notice, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee's situation. PAGA is a distinctly Californian enforcement mechanism; most states have no comparable statute letting a private employee stand in for a state labor agency to pursue civil penalties. The "facts and theories" specificity language quoted above is part of the section's current text (amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 67 (AB 1170), effective January 1, 2026); this research did not independently fetch and compare an archived pre-2024 version of the statute, so whether that exact phrase originated with the 2024 reform (AB 2288/SB 92) or predates it is not confirmed here — only that it is part of the section as currently in force. The two citations below are both drawn from the same statutory section (§ 2699.3), subdivisions (a)(1)(A) and (a)(1)(B), rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was located for this specific point beyond it. What counts as sufficiently specific "facts and theories" has been the subject of considerable litigation not reviewed here; this clause states only the statutory text, not how courts have applied it to any particular notice.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 2699.3, subd. (a)(1)(A)
citations.quote: (1) (A) The aggrieved employee or representative shall give written notice by online filing with the Labor and Workforce Development Agency and by certified mail to the employer of the specific provisions of this code alleged to have been violated, including the facts and theories to support the alleged violation.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 2699.3, subd. (a)(1)(B)
citations.quote: (B) A notice filed with the Labor and Workforce Development Agency pursuant to subparagraph (A) and any employer response to that notice shall be accompanied by a filing fee of seventy-five dollars ($75). The fees required by this subparagraph are subject to waiver in accordance with the requirements of Sections 68632 and 68633 of the Government Code.

clauses.title: The LWDA's 65-Day Response Window
clauses.body: After an aggrieved employee's PAGA notice is filed, Labor Code § 2699.3(a)(2)(A)-(B) gives the LWDA a window to act. If the agency does not intend to investigate, it must notify the employer and the aggrieved employee by certified mail within 60 calendar days of the postmark date of the notice; the aggrieved employee may then commence a civil action once that notice is received, or once 65 calendar days pass from the postmark date of the notice without any agency notice being provided. If the agency does intend to investigate, it must notify the parties of that decision by certified mail within 65 calendar days of the postmark date of the notice, after which it has 120 calendar days to investigate and issue any citation; if no citation issues within these combined periods, or the agency fails to give timely notice, the aggrieved employee may then commence a civil action.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 2699.3) — used as evidence of California's PAGA notice-response timeline, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee's situation. The 65-day figure was checked against the current, most recently amended version of this section (amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 67 (AB 1170), effective January 1, 2026) and confirmed still current — it was not changed by the 2024 PAGA reform (AB 2288/SB 92) or by the 2025 technical amendment. Both citations below are drawn from the same statutory section (§ 2699.3), subdivisions (a)(2)(A) and (a)(2)(B), rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was located for this specific point beyond it. This clause describes only the general notice track under § 2699.3(a); a materially different timeline applies to notices alleging Cal/OSHA (Division 5) violations under § 2699.3(b), which is not addressed here.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 2699.3, subd. (a)(2)(A)
citations.quote: (2) (A) The agency shall notify the employer and the aggrieved employee or representative by certified mail that it does not intend to investigate the alleged violation within 60 calendar days of the postmark date of the notice received pursuant to paragraph (1). Upon receipt of that notice or if no notice is provided within 65 calendar days of the postmark date of the notice given pursuant to paragraph (1), the aggrieved employee may commence a civil action pursuant to Section 2699.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 2699.3, subd. (a)(2)(B)
citations.quote: (B) If the agency intends to investigate the alleged violation, it shall notify the employer and the aggrieved employee or representative by certified mail of its decision within 65 calendar days of the postmark date of the notice received pursuant to paragraph (1). Within 120 calendar days of that decision, the agency may investigate the alleged violation and issue any appropriate citation. If the agency determines that no citation will be issued, it shall notify the employer and aggrieved employee of that decision within five business days thereof by certified mail. Upon receipt of that notice or if no citation is issued by the agency within the time limits prescribed by subparagraph (A) and this subparagraph or if the agency fails to provide timely or any notification, the aggrieved employee may commence a civil action pursuant to Section 2699.

clauses.title: Employer Cure Rights Under the 2024 PAGA Reform
clauses.body: California's 2024 PAGA reform (AB 2288 and SB 92) created cure processes under Labor Code § 2699.3 that differ by employer size, effective as of § 2699.3's operative date of October 1, 2024. An employer that employed fewer than 100 employees in total during the period covered by the notice may, within 33 days of receiving the notice, submit a confidential cure proposal to the LWDA for one or more of the alleged violations, triggering an agency-supervised evaluation process. An employer not eligible for that smaller-employer track — because it employed 100 or more employees during the relevant period — may instead, after being served with a PAGA lawsuit, request a court-supervised early evaluation conference and a stay of proceedings. A separate, narrower cure track exists specifically for wage-statement violations of Labor Code § 226(a).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 2699.3) — used as evidence of how California's 2024 PAGA reform structured employer cure rights, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or which cure track a specific employer qualifies for. PAGA itself, including its cure mechanisms, is a distinctly Californian feature; most states have no comparable statute. All three citations below are drawn from the same statutory section (§ 2699.3) — subdivisions (c)(2)(A), (f)(1)(A), and (g) — rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was located for this specific point beyond it. The full cure procedures are considerably more detailed than what is quoted here — they include conference deadlines, sworn cure-completion notifications, payroll-audit requirements, agency verification timelines, and a right to appeal an adequacy determination to superior court — none of which is restated in this clause. This clause also does not restate the separate, narrower cure track for § 226(a) wage-statement violations (Lab. Code §§ 2699.3(c)(3) and 2699(d)(2)); this project's clause library already covers that narrower mechanism in the Wage Statement Itemization Policy document's `wagestmt_paga_context` clause, which should be cross-referenced rather than duplicated.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 2699.3, subd. (c)(2)(A)
citations.quote: (2) (A) Within 33 days of receipt of the notice sent by the aggrieved employee or representative, an employer that employed fewer than 100 employees in total during the period covered by the notice may submit to the agency a confidential proposal to cure one or more of the alleged violations. The employer shall specify which of the alleged violations it proposes to cure.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 2699.3, subd. (f)(1)(A)
citations.quote: (f) (1) (A) Notwithstanding any other law, an employer not covered by subparagraph (A) of paragraph (2) of subdivision (c), upon being served with a summons and complaint asserting a claim under subdivision (a) or (f) of Section 2699, may file a request for an early evaluation conference in the proceedings of the claim and a request for a stay of court proceedings prior to or simultaneous with that defendant's responsive pleading or other initial appearance in the action that includes the claim.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 2699.3, subd. (g)
citations.quote: (g) This section shall become operative October 1, 2024.

clauses.title: Who Qualifies as an "Aggrieved Employee" Under PAGA
clauses.body: Labor Code § 2699(c)(1) defines who has standing to bring a PAGA action. As currently written, an "aggrieved employee" is any person who was employed by the alleged violator and personally suffered each of the violations alleged, during the period prescribed under Code of Civil Procedure § 340. A separate, narrower definition applies only to civil actions brought by certain long-standing nonprofit legal aid organizations acting as counsel of record under § 2699(c)(2); for those actions, "aggrieved employee" instead means any person employed by the alleged violator against whom one or more of the alleged violations was committed.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 2699) — used as evidence of California's current PAGA standing requirement, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employee's situation. PAGA standing is a distinctly Californian concept; most states have no comparable private-attorney-general standing rule to compare it against. The quoted "personally suffered each of the violations alleged" language reflects the 2024 PAGA reform (AB 2288/SB 92), as further amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 67 (AB 1170), effective January 1, 2026, and is commonly described in legal-reform reporting as narrower than the pre-reform standard, which allowed standing based on any one alleged violation committed against the employee. This research relied on the current statutory text and did not independently fetch and compare an archived pre-June 2024 version of § 2699 to confirm the prior wording word-for-word, so the "narrower than before" characterization rests on the structure of the current text plus general legal-reform reporting, not a second independently fetched historical source. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 2699(c)(1)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 2699, subd. (c)(1)
citations.quote: (c) (1) For purposes of this part, "aggrieved employee" means any person who was employed by the alleged violator and personally suffered each of the violations alleged during the period prescribed under Section 340 of the Code of Civil Procedure, except that for purposes of actions brought pursuant to paragraph (2), "aggrieved employee" means any person who was employed by the alleged violator against whom one or more of the alleged violations was committed within the period prescribed under Section 340 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

clauses.title: Default Civil Penalty Amounts Under PAGA
clauses.body: Labor Code § 2699(f) sets the default civil penalty for a Labor Code violation that does not carry its own specifically-provided civil penalty. If, at the time of the alleged violation, the person does not employ one or more employees, the penalty is $500. If the person employs one or more employees, the general default penalty is $100 for each aggrieved employee per pay period, with several statutory carve-outs: a $25 per-employee, per-pay-period penalty applies to certain wage-statement violations meeting specific conditions under Labor Code § 226(a); a $50 per-employee, per-pay-period penalty applies where the violation resulted from an isolated, nonrecurring event lasting no more than 30 consecutive days or four consecutive pay periods; and a $200 per-employee, per-pay-period penalty applies where, within the preceding five years, the agency or a court already found the employer's underlying policy or practice unlawful, or where the court finds the employer's conduct was malicious, fraudulent, or oppressive.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 2699) — used as evidence of California's current PAGA default civil-penalty structure, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer's exposure or which penalty tier applies to any specific violation. PAGA's civil-penalty scheme is a distinctly Californian mechanism. The penalty structure quoted here reflects the 2024 PAGA reform as further amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 67 (AB 1170), effective January 1, 2026, and it is meaningfully different from the pre-2024 default scheme commonly described as a flat $100-per-employee-per-pay-period penalty for an initial violation and $200 for each subsequent violation; the current text does not use an "initial vs. subsequent violation" framework at all — it instead ties the $100, $200, $50, and $25 tiers to violation type, the employer's prior notice of unlawfulness, and the employer's conduct. This research relied on the current statutory text and did not independently fetch a pre-2024 archived version to compare wording line by line, so the comparison to "the pre-2024 scheme" rests on the structure of the current text plus general legal-reform reporting, not a second independently verified historical source. This clause does not address the separate reduced penalty (no more than 15% or 30% of the amount otherwise available) that applies where an employer took "all reasonable steps" toward compliance either before or within 60 days after the notice, under § 2699(g)-(h), nor the reduced $15-per-employee-per-pay-period cap that applies to a violation an employer actually cures under § 2699(j) — those reductions are separate from, and layered on top of, the default amounts quoted here. This clause has one citation because it quotes a single contiguous statutory subdivision (f) in full, not multiple non-contiguous subsections stitched together; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 2699, subd. (f)
citations.quote: (f) For all provisions of this code except those for which a civil penalty is specifically provided, there is established a civil penalty for a violation of these provisions, as follows:(1) If, at the time of the alleged violation, the person does not employ one or more employees, the civil penalty is five hundred dollars ($500).(2) If, at the time of the alleged violation, the person employs one or more employees, the civil penalty is as follows:(A) One hundred dollars ($100) for each aggrieved employee per pay period, except that:(i) If, at the time of the alleged violation, the person employs one or more employees, and the alleged violation is a violation of paragraphs (1) to (7), inclusive, or paragraph (9) of subdivision (a) of Section 226, the only civil penalty applicable under this part is twenty-five dollars ($25) for each aggrieved employee per pay period if the employee could promptly and easily determine from the wage statement alone the accurate information specified by subdivision (a) of Section 226. If the alleged violation is a violation of paragraph (8) of subdivision (a) of Section 226, the civil penalty applicable under this part for the violation is twenty-five dollars ($25) for each aggrieved employee per pay period if the employee would not be confused or misled about the correct identity of their employer or, if their employer is a farm labor contractor, the legal entity that secured the services of that employer. This subdivision does not apply if the employer has failed to provide an itemized payroll statement during any of the pay periods at issue.(ii) The civil penalty is fifty dollars ($50) for each aggrieved employee per pay period if the alleged violation resulted from an isolated, nonrecurring event that did not extend beyond the lesser of 30 consecutive days or four consecutive pay periods.(B) The civil penalty is two hundred dollars ($200) for each aggrieved employee per pay period if either of the following are met:(i) Within the five years preceding the alleged violation, the agency or any court issued a finding or determination to the employer that its policy or practice giving rise to the violation was unlawful.(ii) The court determines that the employer's conduct giving rise to the violation was malicious, fraudulent, or oppressive.(3) If the alleged violation is a failure to act by the Labor and Workforce Development Agency, or any of its departments, divisions, commissions, boards, agencies, or employees, there shall be no civil penalty.

clauses.title: How a PAGA Recovery Is Split Between the State and Employees
clauses.body: Labor Code § 2699(m) sets the default allocation of civil penalties recovered by aggrieved employees in a PAGA action: 65 percent goes to the Labor and Workforce Development Agency for labor-law enforcement and worker/employer education, and 35 percent goes to the aggrieved employees. A different rule applies to the flat $500 penalty recoverable under § 2699(f)(1), which is not split with employees.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 2699) — used as evidence of California's current PAGA allocation rule, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific recovery. PAGA's state/employee split is a distinctly Californian feature of this enforcement mechanism. The 65%/35% split quoted here reflects the 2024 PAGA reform as further amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 67 (AB 1170), effective January 1, 2026, and differs from the pre-2024 default allocation commonly described in secondary sources as 75% to the LWDA and 25% to employees; this research relied on the current statutory text and did not independently fetch a pre-2024 archived version to confirm the prior percentages, so the "changed from 75/25" characterization rests on the current text plus general legal-reform reporting, not a second independently verified historical source. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 2699(m)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 2699, subd. (m)
citations.quote: (m) Except as provided in subdivision (n), civil penalties recovered by aggrieved employees shall be distributed as follows: 65 percent to the Labor and Workforce Development Agency for enforcement of labor laws, including the administration of this part, and for education of employers and employees about their rights and responsibilities under this code, to be continuously appropriated to supplement and not supplant the funding to the agency for those purposes; and 35 percent to the aggrieved employees.

clauses.title: The One-Year Limitations Period for a PAGA Claim
clauses.body: A PAGA civil action is a statutory penalty action, and Code of Civil Procedure § 340(a) sets a one-year limitations period for an action upon a statute for a penalty or forfeiture given to an individual, or to an individual and the state — the category a PAGA action falls into — except where the statute imposing the penalty prescribes a different limitation. Labor Code § 2699(c)(1) itself measures "aggrieved employee" status by reference to "the period prescribed under Section 340 of the Code of Civil Procedure," confirming that this one-year period is the operative reference point for PAGA. Separately, Labor Code § 2699.3(e) provides that the time spent in the pre-suit notice and any agency cure-review process is not counted against the time limited for commencing the civil action — that is, the running of the limitations period is tolled while those statutory notice and cure procedures play out.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 340 and Cal. Lab. Code § 2699.3) — used as evidence of California's PAGA limitations period, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific claim's timing. A one-year statutory-penalty limitations period, and a private mechanism that tolls it during a mandatory agency pre-suit process, are both distinctly Californian features not found in most other states' law. These two citations are from different codes (the Code of Civil Procedure and the Labor Code) and are treated as independent sources rather than subsections of one statute. The quoted text of § 340(a) itself carves out an exception "if the statute imposing it prescribes a different limitation"; the PAGA statutory text reviewed here (§§ 2699 and 2699.3) was not found to prescribe a different limitations number of its own — it instead cross-references § 340 directly — but this research did not review case law interpreting how the one-year period interacts with a continuing violation, a later-amended PAGA notice, or relation-back to an earlier-filed civil complaint, all of which have been litigated; this clause states only the statutory text, not how courts have applied it.

citations.cite: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 340, subd. (a)
citations.quote: 340. Within one year: (a) An action upon a statute for a penalty or forfeiture, if the action is given to an individual, or to an individual and the state, except if the statute imposing it prescribes a different limitation.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 2699.3, subd. (e)
citations.quote: (e) The periods specified in this section are not counted as part of the time limited for the commencement of the civil action to recover penalties under this part.

clauses.title: Signature and Verification
First-Party (Self-Settled) Special Needs Trusts — Federal Statutory Basis
clauses.body: Federal Medicaid law creates a specific, narrow exception for a trust that holds a disabled individual's own assets: such a trust is excluded from Medicaid's general trust-counting rules if it meets each of several conditions set by statute — the individual is under age 65, the individual meets the federal definition of disability used elsewhere in the Social Security Act, and the trust is established for that individual's benefit by the individual, a parent, grandparent, legal guardian, or a court. This is federal law that applies the same way regardless of which state administers the Medicaid program — in California, Medi-Cal — and every other state's Medicaid program applies this same federal floor, though a state may add its own procedural requirements on top of it.
clauses.gap: This exception is codified at a specific, narrow point in the Medicaid statute — it does not create a general "special needs trust" category, only this one described combination of facts. A trust that departs from these conditions (for example, one established by someone other than the parties this statute lists, or established after the individual turns 65) does not automatically qualify, regardless of how it labels itself. Medicaid separately defines "disabled" for this purpose by cross-reference to the same definition used for Supplemental Security Income eligibility (a functional test tied to a medically determinable impairment and inability to engage in substantial gainful activity). A related paragraph of this same statute creates a separate, additionally-conditioned exception for pooled trusts managed by a non-profit association — a related but distinct arrangement not covered in this clause. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 1396p(d)(4)(A)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: the federal Medicaid statute's exception for a first-party special needs trust
citations.quote: A trust containing the assets of an individual under age 65 who is disabled (as defined in section 1382c(a)(3) of this title) and which is established for the benefit of such individual by the individual, a parent, grandparent, legal guardian of the individual, or a court if the State will receive all amounts remaining in the trust upon the death of such individual up to an amount equal to the total medical assistance paid on behalf of the individual under a State plan under this subchapter.

clauses.title: The Medicaid Payback Requirement
clauses.body: The same statutory exception that allows a first-party special needs trust to hold a disabled individual's own assets without those assets counting against Medicaid eligibility comes with a mandatory condition attached to the same sentence: the state must be repaid, out of whatever remains in the trust when the individual dies, up to the total amount of Medicaid benefits paid on that individual's behalf during their life. This payback obligation runs to the state that administered the Medicaid benefits — in California, the state Department of Health Care Services, which administers Medi-Cal — and applies regardless of who else the trust names as a remainder beneficiary; whatever the trust document says about where the remaining property should go after death, this statutory payback claim applies first, up to the amount owed.
clauses.gap: This condition is not a separate statute — it is part of the same sentence, same statutory subsection, 42 U.S.C. § 1396p(d)(4)(A), as the eligibility conditions in the preceding clause; it is presented separately here because it is one of the most consequential and most often misunderstood features of a first-party special needs trust, not because it comes from an independent source. The statute does not describe a payback capped at some lesser amount — it states the state receives amounts remaining in the trust up to the total medical assistance paid, meaning the payback claim can absorb the entire remainder if that remainder doesn't exceed what Medicaid paid. How this federal payback claim is actually processed, and what (if anything) is deducted before it is satisfied, is governed by the administering state's own Medicaid program rather than by this federal provision itself. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 1396p(d)(4)(A)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: the state Medicaid payback requirement attached to the first-party trust exception
citations.quote: A trust containing the assets of an individual under age 65 who is disabled (as defined in section 1382c(a)(3) of this title) and which is established for the benefit of such individual by the individual, a parent, grandparent, legal guardian of the individual, or a court if the State will receive all amounts remaining in the trust upon the death of such individual up to an amount equal to the total medical assistance paid on behalf of the individual under a State plan under this subchapter.

clauses.title: Third-Party Special Needs Trusts — No Statutory Payback (A Structural, Not a Standalone, Exception)
clauses.body: A trust funded with someone else's own money — for example, a parent's or grandparent's own assets, never owned by the disabled beneficiary — is treated differently under federal Medicaid law than the first-party trust described above. The same subsection that creates Medicaid's trust-counting rules applies, by its own terms, only to a trust the statute treats as "established by" the individual, and the statute defines that phrase to require that the individual's own assets were used to form the trust's corpus. A trust funded exclusively with a third party's own assets, and established by that third party, does not meet the statute's definition of a trust "established by" the individual in the first place — so the trust-counting subsection, including its payback condition, never applies to it at all.
clauses.gap: This is a real and important distinction, but it is honestly a structural consequence of how the statute defines "established by the individual," not a separate, standalone statutory exception written the way the first-party trust exception is — there is no subsection stating, in so many words, that a third-party special needs trust is exempt from payback. If the trust in fact contains any of the beneficiary's own assets — for instance, because the beneficiary contributed some of their own funds — the trust-counting rules can attach to that portion regardless of what the trust calls itself. This clause draws on the same statutory section as the two preceding clauses — 42 U.S.C. § 1396p(d) — but a different paragraph of it (the definitional paragraphs (d)(1) and (d)(2)(A), rather than the specific-exception paragraph (d)(4)(A)); it is not an independently sourced statutory rule. Whether a particular trust actually qualifies as a pure third-party trust under this reasoning is a fact-specific determination the statute does not spell out in a single clean rule. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 1396p(d)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: the definition of a trust 'established by' an individual, and the scope of Medicaid's trust-counting rules
citations.quote: (1) For purposes of determining an individual's eligibility for, or amount of, benefits under a State plan under this subchapter, subject to paragraph (4), the rules specified in paragraph (3) shall apply to a trust established by such individual. (2)(A) For purposes of this subsection, an individual shall be considered to have established a trust if assets of the individual were used to form all or part of the corpus of the trust and if any of the following individuals established such trust other than by will: (i) The individual. (ii) The individual's spouse. (iii) A person, including a court or administrative body, with legal authority to act in place of or on behalf of the individual or the individual's spouse. (iv) A person, including any court or administrative body, acting at the direction or upon the request of the individual or the individual's spouse.

clauses.title: SSI's Resource Limit and When Trust Assets Are Not a Countable Resource
clauses.body: Supplemental Security Income eligibility is subject to a strict cap on countable resources set by Social Security Administration regulation: $2,000 for an individual, and $3,000 for an individual with an eligible spouse — a figure the regulation has held constant since it took effect January 1, 1989. Separately, SSA's general resource-counting regulation defines a "resource" as property the individual owns and could convert to cash for support and maintenance, and it ties that specifically to whether the individual has the legal right, authority, or power to liquidate the property: property a person cannot liquidate is not counted as their resource at all. A properly structured special needs trust is built around that second rule — its terms are meant to ensure the beneficiary has no legal right to demand principal or compel distributions, so trust assets are not something the beneficiary "could convert to cash," rather than around any special trust-specific exclusion written into the resource-limit regulation itself.
clauses.gap: These are two distinct SSA regulations within the same regulatory part (20 C.F.R. Part 416, Subpart L) — the dollar limit (§ 416.1205) and the general availability test (§ 416.1201) — genuinely different sections addressing different questions, not subsections of one provision. Neither regulation specifically defines when trust assets are or are not "available"; SSA's more detailed, trust-specific counting rules for SSI purposes live in a different statutory provision (42 U.S.C. § 1382b(e)) and in the agency's own sub-regulatory guidance (its Program Operations Manual System), which were not independently fetched or verified here and are not cited as authority in this clause. On the dollar figure itself: the source regulation's own citation shows it was last amended in 1985 (50 FR 38982) and its table has not been updated since the $2,000/$3,000 figures took effect in 1989 — this source shows no later change to that number. Whether any particular trust's own terms in fact deny the beneficiary the kind of access this rule turns on — commonly built around "sole benefit of the beneficiary" and fully discretionary, no-demand-right distribution language — is a drafting and administration question the regulation itself does not resolve.

citations.cite: the SSI individual and couple resource limits
citations.quote: (c) Effective January 1, 1985 and later. The resources limits and effective dates for January 1, 1985 and later are as follows: Effective date Individual Individual and spouse Jan. 1, 1985 $1,600 $2,400 Jan. 1, 1986 1,700 $2,550 Jan. 1, 1987 1,800 $2,700 Jan. 1, 1988 1,900 $2,850 Jan. 1, 1989 2,000 $3,000

citations.cite: the general availability / right-to-liquidate test for what counts as a resource
citations.quote: If the individual has the right, authority or power to liquidate the property or his or her share of the property, it is considered a resource. If a property right cannot be liquidated, the property will not be considered a resource of the individual (or spouse).

clauses.title: ABLE Accounts — A Distinct, Simpler Federal Savings Vehicle (Not a Trust)
clauses.body: Separate from any trust, federal tax law authorizes a different kind of vehicle for a person with a disability to save money without losing means-tested benefits: a "qualified ABLE program" account, created by the ABLE Act of 2014 and codified in the Internal Revenue Code. An ABLE account is a state-administered savings account, not a trust — one account per eligible beneficiary, funded with cash contributions, invested and managed by the state program rather than by an individually chosen trustee. Eligibility is limited to a person whose blindness or disability began before a statutory age cutoff — currently age 46 — established either through existing Social Security disability/blindness benefits or a separate disability-certification process. A companion federal provision directs that ABLE account funds are disregarded for most means-tested federal programs, and specifically for SSI, up to $100,000 in an ABLE account is disregarded as a resource; amounts above $100,000 do count as an SSI resource (suspending, rather than terminating, SSI eligibility), while Medicaid eligibility is unaffected by the account's balance regardless of amount.
clauses.gap: Annual contributions to an ABLE account are capped, but the statute sets that cap by cross-reference to the federal annual gift-tax exclusion amount under 26 U.S.C. § 2503(b) — a figure the IRS adjusts for inflation most years — rather than stating a fixed dollar number in the ABLE statute itself; that current inflation-adjusted figure was not independently verified from a primary source here and is not stated as a specific number in this clause. The contribution-structure and eligibility-age citations below are both drawn from the same Internal Revenue Code section, 26 U.S.C. § 529A, just different subsections; the SSI/Medicaid-treatment citation is a genuinely separate source — an uncodified note under Pub. L. 113-295 rather than the operative Code section itself. An ABLE account is materially smaller in what it can hold and simpler to set up than a special needs trust, but it is not a substitute for one in every case — among other differences, it carries its own $100,000 SSI-resource-disregard ceiling and its own age-of-onset eligibility requirement, neither of which applies to a special needs trust.

citations.cite: the qualified ABLE program contribution cap, cross-referenced to the annual gift-tax exclusion
citations.quote: A program shall not be treated as a qualified ABLE program unless it provides that no contribution will be accepted— (A) unless it is in cash, or (B) except in the case of contributions under subsection (c)(1)(C) or received in a qualified ABLE rollover contribution described in section 530A(d)(4)(B), if such contribution to an ABLE account would result in aggregate contributions from all contributors to the ABLE account for the taxable year exceeding the sum of— (i) the amount in effect under section 2503(b) (determined by substituting "1996" for "1997" in paragraph (2)(B) thereof) for the calendar year in which the taxable year begins, plus (ii) in the case of any contribution by a designated beneficiary described in paragraph (7), the lesser of— (I) compensation (as defined by section 219(f)(1)) includible in the designated beneficiary's gross income for the taxable year, or (II) an amount equal to the poverty line for a one-person household, as determined for the calendar year preceding the calendar year in which the taxable year begins.

citations.cite: the age-of-onset eligibility requirement for a designated beneficiary
citations.quote: An individual is an eligible individual for a taxable year if during such taxable year— (A) the individual is entitled to benefits based on blindness or disability under title II or XVI of the Social Security Act, and such blindness or disability occurred before the date on which the individual attained age 46, or (B) a disability certification with respect to such individual is filed with the Secretary for such taxable year.

citations.case: Pub. L. 113-295, div. B, title I, § 103(a)
citations.cite: the federal means-tested-program disregard for ABLE account funds, including the $100,000 SSI resource threshold
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision of Federal law that requires consideration of 1 or more financial circumstances of an individual, for the purpose of determining eligibility to receive, or the amount of, any assistance or benefit authorized by such provision to be provided to or for the benefit of such individual, any amount (including earnings thereon) in the ABLE account (within the meaning of section 529A of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986) of such individual, any contributions to the ABLE account of the individual, and any distribution for qualified disability expenses (as defined in subsection (e)(5) of such section) shall be disregarded for such purpose with respect to any period during which such individual maintains, makes contributions to, or receives distributions from such ABLE account, except that, in the case of the supplemental security income program under title XVI of the Social Security Act [42 U.S.C. 1381 et seq.]— (1) a distribution for housing expenses (within the meaning of such subsection) shall not be so disregarded, and (2) in the case of such program, any amount (including such earnings) in such ABLE account shall be considered a resource of the designated beneficiary to the extent that such amount exceeds $100,000.

clauses.title: California's Special Needs Trust Statute — Narrower Than It Sounds
clauses.body: California's Probate Code does use the specific term "special needs trust," but only within a narrow chapter governing court-approved compromises, settlements, and judgments for a minor or a person with a disability — not as a general estate-planning statute for special needs trusts created outside that litigation context. The chapter applies only when a court approves a compromise or covenant not to sue on a minor's disputed claim, approves a compromise of a pending action involving a minor or person with a disability, or enters judgment for one of them, and the resulting money or property is to be paid or delivered for that person's benefit. Within that chapter, a separate section authorizes the court to order that such money be paid into a special needs trust instead of directly to the minor or person with a disability, requires the court to make specific findings before doing so, and keeps the resulting trust under the court's continuing jurisdiction.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, not a description of special needs trusts generally — its "special needs trust" only exists as a mechanism for money a court is itself directing out of a settlement, covenant, or judgment; it is not a vehicle a family can independently establish outside a lawsuit under this particular statute. A trust created outside this litigation context — for example, funded with a parent's own estate-planning assets rather than a court-approved settlement — is not governed by this chapter, and instead depends on general trust law and the federal Medicaid/SSI rules addressed elsewhere in this document, not on Cal. Prob. Code §§ 3600-3613. The two citations below (§ 3604(a)(1) and § 3604(b)) are subsections of the same code section, presented separately here only for readability, not as independent sources from each other; § 3600 is a genuinely different section.

citations.cite: the scope of Probate Code Chapter 4's protective proceedings for a minor's or disabled person's litigation recovery
citations.quote: This chapter applies whenever both of the following conditions exist: (a) A court (1) approves a compromise of, or the execution of a covenant not to sue on or a covenant not to enforce judgment on, a minor's disputed claim, (2) approves a compromise of a pending action or proceeding to which a minor or person with a disability is a party, or (3) gives judgment for a minor or person with a disability. (b) The compromise, covenant, or judgment provides for the payment or delivery of money or other property for the benefit of the minor or person with a disability.

citations.cite: the court-ordered special needs trust mechanism itself
citations.quote: (a)(1) If a court makes an order under Section 3602 or 3611 that money of a minor or person with a disability be paid to a special needs trust, the terms of the trust shall be reviewed and approved by the court and shall satisfy the requirements of this section. The trust is subject to continuing jurisdiction of the court, and is subject to court supervision to the extent determined by the court. The court may transfer jurisdiction to the court in the proper county for commencement of a proceeding as determined under Section 17005.

citations.cite: the findings the court must make before establishing the trust
citations.quote: (b) A special needs trust may be established and continued under this section only if the court determines all of the following: (1) That the minor or person with a disability has a disability that substantially impairs the individual's ability to provide for the individual's own care or custody and constitutes a substantial handicap. (2) That the minor or person with a disability is likely to have special needs that will not be met without the trust. (3) That money to be paid to the trust does not exceed the amount that appears reasonably necessary to meet the special needs of the minor or person with a disability.

clauses.title: Declaration
clauses.body: I, {{settlorName}}, as settlor, declare that I am creating the {{trustName}} for the benefit of {{beneficiaryName}}, and that I am transferring the property described in the attached schedule to {{trusteeName}}, as initial trustee, to hold, administer, and distribute according to the terms of this trust. This trust is intended to qualify as a special needs trust — a trust structured so that its assets are not treated as available to {{beneficiaryName}} for purposes of eligibility for means-tested government benefits. Upon the death, resignation, or incapacity of {{trusteeName}}, {{successorTrusteeName}} shall serve as successor trustee.

clauses.title: Discretionary Distribution Standard — Sole Benefit
clauses.body: The trustee shall use the trust property solely for the benefit of {{beneficiaryName}} and for no other person's benefit, applying distributions to supplement — and not replace — any benefits {{beneficiaryName}} receives or may become eligible to receive from any government program. All distributions of income or principal are within the trustee's sole and absolute discretion; {{beneficiaryName}} has no right to demand or compel any distribution, and no power to assign, direct, or anticipate any interest in the trust property. ☐ The trustee's discretion is limited as follows: {{distributionLimitations}}

clauses.title: Signature and Notarization
clauses.body:
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, {{settlorName}}, as settlor, and {{trusteeName}}, as trustee, have signed this trust instrument on the date written below.

☐ _________________________ Date: _______________
{{settlorName}}, Settlor

☐ _________________________ Date: _______________
{{trusteeName}}, Trustee

A notary public or other officer completing a notarial certificate for this instrument verifies only the identity of the individual who signed the document, not the truthfulness, accuracy, or validity of that document.

clauses.title: What a Quitclaim Deed Conveys — No Warranty of Title
clauses.body: A quitclaim deed conveys to {{granteeName}} only whatever right, title, and interest {{grantorName}} actually holds in the property at {{propertyAddress}}, described as {{legalDescription}} — if any — as of the date the deed is signed. It carries no covenant or warranty that {{grantorName}} holds good title, that title is free of liens or encumbrances, or that {{grantorName}} holds any interest in the property at all. California's Civil Code sets out a statutory form for a "grant" of an estate in real property, and separately provides that specific covenants of title — that the grantor has not already conveyed the same interest to someone else, and that the estate is free of encumbrances made or suffered by the grantor — are implied only from a conveyance's use of the word "grant." A quitclaim deed's operative language does not use that word.
clauses.gap: California's Civil Code does not set out a distinct statutory form specifically labeled a "quitclaim deed" the way it does for a grant deed — Civil Code § 1092's "I, A B, grant to C D…" language. The customary "convey and quitclaim" (or "remise, release, and forever quitclaim") wording used in a quitclaim deed is a matter of established California conveyancing practice, not itself codified in a numbered section; that specific gap was checked directly against the statutory text rather than assumed. What is codified, and quoted below, is (1) the statutory grant-deed form, and (2) the rule that specific title covenants attach only to a conveyance's use of the word "grant." This clause's statement that a quitclaim deed carries no such covenants is a direct inference from § 1113's own text (covenants are implied "from the use of the word 'grant'" and "none other"), not a quoted statement about quitclaim deeds specifically. §§ 1092 and 1113 are genuinely separate statutory sections in different articles of the same chapter, treated here as two independent sources. This is California's own codification; deed forms and which words of conveyance (if any) imply covenants of title vary from state to state, and this is not a claim about which state's law governs a particular transfer.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, statutory form of a grant of an estate in real property
citations.quote: A grant of an estate in real property may be made in substance as follows: “I, A B, grant to C D all that real property situated in (insert name of county) County, State of California, bounded (or described) as follows: (here insert property description, or if the land sought to be conveyed has a descriptive name, it may be described by the name, as for instance, ‘The Norris Ranch.’) Witness my hand this (insert day) day of (insert month), 20___. _____ AB”

citations.cite: California Civil Code, covenants implied from the word "grant"
citations.quote: From the use of the word “grant” in any conveyance by which an estate of inheritance or fee simple is to be passed, the following covenants, and none other, on the part of the grantor for himself and his heirs to the grantee, his heirs, and assigns, are implied, unless restrained by express terms contained in such conveyance: 1. That previous to the time of the execution of such conveyance, the grantor has not conveyed the same estate, or any right, title, or interest therein, to any person other than the grantee; 2. That such estate is at the time of the execution of such conveyance free from incumbrances done, made, or suffered by the grantor, or any person claiming under him. Such covenants may be sued upon in the same manner as if they had been expressly inserted in the conveyance.

clauses.title: Writing Requirement and Execution by an Attorney in Fact
clauses.body: California law requires that a transfer of an estate in real property — other than a lease for a term of one year or less — be made by a written instrument, signed by the person disposing of the interest, or by that person's agent if the agent is authorized to sign in writing. If {{grantorName}}'s deed is instead signed by an attorney in fact acting on {{grantorName}}'s behalf, California law requires the attorney in fact to sign both {{grantorName}}'s name as the principal and the attorney in fact's own name, identified as attorney in fact.
clauses.gap: This states California's own writing and execution formalities for a transfer of real property generally; it is not specific to quitclaim deeds as a category, and it is not a claim about which state's execution formalities apply to a particular transfer — states differ on whether a deed must be witnessed, how an agent's authority must be documented, and similar mechanics. §§ 1091 and 1095 are genuinely separate statutory sections, treated here as two independent sources. This clause does not address the separate requirement — found in the Government Code, not the Civil Code — that a deed's execution be acknowledged before a notary public in order to be recorded; that requirement is addressed in a separate clause.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, real property transfers must be in writing
citations.quote: An estate in real property, other than an estate at will or for a term not exceeding one year, can be transferred only by operation of law, or by an instrument in writing, subscribed by the party disposing of the same, or by his agent thereunto authorized by writing.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, execution by an attorney in fact
citations.quote: When an attorney in fact executes an instrument transferring an estate in real property, he must subscribe the name of his principal to it, and his own name as attorney in fact.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment Before a Notary and Recorder Acceptance
clauses.body: For a deed to be recorded in California, its execution generally must be acknowledged by the person who signed it. A quitclaim deed is one of the specific instrument types California law does not allow to be recorded merely on "proof" by a subscribing witness in place of acknowledgment — a quitclaim deed's execution must be acknowledged before a notary public or other authorized officer, and that acknowledgment must itself be certified as prescribed by law. Separately, a county recorder must accept a properly acknowledged quitclaim deed for recordation, on payment of the proper fees and taxes, if it contains enough information to be indexed, meets state and local recording requirements, and is photographically reproducible; the recorder may not refuse to record it on the basis of its "lack of legal sufficiency."
clauses.gap: This is California's own recording-formalities framework; acknowledgment and recording mechanics are not uniform across states, and this is not a claim about which state's law governs a particular deed. §§ 27287 and 27201 are genuinely separate Government Code sections, treated here as two independent sources. § 27201's "local recording requirements" language is a direct acknowledgment that individual county recorders impose their own additional formatting rules (margins, page size, first-page content, and similar mechanics) on top of this statewide framework; this clause does not catalog any specific county's additional requirements. Separately, this clause does not address the county documentary transfer tax or Preliminary Change of Ownership Report steps that commonly accompany recording a deed — those are addressed in separate clauses.

citations.cite: California Government Code, acknowledgment required before an instrument can be recorded
citations.quote: Unless it belongs to the class provided for in either Sections 27282 to 27286, inclusive, or Section 1202 or 1203, of the Civil Code, or is a fictitious mortgage or deed of trust as provided in Section 2952 or 2963 of the Civil Code, or is a fictitious oil and gas lease as provided in Section 1219 of the Civil Code, or is a claim of lien under Section 8416 of the Civil Code or a notice of completion under Section 8182 or 9204 of the Civil Code, before an instrument can be recorded its execution shall be acknowledged by the person executing it, or if executed by a corporation, by its president or secretary or other person executing it on behalf of the corporation, or, except for any power of attorney, quitclaim deed, grant deed, mortgage, deed of trust, security agreement, or other document affecting real property, proved by subscribing witness or as provided in Sections 1198 and 1199 of the Civil Code, and the acknowledgment or proof certified as prescribed by law. This section shall not apply to a trustee’s deed resulting from a decree of foreclosure, or a nonjudicial foreclosure pursuant to Section 2924 of the Civil Code, or to a deed of reconveyance.

citations.cite: California Government Code, recorder's duty to accept a conforming instrument for recordation
citations.quote: The recorder shall, upon payment of proper fees and taxes, accept for recordation any instrument, paper, or notice that is authorized or required by statute, or court order to be recorded, or authorized or required to be recorded by a local ordinance that relates to the recordation of any instrument, paper, or notice that relates to real property, if the instrument, paper, or notice contains sufficient information to be indexed as provided by statute, meets recording requirements of state statutes and local ordinances, and is photographically reproducible. The county recorder shall not refuse to record any instrument, paper, or notice that is authorized or required by statute, court order, or local ordinance that relates to the recordation of any instrument, paper, or notice that relates to real property to be recorded on the basis of its lack of legal sufficiency.

clauses.title: Recording: Constructive Notice and California's Race-Notice Rule
clauses.body: A quitclaim deed transfers whatever interest {{grantorName}} has to {{granteeName}} once it is validly executed and delivered, even if it is never recorded; recording is not a condition of the deed's validity between {{grantorName}} and {{granteeName}}. Recording matters for what it does against later claimants: once a conveyance of real property is acknowledged, certified, and recorded as prescribed by law, it serves as constructive notice of its contents to subsequent purchasers and mortgagees, from the time it is filed with the recorder. California is a "race-notice" recording state — an earlier conveyance of the same property that is not recorded is void against a later purchaser or mortgagee who takes the property in good faith, for valuable consideration, and records first.
clauses.gap: California's race-notice recording rule is stated here as evidence of how one state resolves competing claims to the same property, not as a claim about which state's recording rule governs a particular property or transfer — recording statutes vary meaningfully by state, including "pure race" states (first to record wins regardless of notice) and "pure notice" states (a later good-faith purchaser without notice prevails even if they record second). §§ 1213 and 1214 are genuinely separate statutory sections, treated here as two independent sources. This clause does not evaluate whether a particular later claimant on the facts of any specific transfer actually qualifies as a good-faith purchaser for valuable consideration, and it does not address the documentary transfer tax or Preliminary Change of Ownership Report steps a county recorder may separately require at the time of recording — those are addressed in separate clauses.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, recording gives constructive notice
citations.quote: Every conveyance of real property or an estate for years therein acknowledged or proved and certified and recorded as prescribed by law from the time it is filed with the recorder for record is constructive notice of the contents thereof to subsequent purchasers and mortgagees; and a certified copy of such a recorded conveyance may be recorded in any other county and when so recorded the record thereof shall have the same force and effect as though it was of the original conveyance and where the original conveyance has been recorded in any county wherein the property therein mentioned is not situated a certified copy of the recorded conveyance may be recorded in the county where such property is situated with the same force and effect as if the original conveyance had been recorded in that county.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, race-notice recording rule
citations.quote: Every conveyance of real property or an estate for years therein, other than a lease for a term not exceeding one year, is void as against any subsequent purchaser or mortgagee of the same property, or any part thereof, in good faith and for a valuable consideration, whose conveyance is first duly recorded, and as against any judgment affecting the title, unless the conveyance shall have been duly recorded prior to the record of notice of action.

clauses.title: Preliminary Change of Ownership Report
clauses.body: California law directs each county assessor and recorder to make a "Preliminary Change of Ownership Report" form available, which the transferee of real property completes and may file with the recorder at the time a document effecting a change in ownership — such as this deed — is recorded. The report must be signed by the transferee personally, or by an officer of a transferee entity, certifying that the information given is true, correct, and complete to the best of the transferee's knowledge; an agent acting for the transferee may not sign it. If a deed is presented for recording without a report filed concurrently, the recorder may charge an additional recording fee, but noncompliance does not otherwise delay or block recording once that fee is paid. Separately, certain transfers between spouses do not count as a taxable "change in ownership" in the first place, including a transfer that creates, transfers, or terminates a co-owner's interest solely between spouses, and a transfer to a spouse in connection with a marital settlement agreement or a dissolution or legal-separation judgment.
clauses.gap: This states two genuinely separate California statutory sections — § 480.3, governing the PCOR filing mechanic and fee, and § 63, defining an interspousal exclusion from what counts as a taxable "change in ownership" — treated here as independent sources. Whether a particular transfer this deed effects falls inside that interspousal exclusion depends on facts (who the parties are, what interest passes, and why) that this clause does not evaluate for any specific transfer. Being excluded from "change in ownership" for reassessment purposes is not necessarily the same as being excused from filing a PCOR at all — county assessor practice commonly still expects a report to be filed, or a specific exemption to be claimed on it, even for an excluded transfer; this clause states that distinction rather than resolving it. This is California's own reporting regime; other states do not necessarily use an equivalent form or filing mechanic, and this is not a claim about which state's law applies to a given transfer. This clause does not address the separate documentary transfer tax, covered in another clause.

citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, Preliminary Change of Ownership Report
citations.quote: (a) Each county assessor and recorder shall make available, without charge and upon request, a form entitled “Preliminary Change of Ownership Report,” which transferees of real property shall complete and may file with the recorder concurrent with the recordation of any document effecting a change in ownership. The form shall be signed by the transferee or an officer of the transferee certifying that the information provided on the form is, to the best of his or her knowledge and belief, true, correct, and complete. The form shall not be signed by an agent acting for a transferee. (b) If a document evidencing a change in ownership is presented to the recorder for recordation without the concurrent filing of a preliminary change in ownership report, the recorder may charge an additional recording fee of twenty dollars ($20). (c) Noncompliance with this section by the transferee shall not delay or preclude the recordation of documents if the additional fee specified in subdivision (b) is tendered.
