clauses.title: Response to Notice of Claim Filed
clauses.body: {{companyName}} submits this response to the Notice of Claim Filed that the California Employment Development Department (EDD) mailed regarding a claim for unemployment insurance benefits filed by {{employeeName}}, a former employee of {{companyName}} whose employment with {{companyName}} ended on {{separationDate}}. The EDD's notice was mailed on {{claimDate}}.

clauses.title: The Notice of Claim Filed and the Employer's 10-Day Window to Respond
clauses.body: When a former employee files a new or additional unemployment insurance claim, California law requires the EDD to give notice of the filing to the employing unit that last employed the claimant immediately before the claim was filed. That employer must, within 10 days after the notice is mailed, submit to the EDD any facts then known that may affect the claimant's eligibility for benefits — a duty the statute's own text says expressly includes facts relevant to the misconduct/voluntary-quit disqualification standard described below. A related, more specific statute independently gives an employer entitled under that same notice provision up to 10 days after the notice is mailed to submit facts showing that the claimant left employment voluntarily without good cause, was discharged for misconduct connected with the work, or left under several other listed circumstances (for example, to accompany a spouse or domestic partner, or to escape domestic violence abuse). Both 10-day periods described here may be extended by the EDD's director for good cause, and if an employer learns relevant facts only after its 10-day period has run, it has a further 10 days from acquiring that knowledge to submit them.
clauses.gap: This task's research brief asked this document's drafter to verify, rather than assume, which statute sets the commonly-cited 10-day employer response deadline, expecting it to be Unemployment Insurance Code § 1032. That expectation does not match the statutory text: § 1032 was checked directly and contains no response deadline at all — it addresses whether benefits paid are charged to the employer's reserve account, which is a separate, later-in-the-process question addressed in a separate clause below. The real 10-day deadline is set by two overlapping provisions: § 1327 (the general duty on the claimant's last employer to report any fact affecting eligibility) and § 1030(a) (a more specific right, for an employer entitled under § 1327 to receive notice, to submit facts on the voluntary-quit-without-good-cause and misconduct issues listed in that subsection). The commonly-cited '10 days' figure itself is accurate; the section number commonly associated with it in this project's prior assumptions was not. Separately, the brief also asked this drafter to verify whether § 1327 establishes that a non-responding employer loses its status as an 'interested party' to the claim, along with related appeal or relief-from-charges rights. No such text was found: neither § 1327 nor § 1030 uses the phrase 'interested party' to describe an employer's status, and the one appearance of that phrase in § 1030 (subdivision (c)) describes the EDD director's own status on an appeal, not any employer's. This document therefore does not state that an employer forfeits 'interested party' status for a late or missing response; the real, verified consequence of an untimely or missing response — loss of the reserve-account non-charging protection — is described in a separate clause below. This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code §§ 1327 and 1030(a)), used as real evidence of the notice-and-response mechanism a state can build into its unemployment insurance claims process — not a claim about which state's law governs a given employer or claim.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1327 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: The department shall give a notice of the filing of a new or additional claim to the employing unit by which the claimant was last employed immediately preceding the filing of the claim unless the additional claim is the result of the filing of a partial claim as defined by the department, there has not been a subsequent employing unit which is designated as the last employer, and there is no separation issue. The employing unit so notified shall submit within 10 days after the mailing of the notice any facts then known that may affect the claimant’s eligibility for benefits, including, but not limited to, facts pertaining to eligibility under Section 1256. The 10-day period may be extended for good cause. If after the 10-day period the employing unit acquires knowledge of facts that may affect the eligibility of the claimant and facts could not reasonably have been known within the period, the employing unit shall, within 10 days of acquiring the knowledge, submit the facts to the department, and the 10-day period may also be extended for good cause.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1030(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: (a) An employer that is entitled under Section 1327 to receive notice of the filing of a new or additional claim may, within 10 days after mailing of the notice, submit to the department any facts within its possession disclosing whether the claimant left the employer’s employ voluntarily and without good cause or left under one of the following circumstances: (1) The claimant was discharged from the employment for misconduct connected with their work. … The period during which the employer may submit these facts may be extended by the director for good cause.

clauses.title: Reason for Separation: The Misconduct / Voluntary-Quit Standard
clauses.body: A separate statute states the substantive standard the EDD applies in deciding whether a claimant's own reason for leaving disqualifies the claimant from unemployment insurance benefits: an individual is disqualified if the director finds that the individual left the most recent work voluntarily without good cause, or was discharged for misconduct connected with the most recent work. The same statute creates a rebuttable presumption running in the claimant's favor: an individual is presumed to have been discharged for reasons other than misconduct, and not to have voluntarily left without good cause, unless the employer has given written notice to the contrary to the EDD (as provided in the notice-and-response statute described above), setting out facts sufficient to overcome that presumption.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1256), used as real evidence of the substantive eligibility standard and burden-shifting structure a state can attach to an employer's separation-response duty — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular claimant's eligibility, and not a statement about how a specific claimant's separation should be characterized. Neither 'misconduct' nor 'good cause' is defined within the statutory text quoted here; both terms have been the subject of extensive EDD precedent decisions and California appellate case law construing their meaning, which this document does not survey or attempt to summarize. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1256); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1256 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: An individual is disqualified for unemployment compensation benefits if the director finds that he or she left his or her most recent work voluntarily without good cause or that he or she has been discharged for misconduct connected with his or her most recent work. An individual is presumed to have been discharged for reasons other than misconduct in connection with his or her work and not to have voluntarily left his or her work without good cause unless his or her employer has given written notice to the contrary to the department as provided in Section 1327, setting forth facts sufficient to overcome the presumption. The presumption provided by this section is rebuttable.

clauses.title: Reserve-Account Charging Consequence of an Untimely or Missing Response
clauses.body: A further statute ties the outcome of the misconduct/voluntary-quit ruling described above to the employer's own unemployment insurance reserve account. If it is ruled that the claimant left voluntarily without good cause, was discharged for misconduct, or left under one of several other listed circumstances, benefits later paid to the claimant based on wages earned from that employer are, subject to certain exceptions, not charged to the employer's reserve account. That protection from charging does not apply, however, if the employer failed to furnish the facts described above within the applicable time limit, or if the ruling is later reversed on reconsideration.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1032), used as real evidence that a state can condition an employer's protection from reserve-account charging on a timely factual response to a notice of claim — not a claim about which state's law governs a given employer's account or charges. This clause quotes § 1032's operative sentence, which itself cross-references Unemployment Insurance Code §§ 1026, 1026.1, 1030, and 1328; this document does not independently verify the content of §§ 1026, 1026.1, or 1328, and describes only what § 1032's own text says about the consequence of an untimely or missing § 1030 response. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1032); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1032 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: If it is ruled under Section 1030 or 1328 that the claimant left the employer’s employ voluntarily and without good cause, or left under one of the following circumstances, benefits paid to the claimant subsequent to the termination of employment that are based upon wages earned from the employer prior to the date of the termination of employment shall not be charged to the account of the employer, except as provided by Section 1026 or if the department determines pursuant to Section 1026.1 that the employer’s reserve account should not be credited, unless the employer failed to furnish the information specified in Section 1030 within the time limit prescribed in that section or unless that ruling is reversed by a reconsidered ruling: (a) The claimant was discharged by reason of misconduct connected with his or her work.

clauses.title: How Reserve-Account Charges Connect to the Employer's Contribution Rate
clauses.body: A separate statute sets each employer's UI contribution (payroll tax) rate from a statutory schedule keyed to the employer's own 'reserve ratio' — the employer's net reserve-account balance measured against its average base payroll — with rate lines that, depending on which statewide schedule is in effect for the year and where the employer's reserve ratio falls on it, run from a small fraction of a percent up to a statutory maximum of 5.4% of the wage base described in the statute. Because a benefit charge that is not excluded from charging under the provision described in the previous clause is charged to the employer's reserve account, and because that account's balance is a direct input to this rate-setting formula, a charge to the account is capable of moving an employer to a different line on this statutory schedule, and therefore a different contribution rate, in a later year.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 977(a)), used as real evidence that California ties an employer's own future UI contribution rate to that employer's reserve-account balance through a statutory experience-rating formula — not a claim about which state's law governs a given employer's rate, and not a prediction of what will happen to any particular employer's rate. The statute itself sets out the rate-schedule mechanics; it does not contain a sentence stating that a single unanswered claim will raise a given employer's rate, and this document does not calculate or predict the size, timing, or existence of any rate effect for any specific employer — that depends on the employer's full reserve-account history, the statewide schedule in effect for the relevant year, and other statutory provisions (including § 1032, described in the preceding clause) that are not independently modeled here. § 977(a) also incorporates a lengthy numeric rate table with dozens of lines; this clause quotes only the table's structural, operative sentence and does not reproduce the table itself. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 977(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 977(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: (a) Except as provided in subdivision (c), if, as of the computation date, the employer’s net balance of reserve equals or exceeds that percentage of his or her average base payroll which appears on any line in column 1 of the following table, but is less than that percentage of his or her average base payroll which appears on the same line in column 2 of that table, his or her contribution rate shall be the figure appearing on that same line in the appropriate schedule, as defined in subdivision (b), which shall be a percentage of the wages specified in Section 930.

clauses.title: Statement of Facts Regarding Separation
clauses.body: {{companyName}} states that {{employeeName}}'s employment ended for the following reason: {{separationReason}}. In support of this response, {{companyName}} submits the following facts within its knowledge concerning the separation: {{supportingFacts}}. {{companyName}} is submitting this statement within the time period stated in the EDD's notice.

clauses.title: License Versus Sale: Why the Distinction Matters
clauses.body: Federal copyright law treats a license and a sale of software very differently. Under the Copyright Act, the owner of copyright in a work has the exclusive rights to reproduce it, prepare derivative works from it, distribute copies of it, and to authorize others to do those things. This document grants {{licenseeName}} permission to use {{softwareDescription}} under some of {{licensorName}}'s exclusive rights — it is a license, not a sale, and {{licensorName}} retains ownership of the copyright in {{softwareDescription}} unless a separate agreement transfers that ownership. This distinction matters because federal law also gives the owner of a lawfully made copy — someone who bought that copy outright — the right to resell or otherwise dispose of that particular copy without needing the copyright owner's permission, a rule known as the first sale doctrine. Whether {{licenseeName}} qualifies as an "owner" of a copy for purposes of that rule, given that this document is a license rather than a sale, is addressed elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, uniform nationwide. The exclusive-rights list in 17 U.S.C. § 106 is itself expressly made "subject to sections 107 through 122" of the Copyright Act — including fair use and other statutory limitations not addressed by this clause. This clause states the general license/sale distinction and the existence of the first sale doctrine; it does not resolve whether any particular transaction under this agreement will be characterized as a license or a sale, which depends on the specific terms of the agreement and is addressed in the next clause.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, exclusive rights in copyrighted works
citations.quote: Subject to sections 107 through 122, the owner of copyright under this title has the exclusive rights to do and to authorize any of the following: (1) to reproduce the copyrighted work in copies or phonorecords; (2) to prepare derivative works based upon the copyrighted work; (3) to distribute copies or phonorecords of the copyrighted work to the public by sale or other transfer of ownership, or by rental, lease, or lending...

citations.cite: U.S. Code, limitations on exclusive rights — effect of transfer of particular copy or phonorecord (first sale doctrine)
citations.quote: Notwithstanding the provisions of section 106(3), the owner of a particular copy or phonorecord lawfully made under this title, or any person authorized by such owner, is entitled, without the authority of the copyright owner, to sell or otherwise dispose of the possession of that copy or phonorecord.

clauses.title: The Ninth Circuit Test for Whether Software Is Licensed or Sold
clauses.body: The label a software agreement uses for itself is not necessarily the last word on whether the transaction is legally a license or a sale. The Ninth Circuit has articulated a specific test: a software user is a licensee, rather than an owner of a copy — meaning the first sale doctrine does not apply to that copy — where the copyright owner (1) specifies that the user is granted a license, (2) significantly restricts the user's ability to transfer the software, and (3) imposes notable use restrictions. In the case establishing this test, the software publisher's agreement retained title to the software, barred the customer from renting, leasing, or transferring it without consent, barred transfer outside a defined geographic area, and restricted the customer's ability to modify or reverse-engineer the software — and the court held that because of those provisions, the customer was a licensee, not an owner, so a person who later acquired copies from that customer could not invoke the first sale doctrine to justify reselling them. A consequence the same court identified is that a licensee who is not an "owner" of a copy also cannot invoke the separate statutory defense that lets an owner of a copy make the essential copies needed just to run software on a computer.
clauses.gap: This is Ninth Circuit precedent (Vernor v. Autodesk); it is binding within that circuit, including on courts sitting in California, but other federal circuits have not uniformly adopted this same three-factor test for distinguishing a software license from a sale, and the question can be analyzed differently outside the Ninth Circuit. This clause states the three-factor test and its stated consequences as articulated in that case; it does not resolve how any particular license's actual terms would be evaluated under that test, since that depends on close review of the specific provisions at issue — something this clause does not do for this agreement.

citations.quote: We hold today that a software user is a licensee rather than an owner of a copy where the copyright owner (1) specifies that the user is granted a license; (2) significantly restricts the user's ability to transfer the software; and (3) imposes notable use restrictions.

CTA was a licensee rather than an “owner of a particular copy” of Release 14, and it was not entitled to resell its Release 14 copies to Vernor under the first sale doctrine. 17 U.S.C. § 109(a). Therefore, Vernor did not receive title to the copies from CTA and accordingly could not pass ownership on to others.

clauses.title: Clickwrap and Browsewrap: What Makes an Online Agreement Enforceable
clauses.body: When a software license is presented to a user online rather than signed on paper, courts distinguish between two common formats. In a "clickwrap" (or "click-through") agreement, the user must click an "I agree" button after being shown the terms; in a "browsewrap" agreement, the terms are simply posted, often via a hyperlink, and the site states that continuing to use it counts as agreement, without requiring the user to take any affirmative step. The Ninth Circuit has explained that ordinary contract-formation principles — including that mutual assent is the touchstone of a contract — apply to both formats, but they are not treated the same in practice: because a browsewrap agreement doesn't require the user to expressly manifest assent, its enforceability turns on whether the user had actual notice of the terms, or whether the design and placement of the notice would put a reasonably prudent user on inquiry notice of them, and courts have refused to enforce browsewrap terms that were buried or easy to miss. A clickwrap agreement's affirmative "I agree" step is what distinguishes it and is why courts have been more willing to find assent where a browsewrap-style notice resembles a clickwrap flow — for example, requiring an affirmative acknowledgment before proceeding.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on Ninth Circuit case law (Nguyen v. Barnes & Noble); it is binding within that circuit and is frequently cited by California federal and state courts on this point, but it applied New York law under the parties' contractual choice-of-law clause in that specific case (the court noted California and New York law reached the same result on the facts before it, so it did not need to resolve which applied). This clause describes the general clickwrap/browsewrap distinction and the reasoning courts have used; it does not evaluate whether any specific online presentation of this license's terms to the software's licensee would in fact be found enforceable, which depends on the actual design, placement, and required steps of that specific presentation.

citations.quote: Contracts formed on the Internet come primarily in two flavors: “clickwrap” (or “click-through”) agreements, in which website users are required to click on an “I agree” box after being presented with a list of terms and conditions of use; and “browsewrap” agreements, where a website's terms and conditions of use are generally posted on the website via a hyperlink at the bottom of the screen.

Because no affirmative action is required by the website user to agree to the terms of a contract other than his or her use of the website, the determination of the validity of the browsewrap contract depends on whether the user has actual or constructive knowledge of a website's terms and conditions.

clauses.title: Exclusive Licenses Are Treated as Ownership Transfers — and Must Be in Writing
clauses.body: Federal copyright law draws a sharp line between an exclusive license and a nonexclusive one. An exclusive license — one where {{licensorName}} promises not to grant the same rights to anyone else, including {{licensorName}} itself in some cases — is legally treated as a "transfer of copyright ownership," the same category that includes an outright assignment. A nonexclusive license is expressly excluded from that definition. This distinction has a real consequence: like other transfers of copyright ownership, an exclusive license is not valid unless there is a signed writing — an instrument of conveyance, or at least a note or memorandum of the transfer, signed by {{licensorName}} or {{licensorName}}'s authorized agent. A nonexclusive license carries no equivalent federal writing requirement and, under general contract-law principles, can in some circumstances be granted orally or implied from conduct.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, uniform nationwide. This clause cites two provisions that work together — the Copyright Act's definition of "transfer of copyright ownership" in 17 U.S.C. § 101 and its writing requirement for such transfers in 17 U.S.C. § 204(a) — rather than two independent sources, since the definition is what makes the writing requirement apply to an exclusive license in the first place. This clause does not determine whether any particular license granted under this agreement is exclusive or nonexclusive; that depends on the license's actual terms, addressed elsewhere in this document.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, definitions — "transfer of copyright ownership"
citations.quote: A “transfer of copyright ownership” is an assignment, mortgage, exclusive license, or any other conveyance, alienation, or hypothecation of a copyright or of any of the exclusive rights comprised in a copyright, whether or not it is limited in time or place of effect, but not including a nonexclusive license.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, execution of transfers of copyright ownership
citations.quote: A transfer of copyright ownership, other than by operation of law, is not valid unless an instrument of conveyance, or a note or memorandum of the transfer, is in writing and signed by the owner of the rights conveyed or such owner's duly authorized agent.

clauses.title: Whether an Implied Warranty Applies to Licensed Software Is Unsettled
clauses.body: California's Commercial Code implies a warranty that goods are merchantable — fit for their ordinary purpose, among other things — in a contract for the sale of goods, when the seller is a merchant dealing in goods of that kind, unless that warranty is excluded or modified. This warranty, by its own terms, is tied to a "contract for sale" of "goods." Whether software delivered under a license, rather than sold outright, counts as a "sale" of "goods" for purposes of this warranty is a genuinely unsettled and contested question: software is intangible information rather than a tangible item in the traditional sense, and courts in different jurisdictions have not converged on a single answer, including on whether the analysis differs depending on how the software is delivered (for example, on physical media versus downloaded or accessed remotely) or on whether a transaction that bundles software with services is treated under a "predominant purpose" test that looks at the transaction as a whole. This is why software license agreements, including this one, commonly include an express warranty disclaimer: to state the parties' agreement plainly rather than depend on how an unresolved threshold question about the Commercial Code's scope would eventually be answered.
clauses.gap: California's Commercial Code Article 2 (Cal. Com. Code §§ 2101 et seq.) is a state statute; other states' versions of the Uniform Commercial Code contain similar merchantability language, and the same scope question exists under those states' laws as well, so this clause's description of the underlying provision is specific to California but the unresolved-scope problem is not unique to it. This clause is deliberately conservative: it identifies a real, cited textual hook (the "contract for sale" of "goods" limitation in Cal. Com. Code § 2314) and honestly states that whether software licensing satisfies that hook is contested, rather than asserting a definitive answer either way — a case-law search for on-point California and Ninth Circuit authority on this specific question was attempted but could not be completed and quote-verified before this session's legal-research tool access was rate-limited, so no case citation is included here for that narrower question, only the statutory hook itself. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 2314); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Com. Code § 2314 (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Commercial Code, implied warranty of merchantability
citations.quote: Unless excluded or modified (Section 2316), a warranty that the goods shall be merchantable is implied in a contract for their sale if the seller is a merchant with respect to goods of that kind.

clauses.title: Grant of Software License
clauses.body: {{licensorName}} ("Licensor") owns or controls all right, title, and interest in and to the copyright in the following software: {{softwareDescription}} (the "Software"). Subject to {{licenseeName}}'s ("Licensee") compliance with this agreement, Licensor grants Licensee a license to use the Software as described in this agreement. This is a license, not a sale or other transfer of ownership: Licensor retains all right, title, and interest in and to the Software, including all copyright and other intellectual property rights in it, except for the specific rights expressly granted to Licensee under this agreement. No rights in the Software are granted to Licensee by implication, estoppel, or otherwise, other than as expressly stated here.

clauses.title: Disclaimer of Warranties
clauses.body: EXCEPT AS EXPRESSLY STATED IN THIS AGREEMENT, THE SOFTWARE IS PROVIDED "AS IS," WITHOUT WARRANTY OF ANY KIND, WHETHER EXPRESS, IMPLIED, OR STATUTORY, INCLUDING WITHOUT LIMITATION ANY IMPLIED WARRANTY OF MERCHANTABILITY, FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE, TITLE, OR NON-INFRINGEMENT. {{licensorName}} does not warrant that the Software will be error-free, uninterrupted, or free of security vulnerabilities, or that it will meet {{licenseeName}}'s particular requirements. Some jurisdictions do not allow the exclusion or limitation of certain implied warranties, so some of the exclusions in this section may not apply to {{licenseeName}} to the extent prohibited by applicable law.

clauses.title: When a Home Improvement Contract Is Required, and Its Core Written Terms and Disclosures
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of when California requires a home improvement contract to be in writing, what core terms it must contain, and what specific disclosure notices it must include — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular project or contract. All five citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Bus. & Prof. Code section 7159) rather than independently authored sources, so they corroborate one internally consistent statute rather than five separate ones. This clause doesn't state whether a particular job qualifies as a 'home improvement' as the statute defines that term, whether a particular price aggregates multiple contracts, the exact wording of every notice the statute requires (the mechanics lien warning and CSLB notice are lengthy standardized texts, only partially quoted here), or what content requirement applies to a job that instead qualifies as a 'service and repair contract' under a separate, narrower statute.
clauses.body: California's Contractors State License Law defines a "home improvement contract" as an agreement — oral or written, in one or more documents — between a contractor and a homeowner (or, in some cases, a tenant) for a home improvement as statutorily defined, where the aggregate contract price exceeds $500. Once that threshold is met, the contract and any changes to it must be in writing and signed by the parties before work covered by the contract (or a change order) begins. Before any work starts, the contractor must give the buyer a copy of the signed, dated contract, and the buyer's receipt of that copy is what starts the buyer's statutory cancellation-notice period running. The written contract must include, among other things, the contractor's name, business address, and license number; a "Home Improvement" heading; a "Contract Price" heading with the amount in dollars and cents; a description of the project and the significant materials and equipment involved; headings for the approximate start date and approximate completion date; and, in close proximity to the signatures, a notice that the owner or tenant has the right to require the contractor to carry a performance and payment bond. A change-order or extra-work form becomes part of the contract only if it is a separate writing signed by the parties before the change-order work begins. Beyond these core terms, the contract (or an attachment it references) must include several specific disclosure notices: a commercial general liability insurance (CGL) notice stating, correctly, whether the contractor carries CGL insurance, is self-insured, or carries the liability coverage the law requires; a workers' compensation insurance notice stating whether the contractor has no employees and is exempt, or carries coverage for all employees; a "Mechanics Lien Warning" in specific statutory language, telling the owner that even a contractor who has been paid in full may leave unpaid subcontractors, suppliers, or laborers who can still record a lien on the property; and a notice with the Contractors State License Board's (CSLB) contact information, cautioning the buyer that using an unlicensed contractor may leave the buyer's only remedy in civil court, with possible liability for injuries to the unlicensed contractor or that contractor's employees.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, definition of 'home improvement contract' and its $500 price threshold
citations.quote: “home improvement contract” means an agreement, whether oral or written, or contained in one or more documents, between a contractor and an owner or between a contractor and a tenant ... for the performance of a home improvement, as defined in Section 7151, and includes all labor, services, and materials to be furnished and performed thereunder, if the aggregate contract price specified in one or more improvement contracts ... exceeds five hundred dollars ($500).

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159(c)(3)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, contractor's duty to give the buyer a signed copy before work starts
citations.quote: Before any work is started, the contractor shall give the buyer a copy of the contract that is signed and dated by both the contractor and the buyer. The buyer’s receipt of the copy of the contract initiates the buyer’s rights to cancel the contract pursuant to Sections 1689.5 to 1689.14, inclusive, of the Civil Code.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159(d) & (d)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, writing requirement and mandatory contractor-identification term
citations.quote: A home improvement contract and any changes to the contract shall be in writing and signed by the parties to the contract prior to the commencement of work covered by the contract or an applicable change order and ... shall include or comply with all of the following: (1) The name, business address, and license number of the contractor.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159(e)(1)-(e)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, required commercial general liability insurance and workers' compensation insurance notices
citations.quote: A notice concerning commercial general liability insurance. ... The notice shall include the heading “Commercial General Liability Insurance (CGL),” followed by whichever of the following statements is both relevant and correct: (A) “(The name on the license or ‘This contractor’) does not carry commercial general liability insurance.” ... A notice concerning workers’ compensation insurance. ... The notice shall include the heading “Workers’ Compensation Insurance” followed by whichever of the following statements is correct: (A) “(The name on the license or ‘This contractor’) has no employees and is exempt from workers’ compensation requirements.” (B) “(The name on the license or ‘This contractor’) carries workers’ compensation insurance for all employees.”

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159(e)(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, required Contractors State License Board (CSLB) contact and unlicensed-contractor-risk notice
citations.quote: Information about the Contractors State License Board (CSLB): CSLB is the state consumer protection agency that licenses and regulates construction contractors. ... Use only licensed contractors. ... If you use an unlicensed contractor, CSLB may not be able to help you resolve your complaint. Your only remedy may be in civil court, and you may be liable for damages arising out of any injuries to the unlicensed contractor or the unlicensed contractor’s employees.

clauses.title: Down Payment Cap and the Rule Against Paying for Incomplete Work
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's actual down-payment cap and progress-payment rule for a home improvement contract — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular contract's payment terms. Three of the four citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Bus. & Prof. Code section 7159.5(a) and (b)) rather than independently authored sources; the fourth (section 7159(d)(8)(C)) is a companion section requiring the identical dollar cap to appear as boldface contract language. It doesn't state how 'value of the work performed' is measured in a disputed case, and a contractor who furnishes a qualifying performance and payment bond, lien and completion bond, or approved joint control is statutorily exempt from the down payment cap, the progress-payment schedule requirement, and the related boldface warnings.
clauses.body: California law caps the down payment a home improvement contract may require: if any down payment is charged, it may not exceed $1,000 or 10% of the contract price, whichever amount is less, and the contract must display that exact dollar/percentage cap in boldface type. Beyond the down payment, the contractor generally may neither request nor accept payment that exceeds the value of the work actually performed or the materials actually delivered — the schedule of progress payments must be stated in dollars and cents tied to specific phases of work, and the contract must include a boldface statement that it is against the law to collect payment for work not yet completed or materials not yet delivered. A contractor who instead furnishes a qualifying performance and payment bond, lien and completion bond, or an approved joint control is exempt from the down-payment cap and the progress-payment restrictions, and may accept payment before the work is completed. Violating the writing requirement, the down-payment cap, or the rule against accepting payment beyond the value of work performed is a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of not less than $100 nor more than $5,000, by up to one year in county jail, or by both.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159(d)(8)(C) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, required boldface down-payment cap statement
citations.quote: “THE DOWNPAYMENT MAY NOT EXCEED $1,000 OR 10 PERCENT OF THE CONTRACT PRICE, WHICHEVER IS LESS.”

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159.5(a)(3) & (5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, down-payment cap and prohibition on payment exceeding value of work performed
citations.quote: (3) If a downpayment will be charged, the downpayment shall not exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000) or 10 percent of the contract amount, whichever amount is less. ... (5) Except for a downpayment, the contractor shall neither request nor accept payment that exceeds the value of the work performed or material delivered.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159.5(a)(8) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, bonded-contractor exemption from the down-payment and progress-payment rules
citations.quote: A contractor furnishing a performance and payment bond, lien and completion bond, or a bond equivalent or joint control approved by the registrar covering full performance and payment is exempt from paragraphs (3), (4), and (5) ... A contractor furnishing these bonds, bond equivalents, or a joint control approved by the registrar may accept payment prior to completion.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159.5(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, misdemeanor penalty for violating the writing requirement, down-payment cap, or progress-payment rule
citations.quote: A violation of paragraph (1), (3), or (5) of subdivision (a) by a licensee or a person subject to be licensed under this chapter, or by their agent or salesperson, is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of not less than one hundred dollars ($100) nor more than five thousand dollars ($5,000), or by imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding one year, or by both that fine and imprisonment.

clauses.title: The Three-Business-Day (or Five-Day, or Seven-Day) Right to Cancel
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's cancellation-notice requirement for a home improvement contract signed away from the contractor's place of business — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular contract's cancellation rights. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Bus. & Prof. Code section 7159(e)(6) and (e)(7)) rather than independently authored sources. It doesn't state how 'contractor's place of business' is determined on disputed facts, and a separate body of law (Civil Code sections 1689.5 to 1689.14, not researched for this clause) governs the mechanics of exercising this cancellation right in more detail.
clauses.body: Unless a home improvement contract is negotiated at the contractor's place of business, or falls within a narrow set of other exceptions, California law requires the contract to include a "Three-Day Right to Cancel" notice — extended to a "Five-Day Right to Cancel" when the buyer is a senior citizen — allowing the buyer to cancel by emailing, mailing, faxing, or delivering written notice to the contractor by midnight of the third (or fifth) business day after the buyer receives a signed, dated copy of the contract that includes the notice. If the buyer cancels, the contractor must return anything the buyer paid within 10 days of receiving the cancellation notice. The notice must appear in at least 12-point boldface type, in immediate proximity to the owner's signature space, in the same language principally used in any oral sales presentation, and it must be accompanied by a duplicate, easily detachable "Notice of Cancellation" form. A separate "Seven-Day Right to Cancel" notice applies instead — in place of the three/five-day notice — to a contract for the repair or restoration of residential premises damaged by a sudden or catastrophic event for which a state of emergency or local emergency has been declared.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159(e)(6)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, when the Three/Five-Day Right to Cancel notice is required and its exceptions
citations.quote: The notice set forth in subparagraph (B) and entitled “Three-Day Right to Cancel,” or entitled “Five-Day Right to Cancel” for contracts with a senior citizen, shall be provided to the buyer unless the contract is: (i) Negotiated at the contractor’s place of business. (ii) Subject to the ‘Seven-Day Right to Cancel,’ as set forth in paragraph (7). (iii) Subject to licensure under the Alarm Company Act ...

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159(e)(6)(B)(i) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, text of the statutory Three-Day Right to Cancel notice
citations.quote: “Three-Day Right to Cancel: You, the buyer, have the right to cancel this contract within three business days. You may cancel by emailing, mailing, faxing, or delivering a written notice to the contractor at the contractor’s place of business by midnight of the third business day after you received a signed and dated copy of the contract that includes this notice. ... If you cancel, the contractor must return to you anything you paid within 10 days of receiving the notice of cancellation.”

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159(e)(7)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, the Seven-Day Right to Cancel for declared-disaster repair contracts
citations.quote: The following notice entitled “Seven-Day Right to Cancel” shall be provided to the buyer for any contract that is written for the repair or restoration of residential premises damaged by any sudden or catastrophic event for which a state of emergency has been declared by the President of the United States or the Governor, or for which a local emergency has been declared ...

clauses.title: Consequences of Contracting Without a License: § 7031
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual consequences California attaches to unlicensed contracting — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular contractor's licensure or a particular homeowner's remedies. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Bus. & Prof. Code section 7031) rather than independently authored sources. It doesn't state whether a specific person was required to be licensed for specific work, whether a specific person's licensure is genuinely disputed, or how a court would apply the narrow substantial-compliance exception on particular facts.
clauses.body: The Contractors State License Law attaches significant consequences to contracting without a license. With limited exceptions, a person acting as a contractor may not bring or maintain any court action to recover compensation for work requiring a license unless that person alleges — and, if licensure is disputed, proves with a verified certificate of licensure from the Contractors State License Board — that they were duly licensed at all times while performing the work, regardless of the merits of the underlying claim. Separately, and just as significantly, a person who used an unlicensed contractor's services may bring a court action to recover all compensation paid to that unlicensed contractor for the work. A security interest taken to secure payment for work requiring a license is unenforceable if the person who did the work was not duly licensed throughout. A narrow judicial 'substantial compliance' exception can excuse a licensing lapse in limited circumstances — where the person had been duly licensed before doing the work, acted reasonably and in good faith to keep the license current, and acted promptly and in good faith to fix the lapse once aware of it — but that exception is unavailable to someone who was never licensed in California at all.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7031(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, bar on an unlicensed contractor recovering compensation in court
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (e), no person engaged in the business or acting in the capacity of a contractor, may bring or maintain any action, or recover in law or equity in any action, in any court of this state for the collection of compensation for the performance of any act or contract where a license is required by this chapter without alleging that they were a duly licensed contractor at all times during the performance of that act or contract, regardless of the merits of the cause of action brought by the person ...

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7031(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, homeowner's right to recover all compensation paid to an unlicensed contractor
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (e), a person who utilizes the services of an unlicensed contractor may bring an action in any court of competent jurisdiction in this state to recover all compensation paid to the unlicensed contractor for performance of any act or contract.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7031(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, narrow substantial-compliance exception
citations.quote: The judicial doctrine of substantial compliance shall not apply under this section where the person who engaged in the business or acted in the capacity of a contractor has never been a duly licensed contractor in this state. However ... the court may determine that there has been substantial compliance with licensure requirements under this section if it is shown at an evidentiary hearing that the person ... (1) had been duly licensed as a contractor in this state prior to the performance of the act or contract, (2) acted reasonably and in good faith to maintain proper licensure, and (3) acted promptly and in good faith to remedy the failure to comply with the licensure requirements upon learning of the failure.

clauses.title: The Narrower 'Service and Repair Contract' Category, and When It Doesn't Apply
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California treats a small, buyer-initiated repair call as a distinct, more lightly regulated contract category from a full home improvement contract — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular repair job. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Bus. & Prof. Code section 7159.10) rather than independently authored sources. Note for this project specifically: the meaningful HIC-versus-service-and-repair distinction lives in section 7159.10, not section 7159.5 — section 7159.5 instead states payment-related rules (down payment cap, prohibition on paying for incomplete work) that apply to every home improvement contract; it was worth checking directly rather than assumed, and the two sections should not be conflated. This clause doesn't state whether a particular job in fact meets every element of the statutory definition.
clauses.body: Not every small home-repair job is a "home improvement contract" subject to the full requirements described elsewhere in this document. California law separately defines a narrower "service and repair contract" category, but only where every one of several conditions is met: the contract amount is $750 or less; the buyer — not the contractor — initiated contact requesting the work; the contractor doesn't sell the buyer goods or services beyond what's reasonably necessary to address the specific problem that prompted the call; and no payment is due, or accepted by the contractor, until the work is completed. If a contract is written as, or presented to the buyer as, a service and repair contract but any one of those conditions isn't actually met, the full home improvement contract requirements apply instead, regardless of the contract's dollar amount — including whatever right to rescind would otherwise apply. A contract that genuinely qualifies has its own separate, shorter disclosure list (its own required insurance notices and its own right-to-cancel notice), but does not need a down-payment or progress-payment schedule, since payment isn't permitted until the work is done.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159.10(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, definition and conditions of a qualifying 'service and repair contract'
citations.quote: “Service and repair contract” means an agreement ... that conforms to the following requirements: (A) The contract amount is seven hundred fifty dollars ($750) or less. (B) The prospective buyer initiated contact with the contractor to request the work. (C) The contractor does not sell the buyer goods or services beyond those reasonably necessary to take care of the particular problem that caused the buyer to contact the contractor. (D) No payment is due, or accepted by the contractor, until the work is completed.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159.10(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, fallback to full home improvement contract requirements when the conditions aren't met
citations.quote: For any contract written pursuant to subdivision (a) or otherwise presented to the buyer as a service and repair contract, unless all of the conforming requirements for service and repair contracts specified in subdivision (a) are met, the contract requirements for home improvements set forth in subdivisions (c), (d), and (e) of Section 7159 shall be applicable, including any rights to rescind the contract ... regardless of the aggregate contract price.

clauses.title: Home Improvement Contract — Parties, License, and Project Terms
Home Improvement Contract — Three-Day Right to Cancel Notice
clauses.body:
YOUR RIGHT TO CANCEL

Three-Day Right to Cancel

You, the buyer, have the right to cancel this contract within three business days. You may cancel by emailing, mailing, faxing, or delivering a written notice to the contractor at the contractor's place of business by midnight of the third business day after you received a signed and dated copy of the contract that includes this notice. Include your name, your address, and the date you received the signed copy of the contract and this notice.

If you cancel, the contractor must return to you anything you paid within 10 days of receiving the notice of cancellation. For your part, you must make available to the contractor at your residence, in substantially as good condition as you received them, goods delivered to you under this contract or sale. Or, you may, if you wish, comply with the contractor's instructions on how to return the goods at the contractor's expense and risk. If you do make the goods available to the contractor and the contractor does not pick them up within 20 days of the date of your notice of cancellation, you may keep them without any further obligation. If you fail to make the goods available to the contractor, or if you agree to return the goods to the contractor and fail to do so, then you remain liable for performance of all obligations under the contract.

(If the buyer is a senior citizen, references above to "three" and "third" become "five" and "fifth," respectively.)

If you do make the goods available to the seller and the seller does not pick them up within 20 days of the date of your notice of cancellation, you may retain or dispose of the goods without any further obligation. clauses.title: Home Improvement Contract — Mechanics Lien Warning and CSLB Notice
clauses.body:
MECHANICS LIEN WARNING

Anyone who helps improve your property, but who is not paid, may record what is called a mechanics lien on your property. A mechanics lien is a claim, like a mortgage or home equity loan, made against your property and recorded with the county recorder.

Even if you pay your contractor in full, unpaid subcontractors, suppliers, and laborers who helped to improve your property may record mechanics liens and sue you in court to foreclose the lien. If a court finds the lien is valid, you could be forced to pay twice or have a court officer sell your home to pay the lien. Liens can also affect your credit.

To preserve their right to record a lien, each subcontractor and material supplier must provide you with a document called a 'Preliminary Notice.' This notice is not a lien. The purpose of the notice is to let you know that the person who sends you the notice has the right to record a lien on your property if they are not paid.

BE CAREFUL. The Preliminary Notice can be sent up to 20 days after the subcontractor starts work or the supplier provides material. This can be a big problem if you pay your contractor before you have received the Preliminary Notices.

You will not get Preliminary Notices from your prime contractor or from laborers who work on your project. The law assumes that you already know they are improving your property.

PROTECT YOURSELF FROM LIENS. You can protect yourself from liens by getting a list from your contractor of all the subcontractors and material suppliers that work on your project. Find out from your contractor when these subcontractors started work and when these suppliers delivered goods or materials. Then wait 20 days, paying attention to the Preliminary Notices you receive.

PAY WITH JOINT CHECKS. One way to protect yourself is to pay with a joint check. When your contractor tells you it is time to pay for the work of a subcontractor or supplier who has provided you with a Preliminary Notice, write a joint check payable to both the contractor and the subcontractor or material supplier.

For other ways to prevent liens, visit CSLB's internet website at www.cslb.ca.gov or call CSLB at 800-321-CSLB (2752).

REMEMBER, IF YOU DO NOTHING, YOU RISK HAVING A LIEN PLACED ON YOUR HOME. This can mean that you may have to pay twice, or face the forced sale of your home to pay what you owe.

— — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — —

Information about the Contractors State License Board (CSLB): CSLB is the state consumer protection agency that licenses and regulates construction contractors.

Contact CSLB for information about the licensed contractor you are considering, including information about disclosable complaints, disciplinary actions, and civil judgments that are reported to CSLB.

Use only licensed contractors. If you file a complaint against a licensed contractor within the legal deadline (usually four years), CSLB has authority to investigate the complaint. If you use an unlicensed contractor, CSLB may not be able to help you resolve your complaint. Your only remedy may be in civil court, and you may be liable for damages arising out of any injuries to the unlicensed contractor or the unlicensed contractor's employees.

For more information:
Visit CSLB's internet website at www.cslb.ca.gov
Call CSLB at 800-321-CSLB (2752)
Write CSLB at P.O. Box 26000, Sacramento, CA 95826.

clauses.title: This Petition Information Sheet Describes a Contested Court Process, Not the Voluntary Declaration
clauses.body: California recognizes two distinct routes to legally establishing a parent-child relationship. One is the out-of-court, signed voluntary declaration of parentage described in a separate companion document, which depends on both people agreeing to sign. The other — the subject of this information sheet — is a contested court proceeding under California's Uniform Parentage Act (Fam. Code Div. 12, Part 3), used when parentage is disputed or when a party will not voluntarily sign a declaration. Family Code § 7630(a) authorizes specified people to "bring an action" in court to declare the existence or nonexistence of a parent-child relationship regarding {{childName}}. Completing this information sheet does not itself establish or disestablish {{allegedParentName}}'s parentage of {{childName}}; only a court judgment issued after the statutory petition, notice, and hearing process under the Uniform Parentage Act can do that.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can maintain two legally distinct pathways to establishing parentage — an out-of-court signed declaration and a separate contested court action — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific child's situation, nor a claim that every jurisdiction structures its parentage law this same way. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 7630(a) introductory clause); no additional independent source was found for this specific framing. Whether a voluntary out-of-court declaration process exists at all, whether a separate contested court action exists, and how the two interact varies by state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7630(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the introductory clause identifying who may bring an action
citations.quote: A child, the child’s natural mother, a person presumed to be the child’s parent under subdivision (a), (b), or (c) of Section 7611, a person seeking to be adjudicated as a parent or donor under Section 7613, an adoption agency to whom the child has been relinquished, or a prospective adoptive parent of the child may bring an action as follows:

clauses.title: Who May Bring an Action to Establish or Disestablish Parentage
clauses.body: California's Uniform Parentage Act lists specific categories of people who may file a court action to determine parentage; not everyone with an interest in {{childName}}'s parentage has standing to do so. Family Code § 7630(a) authorizes the child, the child's natural mother, a person already presumed to be the child's parent under specific marital or holding-out categories, a person seeking to be adjudicated a parent or donor in an assisted-reproduction context, an adoption agency, or a prospective adoptive parent to bring an action regarding the existence or nonexistence of a parent-child relationship. Separately, § 7630(c) authorizes a broader general "action to determine parentage" — outside the marital-presumption chapter — to be brought by the child, a personal representative of the child, the Department of Child Support Services, a presumed parent (or that parent's representative if the presumed parent has died or is a minor), and, only when the natural mother is the only presumed parent, a dependency action is pending, or an adoption is pending, a man alleged or claiming to be the father (or his representative if he has died or is a minor).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a state can define a specific, limited list of people with standing to bring a contested parentage action — not a claim about which state's law governs standing in any specific case, nor a claim that any particular person does or does not have standing. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7630(a) and § 7630(c)); no additional independent source beyond § 7630 itself was found for this list. This corrects a framing assumption in the research request that prompted this clause: an alleged father's standing to bring a general parentage action under § 7630(c) is not unconditional — the statute's own text limits it to circumstances where the natural mother is the only presumed parent, or a Welfare and Institutions Code § 300 dependency action or an adoption is pending. Who has standing to bring a contested parentage action, and under what conditions, varies by state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7630(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: standing to bring an action regarding existence or nonexistence of the relationship
citations.quote: A child, the child’s natural mother, a person presumed to be the child’s parent under subdivision (a), (b), or (c) of Section 7611, a person seeking to be adjudicated as a parent or donor under Section 7613, an adoption agency to whom the child has been relinquished, or a prospective adoptive parent of the child may bring an action as follows:

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7630(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: standing for a general action to determine parentage, including DCSS and a conditioned alleged-father category
citations.quote: Except as to cases coming within Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 7540) of Part 2 or when paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) applies, an action to determine parentage may be brought by the child, a personal representative of the child, the Department of Child Support Services, a presumed parent or the personal representative or a parent of that presumed parent if that parent has died or is a minor, or, when the natural mother is the only presumed parent or an action under Section 300 of the Welfare and Institutions Code or adoption is pending, a man alleged or claiming to be the father or the personal representative or a parent of the alleged father if the alleged father has died or is a minor.

clauses.title: The Marital Presumption and Its Two-Year Deadline to Disestablish
clauses.body: California law starts from a strong marital presumption: Family Code § 7540(a) provides that, except as provided in § 7541, "the child of spouses who cohabited at the time of conception and birth is conclusively presumed to be a child of the marriage." That presumption is not absolute. Section 7541(a) provides that if the court finds, based on genetic testing, that the spouse presumed to be a parent under § 7540 is not a genetic parent of the child, the question of parentage is resolved under the Uniform Parentage Act's other applicable provisions. But § 7541(b) attaches a firm outer deadline to that challenge: "An action to challenge the parentage of the spouse who is a presumed parent under Section 7540 shall be filed and served not later than two years from the child's date of birth," and may be filed only by either spouse, or by a person presumed to be a parent under § 7611, or by the child (through a guardian ad litem) to establish that § 7611-presumed person's parentage.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can pair a strong, birth-during-marriage presumption of parentage with a fixed, short outer deadline for challenging it — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage, birth, or challenge, and not a claim about whether the petitioner, respondent, or alleged parent in any specific matter falls within any of these categories. This clause cites two different statutory sections (§ 7540(a) and § 7541(a)-(b)); the citations from § 7541 are two subsections of that same section, and no additional independent source beyond § 7541 itself was found for the two-year deadline and who may invoke it. Whether a marital presumption of parentage exists, how strong it is, whether and how it can be rebutted, and any deadline for doing so all vary substantially by state — this is exactly the kind of date-sensitive, jurisdiction-specific rule that does not transfer across state lines.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7540(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the conclusive marital presumption
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 7541, the child of spouses who cohabited at the time of conception and birth is conclusively presumed to be a child of the marriage.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7541(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: genetic testing overcoming the presumption
citations.quote: If the court finds that the spouse who is a presumed parent under Section 7540 is not a genetic parent of the child pursuant to Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 7550), the question of parentage shall be resolved in accordance with all other applicable provisions of this division, including, but not limited to, Section 7612.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7541(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the two-year filing deadline and who may bring the challenge
citations.quote: An action to challenge the parentage of the spouse who is a presumed parent under Section 7540 shall be filed and served not later than two years from the child’s date of birth and may only be filed by any of the following: (1) By either spouse. (2) By a person who is a presumed parent under Section 7611 or by the child, through or by the child’s guardian ad litem, to establish the parentage of the person who is a presumed parent under Section 7611.

clauses.title: Genetic Testing: When the Court Must Order It, and the Statutory Threshold for Identifying a Genetic Parent
clauses.body: Genetic testing plays a defined, but not unlimited, role in a contested parentage action. Family Code § 7551(a) provides that in a civil action or proceeding in which parentage is a relevant fact, "the court may, upon its own initiative or upon suggestion made by or on behalf of any person who is involved, and shall upon motion of any party to the action or proceeding made at a time so as not to delay the proceedings unduly, order the woman who gave birth, the child, and the alleged genetic parent to submit to genetic testing." Once testing occurs, § 7555(a) sets a specific statistical threshold for what counts as identifying someone as a genetic parent: the testing must disclose "at least a 99 percent probability of parentage, using a prior probability of 0.50," and "a combined relationship index of at least 100 to 1."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific court-ordered-testing trigger and a specific statistical threshold for genetic-parent identification — not a claim about which state's law governs whether, or under what threshold, genetic testing would be ordered or would identify anyone as a genetic parent of any specific child. This clause cites two different statutory sections (§ 7551(a) and § 7555(a)); each citation is a single subsection of its respective section. Section 7551 itself notes that where the child already has a presumed parent under § 7540 (the marital presumption), a motion for genetic testing is instead governed by § 7541, addressed in this document's companion clause — this clause does not restate that separate pathway. Whether courts order genetic testing, on what trigger, and what statistical threshold identifies a genetic parent all vary by state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7551(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: when the court may, and on a party's motion shall, order genetic testing
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivisions (b) and (c), in a civil action or proceeding in which parentage is a relevant fact, the court may, upon its own initiative or upon suggestion made by or on behalf of any person who is involved, and shall upon motion of any party to the action or proceeding made at a time so as not to delay the proceedings unduly, order the woman who gave birth, the child, and the alleged genetic parent to submit to genetic testing.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7555(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statistical threshold for identifying a genetic parent
citations.quote: Subject to a challenge under subdivision (b), a person is identified under this part as a genetic parent of a child if genetic testing complies with this part and the results of the testing disclose both of the following: (1) The person has at least a 99 percent probability of parentage, using a prior probability of 0.50, as calculated by using the combined relationship index obtained in the testing. (2) A combined relationship index of at least 100 to 1.

clauses.title: Competing Presumptions and Genetic Evidence — the "Weightier Considerations" Standard
clauses.body: A person can qualify as a presumed parent under Family Code § 7611 through several routes — marriage or an attempted marriage around the time of the child's birth, later marrying and being named on the birth certificate or undertaking support, or receiving the child into the home and openly holding the child out as the person's own. Section 7612(a) makes that presumption rebuttable, and only "by clear and convincing evidence." Where more than one of these presumptions could apply to {{childName}}, or where a § 7611 presumption conflicts with a claim by a person identified as a genetic parent under § 7555, § 7612(b) does not automatically favor genetic evidence: instead, "the presumption that on the facts is founded on the weightier considerations of policy and logic controls," and if one of the competing presumed parents is also a presumed parent under the marital-presumption statute (§ 7540), that particular presumption can only be rebutted through the § 7541 process described in this document's companion clause.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can resolve competing parentage presumptions — including a conflict with genetic-testing evidence — through a case-specific policy-and-logic balancing test rather than a fixed rule automatically favoring either the presumption or the genetic result, not a claim about which state's law governs, or how any such conflict would be resolved for, any specific child. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7612(a) and § 7612(b)); no additional independent source beyond § 7612 itself was found for the weightier-considerations standard. This corrects a framing assumption in the research request that prompted this clause: on the statute's actual text, a genetic-parent identification under § 7555 does not itself create a separate rebuttable or conclusive presumption that automatically controls over a conflicting § 7611 presumption — it is instead one input the court weighs under the same weightier-considerations balancing test used for conflicts between two § 7611 presumptions. Whether, and how, competing parentage presumptions and genetic evidence are reconciled varies by state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7612(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence
citations.quote: Except as provided in Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 7540) and Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 7570) of Part 2, a presumption under Section 7611 is a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof and may be rebutted in an appropriate action only by clear and convincing evidence.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7612(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the weightier-considerations standard for competing presumptions or genetic evidence
citations.quote: If two or more presumptions arise under Section 7611 that conflict with each other, or if one or more presumptions under Section 7611 conflict with a claim by a person identified as a genetic parent pursuant to Section 7555, the presumption that on the facts is founded on the weightier considerations of policy and logic controls. If one of the presumed parents is also a presumed parent under Section 7540, the presumption arising under Section 7540 may only be rebutted pursuant to Section 7541.

clauses.title: Timing Rules for Actions to Establish or Disestablish the Existence of a Parent-Child Relationship
clauses.body: California's Uniform Parentage Act does not apply one single statute of limitations to every kind of parentage action; the timing rule depends on what is being asked of the court. Family Code § 7630(a)(1) allows an action "[a]t any time for the purpose of declaring the existence of" a presumed or established parent-child relationship regarding {{childName}} — no fixed filing deadline applies to establishing that relationship under this provision. By contrast, § 7630(a)(2) allows an action to declare the nonexistence of a § 7611(a)-(c) presumed relationship "only if the action is brought within a reasonable time after obtaining knowledge of relevant facts" — a flexible, fact-dependent limit rather than a fixed number of days or years. A different, fixed rule applies specifically to challenging the separate marital presumption under § 7540: as described in this document's companion clause, § 7541(b) requires that specific challenge to be filed and served within a hard two-year deadline running from the child's date of birth.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can apply different timing rules — no deadline, a flexible reasonable-time standard, and a fixed deadline — to different categories of parentage action within a single statutory scheme, not a claim about which state's law governs the timing of any specific petitioner's, respondent's, or alleged parent's claim. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7630(a)(1) and § 7630(a)(2)); the cross-reference to § 7541(b)'s two-year deadline is addressed independently, and in full, in this document's companion clause on the marital presumption, and is not re-quoted here. No general, catch-all limitations period for a § 7630(c) action to determine parentage (outside the marital-presumption and nonexistence-challenge categories addressed above) was located in the sections reviewed for this document; this document does not represent that no such rule exists elsewhere in California law, only that this research did not locate one within the sections reviewed. Whether, and how, a state limits the time to bring or challenge a parentage action varies substantially and is exactly the kind of date-sensitive fact that does not transfer across jurisdictions.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7630(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: no fixed deadline to declare the existence of the relationship
citations.quote: At any time for the purpose of declaring the existence of the parent and child relationship presumed under subdivision (a), (b), or (c) of Section 7611, or established pursuant to Section 7613.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7630(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the reasonable-time standard to declare nonexistence
citations.quote: For the purpose of declaring the nonexistence of the parent and child relationship presumed under subdivision (a), (b), or (c) of Section 7611 only if the action is brought within a reasonable time after obtaining knowledge of relevant facts. After the presumption has been rebutted, parentage of the child by another person may be determined in the same action, if that person has been made a party.

clauses.title: Petitioner — Information and Declaration in Support of Petition to Establish Parental Relationship
clauses.body: I, {{petitionerName}}, seek to establish, through the California court process described in this document, the parent-child relationship between {{allegedParentName}} and {{childName}}, a minor born {{childDOB}}. {{childName}}'s other parent or presumed parent of record, so far as known, is {{respondentName}}. This declaration provides background information for use with an actual petition to establish (or, where applicable, to determine the nonexistence of) a parental relationship, to be filed in California superior court under the Uniform Parentage Act, Family Code Division 12, Part 3. This declaration is not itself a court filing, and signing it does not establish, disestablish, or confirm {{allegedParentName}}'s legal parentage of {{childName}}. Only a court judgment issued after the statutory petition, notice, and hearing process — which may include court-ordered genetic testing — can actually establish or disestablish that relationship.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment Block — Paternity Action Information Sheet
clauses.body:

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual petition to establish a parental relationship, filed in California superior court under the Uniform Parentage Act. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that petition, and it does not establish or disestablish parentage of {{childName}}; only a court judgment does that.]

clauses.title: Required Content of Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Articles
clauses.body: California's Nonprofit Corporation Law contains its own, separate required-content statute for a nonprofit public benefit corporation's articles of incorporation, distinct from the required-content statute that governs an ordinary for-profit corporation.
