The notice shall state the due date for compliance and shall be sent to the last address of the corporation according to the records of the Secretary of State or to the last electronic mail address according to the records of the Secretary of State if the corporation has elected to receive notices from the Secretary of State by electronic mail. The failure of the corporation to receive the notice is not an excuse for failure to comply with this section.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, initial and biennial statement of information
citations.quote: Every limited liability company and every foreign limited liability company registered to transact intrastate business in this state shall deliver to the Secretary of State for filing within 90 days after the filing of its original articles of organization or registering to transact intrastate business and biennially thereafter during the applicable filing period, on a form prescribed by the Secretary of State, a statement of information containing:

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, how the two-year filing period is measured
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, the applicable filing period for a limited liability company shall be the calendar month during which its original articles of organization was filed or, in the case of a foreign limited liability company, the month during which its application for registration was filed, and the immediately preceding five calendar months. The Secretary of State shall provide a notice to each limited liability company or foreign limited liability company to comply with this section approximately three months prior to the close of the applicable filing period. The notice shall state the due date for compliance and shall be sent to the last mailing address of the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company according to the records of the Secretary of State, or if none, to the street address of the principal office, or, in the case of a domestic limited liability company, the office required to be maintained pursuant to Section 17701.13, or to the last electronic mail address according to the records of the Secretary of State if the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company has elected to receive notices from the Secretary of State by electronic mail. The failure of the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company to receive the notice shall not exempt the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company from complying with this section.

clauses.title: Information a Corporation's Statement Must Report
clauses.body: For a domestic stock corporation, the statement California requires must include: the corporation's name and Secretary of State file number; the names and complete business or residence addresses of its incumbent directors, and the number of any board vacancies; the names and complete business or residence addresses of its chief executive officer, secretary, and chief financial officer; the street address of its principal executive office and, if different, its mailing address; a statement of the general type of business that constitutes the corporation's principal business activity; and a statement disclosing whether any officer or director has an outstanding, non-appealable judgment against them for violating a wage order or the Labor Code. The statement must also designate the corporation's agent for service of process — either a natural person residing in California, whose complete business or residence street address must also be listed, or a qualifying corporate agent, for whom no address is listed.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's periodic filing requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific entity; other states impose different periodic-report requirements with different names, deadlines, and forms. Both quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 1502 — subsection (a) for the content list and subsection (b) for the agent-designation rule — and are treated as one source, not two independent ones. This section sits in Division 1 (General Corporation Law), which governs domestic stock (for-profit) corporations; nonprofit corporations are formed and governed under a different division of the Corporations Code with their own statement-of-information provisions, which this research did not examine and which this document does not address.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, required content of the statement
citations.quote: (1) The name of the corporation and the Secretary of State’s file number. (2) The names and complete business or residence addresses of its incumbent directors. (3) The number of vacancies on the board, if any. (4) The names and complete business or residence addresses of its chief executive officer, secretary, and chief financial officer. (5) The street address of its principal executive office. (6) The mailing address of the corporation, if different from the street address of its principal executive office. (7) If the address of its principal executive office is not in this state, the street address of its principal business office in this state, if any. (8) If the corporation chooses to receive renewal notices and any other notifications from the Secretary of State by electronic mail instead of by United States mail, the corporation shall include a valid electronic mail address for the corporation or for the corporation’s designee to receive those notices. (9) A statement of the general type of business that constitutes the principal business activity of the corporation, such as, for example, manufacturer of aircraft, wholesale liquor distributor, or retail department store. (10) A statement indicating whether any officer or any director has an outstanding final judgment issued by the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement or a court of law, for which no appeal therefrom is pending, for the violation of any wage order or provision of the Labor Code.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, agent-for-service-of-process designation rule
citations.quote: The statement required by subdivision (a) shall also designate, as the agent of the corporation for the purpose of service of process, a natural person residing in this state or a corporation that has complied with Section 1505 and whose capacity to act as an agent has not terminated. If a natural person is designated, the statement shall set forth that person’s complete business or residence street address. If a corporate agent is designated, no address for it shall be set forth.

clauses.title: Information an LLC's Statement Must Report
clauses.body: For a California LLC, the statement must include: the LLC's name and Secretary of State file number; the name and street address of its agent for service of process (if the agent is a corporate agent, only the agent's name is listed, not an address); the street address of its principal office and, if different, its mailing address; the names and complete business or residence addresses of its manager or managers and chief executive officer, if any — or, if the LLC has no manager, the name and business or residence address of each member; and a statement of the general type of business that constitutes the LLC's principal business activity. The statement must also disclose whether any manager, in a manager-managed LLC, or any member, in a member-managed LLC, has an outstanding, non-appealable judgment against them for violating a wage order or the Labor Code.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's periodic filing requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific entity; other states impose different periodic-report requirements with different names, deadlines, and forms. This clause quotes a single subsection, Cal. Corp. Code § 17702.09(a), which is one source.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, required content of the statement
citations.quote: (1) The name of the limited liability company and the Secretary of State’s file number and, in the case of a foreign limited liability company, the name under which the foreign limited liability company is authorized to transact intrastate business in this state and the state or other jurisdiction under the laws of which it is organized. (2) The name and street address of the agent in this state for service of process required to be maintained pursuant to Section 17701.13. If a corporate agent is designated, only the name of the agent shall be set forth. (3) The street address of its principal office. In the case of a foreign limited liability company, the street address of its principal business office in this state, if any, and, in the case of a domestic limited liability company, the street address of the office required to be maintained pursuant to Section 17701.13. (4) The mailing address of the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company, if different from the street address of its principal office, or principal business office in this state, or, in the case of a domestic limited liability company, the street address of the office required to be maintained pursuant to Section 17701.13. (5) The name and complete business or residence addresses of any manager or managers and the chief executive officer, if any, appointed or elected in accordance with the articles of organization or operating agreement or, if no manager has been so elected or appointed, the name and business or residence address of each member. (6) If the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company chooses to receive renewal notices and any other notifications from the Secretary of State by electronic mail instead of by United States mail, the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company shall include a valid electronic mail address for the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company, or for the limited liability company’s or foreign limited liability company’s designee to receive those notices. (7) The general type of business that constitutes the principal business activity of the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company, such as, for example, manufacturer of aircraft, wholesale liquor distributor, or retail department store. (8) (A) For a manager-managed limited liability company or a manager-managed foreign limited liability company, a statement indicating whether any manager has an outstanding final judgment issued by the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement or a court of law, for which no appeal therefrom is pending, for the violation of any wage order or provision of the Labor Code. (B) For a member-managed limited liability company, a statement indicating whether any member has an outstanding final judgment issued by the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement or a court of law, for which no appeal therefrom is pending, for the violation of any wage order or provision of the Labor Code, unless, pursuant to subdivision (d) of Section 17701.10, a written operating agreement limits the members who are agents of the limited liability company for the purpose of its business and affairs to a specified member or specified members, in which case the statement is only required with respect to the specified member or members. (C) For a foreign limited liability company that is not managed by a manager or managers, a statement indicating whether any member has an outstanding final judgment issued by the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement or a court of law, for which no appeal therefrom is pending, for the violation of any wage order or provision of the Labor Code, unless the member is not an agent of the foreign limited liability company for purposes of its business and affairs, in which case the statement is only required with respect to the member or members who are agents of the foreign limited liability company.

clauses.title: The 'No Change' Alternative to Refiling
clauses.body: When nothing reported in an entity's most recently filed statement has changed, California does not require the entity to prepare and refile a full new Statement of Information for the next filing period. Instead, both corporations and LLCs may, in lieu of refiling, advise the Secretary of State — on a form the Secretary of State prescribes — that no changes to the previously reported information have occurred during the applicable filing period.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's periodic filing requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific entity; other states impose different periodic-report requirements with different names, deadlines, and forms. This clause cites two different statutory sections, one for each entity type: Cal. Corp. Code § 1502(c) for corporations and Cal. Corp. Code § 17702.09(b) for LLCs. Each is a single subsection of its own section, so no same-section multiple-citation issue arises within either citation, though the two provisions are textually near-identical and are being used here as parallel, independently verified evidence for the two different entity types, not as one source standing in for the other.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, certifying no changes in lieu of refiling
citations.quote: If there has been no change in the information in the last filed statement of the corporation on file in the Secretary of State’s office, the corporation may, in lieu of filing the statement required by subdivisions (a) and (b), advise the Secretary of State, on a form prescribed by the Secretary of State, that no changes in the required information have occurred during the applicable filing period.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, certifying no changes in lieu of refiling
citations.quote: If there has been no change in the information contained in the last filed statement of information of the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company on file in the office of Secretary of State, the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company may, in lieu of filing the statement of information required by subdivision (a), advise the Secretary of State, on a form prescribed by the Secretary of State, that no changes in the required information have occurred during the applicable filing period.

clauses.title: The $250 Penalty for a Delinquent Filing
clauses.body: Failing to file a required Statement of Information carries a specific statutory monetary penalty, separate from any Secretary of State filing fee. If a corporation or LLC does not file, the Secretary of State first sends the entity a notice of delinquency describing the penalty and the entity's right to request relief for reasonable cause or unusual circumstances that justify the failure to file. If the required statement still has not been filed 60 days after that notice, the Secretary of State certifies the entity's name to the Franchise Tax Board. Upon that certification, the Franchise Tax Board assesses a penalty of two hundred fifty dollars ($250). The same $250 penalty applies to corporations and to LLCs, each under its own, separately worded certification statute; if the required statement is filed before the 60-day period expires, or the Secretary of State finds its own delinquency notice was sent in error, the certification — and any penalty already assessed — is withdrawn.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's periodic filing requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific entity; other states impose different periodic-report requirements with different names, deadlines, and forms. This clause cites three different statutory sections: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 19141, which sets the $250 penalty amount and is triggered by certification under either of two Corporations Code provisions; Cal. Corp. Code § 2204(a), the corporation-specific notice-and-certification procedure; and Cal. Corp. Code § 17713.09(a), the separately worded but structurally identical LLC-specific notice-and-certification procedure. These are three independent sources, not subsections of one section. Separately, § 19141 also sets a lower, $50 penalty tied to certification under two other Corporations Code sections (§ 6810 and § 8810), which concern nonprofit mutual benefit and religious corporations; this document does not address nonprofit entities or that $50 penalty, since nonprofit formation is already covered by this project's separate Nonprofit Articles of Incorporation document and was outside this research's scope.

citations.cite: Penalties and Additions to Tax, the $250 penalty for corporations and LLCs
citations.quote: Upon certification by the Secretary of State pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 2204 or subdivision (a) of Section 17713.09 of the Corporations Code, the Franchise Tax Board shall assess a penalty of two hundred fifty dollars ($250).

citations.cite: Crimes and Penalties, the corporation delinquency-notice and certification procedure
citations.quote: Upon the failure of a corporation to file the statement required by Section 1502, the Secretary of State shall provide a notice of that delinquency to the corporation. The notice shall also contain information concerning the application of this section, advise the corporation of the penalty imposed by Section 19141 of the Revenue and Taxation Code for failure to timely file the required statement after notice of the delinquency has been provided by the Secretary of State, and shall advise the corporation of its right to request relief from the Secretary of State because of reasonable cause or unusual circumstances that justify the failure to file. If, within 60 days of providing notice of the delinquency, a statement pursuant to Section 1502 has not been filed by the corporation, the Secretary of State shall certify the name of the corporation to the Franchise Tax Board.

citations.cite: Miscellaneous Provisions, the LLC delinquency-notice and certification procedure
citations.quote: Upon the failure of a limited liability company to file the statement required by Section 17702.09, the Secretary of State shall provide a notice of the delinquency to the limited liability company. The notice shall also contain information concerning the application of this section, advise the limited liability company of the penalty imposed by Section 19141 of the Revenue and Taxation Code for failure to timely file the required statement after notice of delinquency has been mailed by the Secretary of State, and shall advise the limited liability company of its right to request relief from the Secretary of State because of reasonable cause or unusual circumstances that justify such failure to file. If, within 60 days after providing notice of the delinquency, a statement pursuant to Section 17702.09 has not been filed by the limited liability company, the Secretary of State shall certify the name of such limited liability company to the Franchise Tax Board.

clauses.title: Suspension of the Entity's Powers for Sustained Non-Filing
clauses.body: Beyond the $250 penalty, California law provides a separate, more serious consequence for an entity that keeps failing to file. If an entity fails to file its Statement of Information for a given filing period, has not filed one at all during the preceding 24 months, and was already certified to the Franchise Tax Board for the $250 penalty for that same period, the statute switches from a monetary penalty to suspension of the entity's powers: the Secretary of State warns the entity that its powers, rights, and privileges will be suspended in 60 days unless it files, and if the entity still has not filed when that period ends, the Secretary of State notifies the Franchise Tax Board and the entity's powers, rights, and privileges are suspended. Filing the required statement can lift a suspension imposed on this basis, unless the entity is also separately held in suspension by the Franchise Tax Board for unpaid tax, penalty, or interest — a related but legally distinct suspension mechanism, triggered by nonpayment rather than non-filing, under which the same broad phrase — the entity's 'powers, rights, and privileges' — is likewise suspended.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's periodic filing requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific entity; other states impose different periodic-report requirements with different names, deadlines, and forms. This clause cites three different statutory sections, not subsections of one section: Cal. Corp. Code § 2205 and Cal. Corp. Code § 17713.10 are separately worded but structurally parallel statutes — the first for corporations, the second for LLCs — and Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23301 is the distinct, tax-nonpayment-based suspension mechanism referenced inside both of the others. An honest limit on what this clause verified: the statutes themselves state only that a suspended entity's 'powers, rights, and privileges' are suspended, without spelling out the practical legal consequences of that suspension. It is commonly discussed, including in California case law, that a suspended corporation or LLC loses the capacity to prosecute or defend a civil action in California courts while suspended — but this research did not independently fetch and verify any court opinion stating that rule, so this clause does not cite one, and that specific consequence should be treated as unverified by this document rather than confirmed.

citations.cite: Crimes and Penalties, Secretary of State suspension of a corporation for sustained non-filing
citations.quote: (a) A corporation that (1) fails to file a statement pursuant to Section 1502 for an applicable filing period, (2) has not filed a statement pursuant to Section 1502 during the preceding 24 months, and (3) was certified for penalty pursuant to Section 2204 for the same filing period, is subject to suspension pursuant to this section rather than to penalty pursuant to Section 2204. (b) When subdivision (a) is applicable, the Secretary of State shall provide a notice to the corporation informing the corporation that its corporate powers, rights, and privileges will be suspended after 60 days if it fails to file a statement pursuant to Section 1502. (c) After the expiration of the 60-day period without any statement filed pursuant to Section 1502, the Secretary of State shall notify the Franchise Tax Board of the suspension and provide a notice of the suspension to the corporation, and thereupon, the corporate powers, rights, and privileges of the corporation are suspended, except for the purpose of filing an application for exempt status or amending the articles of incorporation as necessary either to perfect that application or to set forth a new name.

citations.cite: Miscellaneous Provisions, Secretary of State suspension of an LLC for sustained non-filing
citations.quote: (a) A limited liability company that (1) fails to file a statement pursuant to Section 17702.09 for an applicable filing period, (2) has not filed a statement pursuant to Section 17702.09 during the preceding 24 months, and (3) was certified for penalty pursuant to Section 17713.09 for the same filing period, shall be subject to suspension pursuant to this section rather than to penalty pursuant to Section 17713.09. (b) When subdivision (a) is applicable, the Secretary of State shall notify the limited liability company that its powers, rights, and privileges will be suspended after 60 days if it fails to file a statement pursuant to Section 17702.09. (c) After the expiration of the 60-day period without any statement filed pursuant to Section 17702.09, the Secretary of State shall notify the Franchise Tax Board of the suspension, and shall provide a notice of the suspension to the limited liability company and thereupon, except for the purpose of amending the articles of organization to set forth a new name, the powers, rights, and privileges of the limited liability company are suspended.

citations.cite: Suspension and Revivor, the separate tax-nonpayment suspension mechanism
citations.quote: Except for the purposes of filing an application for exempt status or amending the articles of incorporation or organization as necessary either to perfect that application or to set forth a new name, the powers, rights, and privileges of a domestic taxpayer may be suspended, and the exercise of the powers, rights, and privileges of a foreign taxpayer in this state may be forfeited, if any of the following conditions occur:

clauses.title: Request to Inspect and Copy Records
clauses.body:
This is a written request from {{employeeName}} to {{companyName}}, submitted on {{requestDate}}. As of the date of this request, {{employeeName}}'s employment status is: {{employmentStatus}}.

{{employeeName}} requests the following records: {{recordsRequested}}.

This request references rights described under California Labor Code sections 1198.5 and 226, addressed in the informational sections of this document. Nothing in this letter is a claim that any particular record exists in {{companyName}}'s files, or a demand for records beyond what California law makes available under those statutes.

clauses.title: Two Separate Statutory Rights: Personnel Records and Payroll Records
clauses.body: California law recognizes two separate statutory rights that let {{employeeName}} inspect and obtain copies of employment-related records held by {{companyName}}. Labor Code § 1198.5 gives every current and former employee, or their representative, the right to inspect and receive a copy of the personnel records the employer maintains relating to the employee's performance, including education or training records, or to any grievance concerning the employee; an employer receiving a written request under § 1198.5 must make those records available no later than 30 calendar days from the date of the request (or up to 35 calendar days if the employee or representative and the employer agree in writing to a later date). Separately, Labor Code § 226(b)-(c) gives a current or former employee the right to inspect or receive a copy of records the employer is required to keep in connection with itemized wage statements — payroll records — and requires the employer to comply as soon as practicable but no later than 21 calendar days from the date of the request. These are two different statutes, reaching two different categories of records, with two different compliance deadlines; a request that names only one of the two statutes, or that describes only one category of records, does not automatically function as a request under the other.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's personnel/payroll records inspection rights — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. The two citations below are to two different California statutes (Labor Code §§ 1198.5 and 226), not two subsections of the same statute, so no same-section duplication is being treated as two independent sources. This clause states the general distinction; it does not resolve, for a specific document a reader believes the employer holds, which of the two statutes (if either) actually covers that document — that depends on whether the document is a 'personnel record' relating to performance or a grievance under § 1198.5, a payroll record of the kind § 226(a) requires an employer to keep, both, or neither, none of which this clause determines. This document does not re-derive the full text or mechanics of the § 226 wage-statement itemization requirement itself, which this project's separate Wage Statement Itemization Policy document already covers in more detail.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Every current and former employee, or their representative, has the right to inspect and receive a copy of the personnel records that the employer maintains relating to the employee’s performance, including education or training records, or to any grievance concerning the employee.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: An employer who receives a written or oral request to inspect or receive a copy of records pursuant to subdivision (b) pertaining to a current or former employee shall comply with the request as soon as practicable, but no later than 21 calendar days from the date of the request.

clauses.title: Who May Request Personnel Records, and How Often
clauses.body: Labor Code § 1198.5 gives the right to inspect and copy personnel records to every current and former employee, or their representative — a right that is not limited to employees who are actively employed at the time of the request. A "representative," for these purposes, means a person {{employeeName}} authorizes in writing to inspect or receive a copy of {{employeeName}}'s personnel records on {{employeeName}}'s behalf; {{companyName}} may take reasonable steps to verify the identity of the current or former employee or authorized representative making the request. If {{employeeName}} is a former employee of {{companyName}}, California law limits {{companyName}}'s obligation to comply with more than one request per year from that former employee (or their representative) to inspect or receive a copy of personnel records.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's personnel/payroll records inspection rights — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. The three citations below are to three different subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5 — subdivisions (a)(1), (d), and (e) — so they are treated as one source, not three independent ones. This clause does not address the statute's separate 50-request-per-calendar-month cap on requests filed by a representative or representatives of employees generally (§ 1198.5(p)), nor the statute's exemption for an employee covered by a qualifying collective bargaining agreement (§ 1198.5(q)); neither is quoted or relied on here.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Every current and former employee, or their representative, has the right to inspect and receive a copy of the personnel records that the employer maintains relating to the employee’s performance, including education or training records, or to any grievance concerning the employee.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: An employer is required to comply with only one request per year by a former employee to inspect or receive a copy of their personnel records.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: The employer may take reasonable steps to verify the identity of a current or former employee or their authorized representative. For purposes of this section, “representative” means a person authorized in writing by the employee to inspect, or receive a copy of, their personnel records.

clauses.title: The Response Timeframe Under § 1198.5: 30 Calendar Days, Up to 35 by Written Agreement
clauses.body: Once {{companyName}} receives a written request from {{employeeName}} (or {{employeeName}}'s representative) to inspect personnel records covered by Labor Code § 1198.5, California law requires {{companyName}} to make those records available for inspection no later than 30 calendar days from the date {{companyName}} receives the request — unless {{employeeName}} (or the representative) and {{companyName}} agree in writing to a later date, which cannot exceed 35 calendar days from {{companyName}}'s receipt of the request. The same 30-calendar-day deadline, extendable to 35 calendar days by the same kind of written agreement, applies separately to a request for a copy of the records. Where {{companyName}} provides copies, California law lets {{companyName}} charge {{employeeName}} an amount not to exceed the actual cost of reproduction.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's personnel/payroll records inspection rights — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision, § 1198.5(b)(1); no additional independent source was sought for this specific point. That same subdivision also states that, except as provided in § 1198.5(c)(2), an employer is not required to make personnel records or a copy of them available at a time when the employee is actually required to render service to the employer, if the requester is the employee — a timing nuance this clause does not separately restate. This clause does not address the statute's distinct requirement (§ 1198.5(c)(1)) that an employer keep a copy of each employee's personnel records for at least three years after termination of employment, which bears on record retention rather than on the response deadline described here.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: The employer shall make the contents of those personnel records available for inspection to the current or former employee, or their representative, at reasonable intervals and at reasonable times, but not later than 30 calendar days from the date the employer receives a written request, unless the current or former employee, or their representative, and the employer agree in writing to a date beyond 30 calendar days to inspect the records, and the agreed-upon date does not exceed 35 calendar days from the employer’s receipt of the written request. Upon a written request from a current or former employee, or their representative, the employer shall also provide a copy of the personnel records, at a charge not to exceed the actual cost of reproduction, not later than 30 calendar days from the date the employer receives the request, unless the current or former employee, or their representative, and the employer agree in writing to a date beyond 30 calendar days to produce a copy of the records, as long as the agreed-upon date does not exceed 35 calendar days from the employer’s receipt of the written request.

clauses.title: What § 1198.5 Does Not Reach: Statutory Exclusions
clauses.body: Labor Code § 1198.5's inspection-and-copy right does not extend to every document that might exist somewhere in {{employeeName}}'s file at {{companyName}}. By its own terms, the statute does not apply to: records relating to the investigation of a possible criminal offense; letters of reference; and ratings, reports, or records that were obtained before {{employeeName}}'s employment began, prepared by identifiable examination committee members, or obtained in connection with a promotional examination. The statute also excludes two categories of employees from its coverage altogether: employees subject to the Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights, and employees of agencies subject to the Information Practices Act of 1977.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's personnel/payroll records inspection rights — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision, § 1198.5(h) (paragraphs (1) through (5)); no additional independent source was sought for this exclusions list. Whether a specific document in the employee's personnel file actually falls within one of these exclusions — for example, whether a given report was in fact "obtained prior to the employee's employment" or instead prepared afterward — is a factual question this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(h) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: The requirements of this section do not apply to: (1) Records relating to the investigation of a possible criminal offense. (2) Letters of reference. (3) Ratings, reports, or records that were: (A) Obtained prior to the employee’s employment. (B) Prepared by identifiable examination committee members. (C) Obtained in connection with a promotional examination. (4) Employees who are subject to the Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights (Chapter 9.7 (commencing with Section 3300) of Division 4 of Title 1 of the Government Code). (5) Employees of agencies subject to the Information Practices Act of 1977 (Title 1.8 (commencing with Section 1798) of Part 4 of Division 3 of the Civil Code).

clauses.title: Remedies for Noncompliance Under § 1198.5: $750 Penalty, Injunctive Relief, and Infraction Status
clauses.body: If {{companyName}} fails to permit {{employeeName}} (or {{employeeName}}'s representative) to inspect or copy personnel records within the time Labor Code § 1198.5 allows — including a time agreed to in writing under that statute — California law lets {{employeeName}}, or separately the Labor Commissioner, recover a $750 penalty from {{companyName}}. {{employeeName}} may also bring a civil action for injunctive relief to obtain compliance with § 1198.5, and may recover costs and reasonable attorney's fees in that action. Separately, a violation of § 1198.5 is an infraction, though "impossibility of performance," not caused by or resulting from a violation of law, is available to {{companyName}} as an affirmative defense in any action alleging a violation of the statute.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's personnel/payroll records inspection rights — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. The three citations below are to three different subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5 — subdivisions (k), (l), and (m) — so they are treated as one source, not three independent ones. The statutory text of § 1198.5(k) names the current or former employee and the Labor Commissioner as the parties who "may recover" the $750 penalty, but does not, on its own text, specify the procedural mechanism through which the employee's own recovery proceeds — for example, whether it is pursued through a Labor Commissioner wage claim, a direct civil action, or either; that procedural question was not independently resolved this session (no case law or Division of Labor Standards Enforcement guidance on the point was verified), and is disclosed here rather than assumed. Whether a specific failure to comply within the statutory time actually occurred, and whether the circumstances could support an "impossibility of performance" defense, are factual questions this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(k) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: If an employer fails to permit a current or former employee, or their representative, to inspect or copy personnel records within the times specified in this section, or times agreed to by mutual agreement as provided in this section, the current or former employee or the Labor Commissioner may recover a penalty of seven hundred fifty dollars ($750) from the employer.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(l) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: A current or former employee may also bring an action for injunctive relief to obtain compliance with this section, and may recover costs and reasonable attorney’s fees in such an action.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(m) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Notwithstanding Section 1199, a violation of this section is an infraction. Impossibility of performance, not caused by or resulting from a violation of law, may be asserted as an affirmative defense by an employer in any action alleging a violation of this section.

clauses.title: The Separate Payroll-Records Right Under § 226, and Its 21-Day Deadline
clauses.body: Separately from the personnel-records right described above, Labor Code § 226(b) gives {{employeeName}}, as a current or former employee of {{companyName}}, the right to inspect or receive a copy of records pertaining to {{employeeName}}'s employment that {{companyName}} is required to keep under the itemized-wage-statement statute — {{companyName}}'s payroll records — upon reasonable request. {{companyName}} may take reasonable steps to verify {{employeeName}}'s identity, and may charge {{employeeName}} the actual cost of reproduction for copies. {{companyName}} must comply with a request as soon as practicable but no later than 21 calendar days from the date of the request — a shorter deadline than the 30-to-35-calendar-day deadline that applies to a personnel-records request under § 1198.5. If {{companyName}} fails to permit inspection or copying of payroll records within that 21-day window, California law lets {{employeeName}} or the Labor Commissioner recover a $750 penalty from {{companyName}} — the same dollar figure as the personnel-records penalty described elsewhere in this document, though the two $750 penalties arise under two different statutes and correspond to two different categories of records and two different deadlines.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's personnel/payroll records inspection rights — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. The three citations below are to three different subdivisions of the same statutory section, Cal. Labor Code § 226 — subdivisions (b), (c), and (f) — so they are treated as one source, not three independent ones; this same statutory language is also cited, independently verified, in this project's separate Wage Statement Itemization Policy document, and the two clauses are not meant to be read as reaching a different textual conclusion from one another. This clause does not restate what records an employer is required to keep under § 226(a) in the first place (the nine-item wage-statement content requirement), which that separate document covers in full; it addresses only the inspection-and-copy right and its deadline and penalty.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: An employer that is required by this code or any regulation adopted pursuant to this code to keep the information required by subdivision (a) shall afford current and former employees the right to inspect or receive a copy of records pertaining to their employment, upon reasonable request to the employer. The employer may take reasonable steps to ensure the identity of a current or former employee. If the employer provides copies of the records, the actual cost of reproduction may be charged to the current or former employee.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: An employer who receives a written or oral request to inspect or receive a copy of records pursuant to subdivision (b) pertaining to a current or former employee shall comply with the request as soon as practicable, but no later than 21 calendar days from the date of the request. A violation of this subdivision is an infraction. Impossibility of performance, not caused by or a result of a violation of law, shall be an affirmative defense for an employer in any action alleging a violation of this subdivision. An employer may designate the person to whom a request under this subdivision will be made.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: A failure by an employer to permit a current or former employee to inspect or receive a copy of records within the time set forth in subdivision (c) entitles the current or former employee or the Labor Commissioner to recover a seven-hundred-fifty-dollar ($750) penalty from the employer.

clauses.title: Closing and Signature
This Petition Information Sheet Describes a Court Proceeding, Not an Automatic Transfer
clauses.body: Opening a formal probate proceeding for {{decedentName}}'s estate under California law happens only through an actual proceeding in superior court under Probate Code Division 7 — a filed petition, notice to interested persons, and a court order — not through the act of preparing or signing this document. Probate Code § 8000(a) provides that at any time after a decedent’s death, any interested person may commence proceedings for administration of the estate by a petition to the court for an order determining the date and place of death and for either or both appointment of a personal representative and probate of the decedent’s will. Probate Code § 48(a) separately defines “interested person,” for this and other probate purposes, to include an heir, devisee, child, spouse, creditor, beneficiary, and any other person having a property right in or claim against the estate that may be affected by the proceeding, as well as any person having priority for appointment as personal representative, and a fiduciary representing an interested person.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's formal probate process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. This document is informational: it describes the statutory probate petition process for estates that do not qualify for, or are not using, California's separate small-estate procedures (Prob. Code §§ 13100-13210); it does not itself open probate, appoint a personal representative, or determine the value of any specific estate or the identity of any specific decedent's heirs — only a court order issued after the statutory petition, notice, and hearing process can do that. This clause cites two different statutory sections (§ 8000(a) and § 48(a)); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. § 48(b) further notes that the meaning of “interested person” as applied to particular persons can vary by the purpose and matter involved in a given proceeding; this clause does not attempt to resolve that variation for any specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8000(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8000(a)
citations.quote: At any time after a decedent’s death, any interested person may commence proceedings for administration of the estate of the decedent by a petition to the court for an order determining the date and place of the decedent’s death and for either or both of the following: (1) Appointment of a personal representative. (2) Probate of the decedent’s will.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 48(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 48(a)
citations.quote: Subject to subdivision (b), “interested person” includes any of the following: (1) An heir, devisee, child, spouse, creditor, beneficiary, and any other person having a property right in or claim against a trust estate or the estate of a decedent which may be affected by the proceeding. (2) Any person having priority for appointment as personal representative. (3) A fiduciary representing an interested person.

clauses.title: California Does Not Set a General Deadline to File a Probate Petition — Only a Narrow 30-Day Rule for a Named Executor
clauses.body: Probate Code § 8001 does not impose a general deadline, running from {{decedentName}}'s date of death, by which a petition to open probate must be filed. The only timing rule found in this part of the code is narrower: unless good cause for the delay is shown, a person named as executor in a will who fails to petition the court for administration of the estate within 30 days after that person has knowledge of the decedent's death and of being named as executor may be held to have waived the right to appointment as personal representative. That 30-day rule applies only to a person named as executor in a will; it does not set a deadline for heirs or other interested persons to petition, and it does not itself bar the estate from being probated — it addresses only whether that particular named executor may lose priority for appointment.
clauses.gap: This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: California law does not impose a general, estate-wide filing deadline for opening probate after a decedent's death. § 8001 is a narrow, waiver-only rule aimed specifically at a person named as executor in a will, subject to a good-cause exception, and it does not itself bar probate or set a deadline applicable to heirs or other interested persons who are not named as executor. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's formal probate process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. This document is informational: it does not itself open probate, appoint a personal representative, or determine the value of any specific estate or the identity of any specific decedent's heirs — only a court order issued after the statutory petition, notice, and hearing process can do that. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 8001); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8001 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8001
citations.quote: Unless good cause for delay is shown, if a person named in a will as executor fails to petition the court for administration of the estate within 30 days after the person has knowledge of the death of the decedent and that the person is named as executor, the person may be held to have waived the right to appointment as personal representative.

clauses.title: What the Petition Must State
clauses.body: Probate Code § 8002(a) requires a petition for administration of {{decedentName}}'s estate to contain: the date and place of {{decedentName}}'s death; the street address and county of {{decedentName}}'s residence at the time of death; the name, age, address, and relation to {{decedentName}} of each heir and devisee, so far as known to or reasonably ascertainable by the petitioner; the character and estimated value of the property in the estate; and the name of the person for whom appointment as personal representative is petitioned. If {{decedentName}} left a will, § 8002(b) separately requires the petitioner to attach a photographic copy of the will (plus a typed copy, if it is holographic or otherwise has handwritten material provisions, and an English translation if it is in a foreign language), and to state in the petition whether the person named as executor in the will consents to act or waives the right to appointment.
clauses.gap: This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: the required contents of a California probate petition are set out in Probate Code § 8002, not in the §§ 8100-8110 range — that range instead governs the separate notice of hearing that must be given after the petition is filed (its required contents at § 8100, and service of that notice at § 8110), addressed in this document's companion clause on notice. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 8002(a) and § 8002(b)). Honest gap: § 8002 does not, on its own text, list “whether the decedent left a will” as a separate item the petition must affirmatively state; instead, § 8002(b)'s attachment and consent-or-waiver obligations are conditioned on a will having been left, which in practice discloses that fact through the petition's structure and attachments (and through the statewide Judicial Council petition form, which this clause does not independently verify). This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's formal probate process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. This document is informational: it does not itself open probate, appoint a personal representative, or determine the value of any specific estate or the identity of any specific decedent's heirs — only a court order issued after the statutory petition, notice, and hearing process can do that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8002(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8002(a)
citations.quote: The petition shall contain all of the following information: (1) The date and place of the decedent’s death. (2) The street number, street, and city, or other address, and the county, of the decedent’s residence at the time of death. (3) The name, age, address, and relation to the decedent of each heir and devisee of the decedent, so far as known to or reasonably ascertainable by the petitioner. (4) The character and estimated value of the property in the estate. (5) The name of the person for whom appointment as personal representative is petitioned.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8002(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8002(b)
citations.quote: If the decedent left a will: (1) The petitioner shall attach to the petition a photographic copy of the will. In the case of a holographic will or other will of which material provisions are handwritten, the petitioner shall also attach a typed copy of the will. (2) If the will is in a foreign language, the petitioner shall attach an English language translation. On admission of the will to probate, the court shall certify to a correct translation into English, and the certified translation shall be filed with the will. (3) The petition shall state whether the person named as executor in the will consents to act or waives the right to appointment.

clauses.title: Notice Before the Hearing, and the Creditor Claim-Filing Period It Starts
clauses.body: At least 15 days before the hearing on a petition for administration of {{decedentName}}'s estate, Probate Code § 8110 requires the petitioner to deliver notice of the hearing to each heir of {{decedentName}}, so far as known to or reasonably ascertainable by the petitioner, and to each devisee, executor, and alternate executor named in any will being offered for probate, regardless of whether that devise or appointment is purportedly revoked by a later instrument. The statutory notice form set out at Probate Code § 8100 also fixes the outer limit for a creditor or contingent creditor of {{decedentName}} to file a claim: within the later of four months from the date letters are first issued to a general personal representative, or 60 days from the date a particular creditor is delivered notice under Probate Code § 9052.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's formal probate process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. This clause cites two different statutory sections (§ 8110 and § 8100); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. This clause does not address the separate publication requirement for notice under Probate Code Article 3 (commencing with § 8120), which applies in addition to the delivered notice described here. This document is informational: it does not itself open probate, appoint a personal representative, or determine the value of any specific estate or the identity of any specific decedent's heirs — only a court order issued after the statutory petition, notice, and hearing process can do that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8110 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8110
citations.quote: At least 15 days before the hearing of a petition for administration of a decedent’s estate, the petitioner shall deliver notice of the hearing pursuant to Section 1215 on all of the following persons: (a) Each heir of the decedent, so far as known to or reasonably ascertainable by the petitioner. (b) Each devisee, executor, and alternative executor named in any will being offered for probate, regardless of whether the devise or appointment is purportedly revoked in a subsequent instrument.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8100 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8100
citations.quote: IF YOU ARE A CREDITOR or a contingent creditor of the deceased, you must file your claim with the court and mail a copy to the personal representative appointed by the court within the later of either (1) four months from the date of first issuance of letters to a general personal representative, as defined in subdivision (b) of Section 58 of the California Probate Code, or (2) 60 days from the date of delivery of the notice to you under Section 9052 of the California Probate Code.

clauses.title: Who the Court May Appoint as Administrator When There Is No Will, and in What Order
clauses.body: If {{decedentName}} died intestate (without a valid will), Probate Code § 8460(a) requires the court to appoint an administrator as personal representative, and § 8460(b) allows the court to appoint more than one person to serve in that role. Probate Code § 8461 fixes the order of priority among persons entitled to that appointment: (a) surviving spouse or domestic partner; (b) children; (c) grandchildren; (d) other issue; (e) parents; (f) brothers and sisters; (g) issue of brothers and sisters; (h) grandparents; (i) issue of grandparents; (j) children of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner; (k) other issue of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner; (l) other next of kin; (m) parents of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner; (n) issue of parents of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner; (o) a conservator or guardian of the estate acting in that capacity at {{decedentName}}'s death who has filed a first account and is not acting as conservator or guardian for anyone else; (p) the public administrator; (q) creditors; and (r) any other person.
clauses.gap: This corrects and confirms an assumption in the original research brief: § 8461's priority order runs considerably further than spouse, children, grandchildren, parents, and siblings alone — it continues through issue of siblings, grandparents and their issue, several categories tied to a predeceased spouse or domestic partner, other next of kin, an acting conservator or guardian of the estate, the public administrator, creditors, and finally any other person. This clause cites two different statutory sections (§ 8460 and § 8461); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. Several conditioning provisions in the same article are not quoted here and are honestly disclosed rather than described: § 8462 limits a spouse's, domestic partner's, or relative's priority to situations where that person is entitled to succeed to all or part of the estate (directly, or through another deceased person's entitlement); § 8463 gives a surviving spouse who was living apart from the decedent at death, while a party to a separate maintenance, annulment, or dissolution action, priority next after brothers and sisters instead of the priority § 8461 would otherwise give a spouse; and § 8464 lets the court, in its discretion, appoint a guardian or conservator (or another qualified person) in place of someone otherwise entitled to appointment who is a minor or has their own conservator of the estate. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's formal probate process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. This document is informational: it does not itself appoint any administrator or determine the identity of any specific decedent's heirs — only a court order issued after the statutory petition, notice, and hearing process can do that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8460 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8460
citations.quote: (a) If the decedent dies intestate, the court shall appoint an administrator as personal representative. (b) The court may appoint one or more persons as administrator.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8461 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8461
citations.quote: Subject to the provisions of this article, a person in the following relation to the decedent is entitled to appointment as administrator in the following order of priority: (a) Surviving spouse or domestic partner as defined in Section 37. (b) Children. (c) Grandchildren. (d) Other issue. (e) Parents. (f) Brothers and sisters. (g) Issue of brothers and sisters. (h) Grandparents. (i) Issue of grandparents. (j) Children of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner. (k) Other issue of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner. (l) Other next of kin. (m) Parents of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner. (n) Issue of parents of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner. (o) Conservator or guardian of the estate acting in that capacity at the time of death who has filed a first account and is not acting as conservator or guardian for any other person. (p) Public administrator. (q) Creditors. (r) Any other person.

clauses.title: A Personal Representative Has No Authority to Act Until Letters Are Issued
clauses.body: Probate Code § 8400(a) provides that a person has no power to administer {{decedentName}}'s estate until that person is appointed personal representative and the appointment becomes effective, and that the appointment becomes effective only when the person appointed is issued letters. § 8400(b) makes this true whether or not the person is named executor in {{decedentName}}'s will, with one narrow exception: a person named executor may, before the appointment is made or becomes effective, pay funeral expenses and take necessary measures for the maintenance and preservation of the estate. § 8400(c) requires the court's order appointing a personal representative to carry, in capital letters on its first page, the warning that the appointment is not effective until letters have issued. Before letters are issued, Probate Code § 8403(a) separately requires the personal representative to take and subscribe an oath to perform the duties of the office according to law; § 8403(b) provides that the oath constitutes acceptance of the office and must be attached to or endorsed on the letters.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's formal probate process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. This clause cites two different statutory sections (§ 8400 and § 8403); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. This document is informational: it does not itself appoint any personal representative or issue Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration, and signing any declaration prepared alongside this document gives no one authority to act for the decedent's estate — only a court order followed by the actual issuance of letters, as described here, does that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8400 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8400
citations.quote: (a) A person has no power to administer the estate until the person is appointed personal representative and the appointment becomes effective. Appointment of a personal representative becomes effective when the person appointed is issued letters. (b) Subdivision (a) applies whether or not the person is named executor in the decedent’s will, except that a person named executor in the decedent’s will may, before the appointment is made or becomes effective, pay funeral expenses and take necessary measures for the maintenance and preservation of the estate. (c) The order appointing a personal representative shall state in capital letters on the first page of the order, in at least 12-point type, the following: “WARNING: THIS APPOINTMENT IS NOT EFFECTIVE UNTIL LETTERS HAVE ISSUED.”

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8403 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8403
citations.quote: (a) Before letters are issued, the personal representative shall take and subscribe an oath to perform, according to law, the duties of the office. The oath may be taken and dated on or after the time the petition for appointment as personal representative is signed, and may be filed with the clerk at any time after the petition is granted. (b) The oath constitutes an acceptance of the office and shall be attached to or endorsed on the letters.

clauses.title: Independent Administration Under the IAEA, and the Matters That Still Require Court Supervision Even Then
clauses.body: Once appointed, a personal representative for {{decedentName}}'s estate does not automatically administer that estate under full court supervision for every act. Probate Code § 10450(a) lets a personal representative petition the court — either in the petition for appointment or in a separate petition filed later in the estate proceeding — for authority to administer the estate under the Independent Administration of Estates Act (IAEA), and § 10450(b) lets that petition request either full or limited IAEA authority. Even where full or limited IAEA authority is granted, Probate Code § 10501(a) still requires the personal representative to obtain court supervision, in the manner otherwise provided by the Probate Code, for specified matters — among them, allowance of the personal representative's or their attorney's compensation, settlement of accounts, and preliminary or final distributions and discharge; § 10501(b) requires court supervision for sale or exchange of real property, and certain other real-property transactions, whenever only limited (rather than full) IAEA authority has been granted. Separately, Probate Code § 10404 provides that a personal representative may not be granted IAEA authority at all if {{decedentName}}'s will provides that the estate shall not be administered under the Act.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's formal probate process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. This clause cites three different statutory sections (§ 10450, § 10501, and § 10404); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. § 10501(a) lists ten specific categories of action requiring court supervision even under full IAEA authority, and § 10501(b) lists four further categories requiring it under limited authority alone; this clause summarizes rather than reproduces every listed category, and § 10501(c) sets out a narrow exception to some of those categories (for certain sole-beneficiary or fully-consented transactions after the creditor-claim period has run) that this clause does not otherwise describe. This document does not describe the separate notice-of-proposed-action procedure (Probate Code §§ 10580-10592) that IAEA administration otherwise substitutes for many court petitions. This document is informational: it does not itself grant IAEA authority, open probate, or appoint a personal representative — only a court order does that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10450 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) To obtain authority to administer the estate under this part, the personal representative shall petition the court for that authority either in the petition for appointment of the personal representative or in a separate petition filed in the estate proceedings. (b) The petition may request either of the following: (1) Full authority to administer the estate under this part. (2) Limited authority to administer the estate under this part.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10501(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision of this part, whether the personal representative has been granted full authority or limited authority, a personal representative who has obtained authority to administer the estate under this part is required to obtain court supervision, in the manner provided in this code, for any of the following actions: (1) Allowance of the personal representative’s compensation. (2) Allowance of compensation of the attorney for the personal representative. (3) Settlement of accounts. (4) Subject to Section 10520, preliminary and final distributions and discharge.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10404 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The personal representative may not be granted authority to administer the estate under this part if the decedent’s will provides that the estate shall not be administered under this part.

clauses.title: Proposed Petitioner — Information and Declaration in Support of Petition
clauses.body: I, {{petitionerName}}, am the person petitioning the California superior court to open a probate proceeding for the estate of {{decedentName}}, who died on {{dateOfDeath}} at {{placeOfDeath}}. My relationship to {{decedentName}} is: {{relationshipToDecedent}}. I am petitioning for appointment of {{petitionerName}} as personal representative of {{decedentName}}'s estate. The character and estimated value of the property in the estate is: {{estimatedEstateValue}}. This declaration provides background information for use with an actual petition for probate, to be filed in California superior court under Probate Code Division 7, Part 2. This declaration is not itself a court filing, and signing it does not open probate, appoint {{petitionerName}} — or anyone else — as personal representative, or determine the value of {{decedentName}}'s estate or the identity of {{decedentName}}'s heirs or devisees for any purpose. Only a court order issued after the statutory petition, notice, and hearing process described in this document can open probate or appoint a personal representative, and only the subsequent issuance of Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration gives that personal representative actual authority to act for the estate.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment Block — Petition for Probate Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{petitionerName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual petition for probate filed with the California superior court. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that petition, and it does not open probate, appoint a personal representative, or issue Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration; only a court order, followed by the issuance of Letters, does that.]

clauses.title: Grant of Easement, Purpose, and Location
clauses.body:
{{grantorName}} ("Grantor"), as owner of the real property located at {{servientPropertyAddress}}, described as {{servientLegalDescription}} (the "Servient Property"), grants to {{granteeName}} ("Grantee") an easement over, across, or upon the Servient Property for the purpose of {{easementPurpose}}. The specific area, route, or location within the Servient Property that is subject to this easement is described as follows: {{easementLocationDescription}}.
