clauses.title: Servitudes California's Civil Code Recognizes as Easements
clauses.body: California's Civil Code, in a chapter titled "Servitudes," sets out a specific statutory list of the land burdens that can be created over one parcel of real property for the benefit of another. That list includes, among others, a right-of-way, the right of pasture, the right of fishing or of taking game, the right of taking water, wood, minerals, and other things, the right of transacting business or conducting lawful sports upon land, the right of receiving air, light, or heat from or over land (or of discharging the same), the right of receiving or discharging water, the right of flooding land, the right of having water flow without diminution or disturbance, the right of using a wall as a party wall, the right of receiving more than natural support from adjacent land, the right of having a division fence maintained, and several others including a right of burial and a right of receiving sunlight as separately specified elsewhere in the Code. California's Civil Code states that when this same list of land burdens is "attached to other land as incidents or appurtenances," it is "then called easements." The Code separately states, in the same chapter, that much of that same list of land burdens "may be granted and held, though not attached to land." This easement, stated to be for the purpose of {{easementPurpose}} over the real property at {{servientPropertyAddress}}, is created as one of these statutory servitudes.
clauses.gap: §§ 801 and 802 are genuinely separate statutory sections within the same chapter (Civil Code Chapter 3, Servitudes), treated here as two independent sources. § 801 and § 802 list overlapping but not identical items — § 801's list of eighteen items is longer than § 802's list of six — and this clause quotes each list as its own section states, without asserting that every item on § 801's list also appears on § 802's list or vice versa. Neither section uses the modern shorthand terms "easement appurtenant" or "easement in gross"; those terms are common conveyancing and case-law shorthand for the distinction § 801 and § 802 draw in their own words — a servitude "attached to other land as incidents or appurtenances" (§ 801) versus one "granted and held, though not attached to land" (§ 802) — and that correspondence was checked directly against each section's statutory text rather than assumed. § 802 is a 19th-century section (last amended in 1873-74) whose own text begins with the words "Section Eight Hundred and Two," which are quoted here because they are part of the verified statutory text as currently published, not because they add substantive meaning; the quoted text also runs "land:One—" with no space, exactly as the publisher's markup renders it, rather than starting a new sentence. This clause does not determine whether this document's particular grant is appurtenant or in gross on its own facts; that depends on whether a Dominant Property is identified and on the document's own terms. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's law on easements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, statutory list of servitudes attached to land (easements appurtenant)
citations.quote: The following land burdens, or servitudes upon land, may be attached to other land as incidents or appurtenances, and are then called easements: 1. The right of pasture; 2. The right of fishing; 3. The right of taking game; 4. The right-of-way; 5. The right of taking water, wood, minerals, and other things; 6. The right of transacting business upon land; 7. The right of conducting lawful sports upon land; 8. The right of receiving air, light, or heat from or over, or discharging the same upon or over land; 9. The right of receiving water from or discharging the same upon land; 10. The right of flooding land; 11. The right of having water flow without diminution or disturbance of any kind; 12. The right of using a wall as a party wall; 13. The right of receiving more than natural support from adjacent land or things affixed thereto; 14. The right of having the whole of a division fence maintained by a coterminous owner; 15. The right of having public conveyances stopped, or of stopping the same on land; 16. The right of a seat in church; 17. The right of burial; 18. The right of receiving sunlight upon or over land as specified in Section 801.5.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, statutory list of servitudes held without attachment to land (easements in gross)
citations.quote: Section Eight Hundred and Two. The following land burdens, or servitudes upon land, may be granted and held, though not attached to land:One—The right to pasture, and of fishing and taking game. Two—The right of a seat in church. Third—The right of burial. Four—The right of taking rents and tolls. Five—The right of way. Six—The right of taking water, wood, minerals, or other things.

clauses.title: Extent of an Easement: Terms of the Grant
clauses.body: California law states that the extent of a servitude — how broadly or narrowly an easement may be used — is determined by the terms of the grant that created it, or, for an easement that arose some other way, by the nature of the enjoyment by which it was acquired. For an easement created by an express written grant, such as this one, the extent of {{granteeName}}'s rights over the Servient Property at {{servientPropertyAddress}}, for the stated purpose of {{easementPurpose}}, is fixed by the words of this grant itself, including the purpose, location, and any other terms this document states.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 806); no additional independent statutory source was located for the extent-of-servitude rule itself. § 806's rule has two branches — "the terms of the grant" and "the nature of the enjoyment by which it was acquired" — and this clause addresses only the first branch, which governs an easement created by an express grant such as this document; the second branch concerns easements acquired other ways (for example, by continued use), which this clause does not independently research or address. This clause does not determine, on the facts of any particular use, what a particular grant's terms actually permit or forbid. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's law on easements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, extent of a servitude
citations.quote: The extent of a servitude is determined by the terms of the grant, or the nature of the enjoyment by which it was acquired.

clauses.title: Interpreting an Easement Grant: In Favor of the Grantee, Except a Reservation
clauses.body: California law states a general rule for interpreting a grant of an interest in real property: a grant is to be interpreted in favor of the grantee. The same statute states an exception: a reservation contained within a grant — language by which the person conveying property keeps some interest for themselves rather than granting it away — is interpreted in favor of the grantor instead, as is any grant made by a public officer or public body, acting as such, to a private party. An easement is itself a grant of an interest in real property — a right to use another's land for a stated purpose. This rule applies to an easement granted outright by {{grantorName}} to {{granteeName}}, and applies in the opposite direction to the extent this document instead reserves an easement in favor of {{grantorName}} rather than granting one to {{granteeName}}.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 1069); no additional independent statutory source was located for this interpretive rule. § 1069 is an interpretive rule that operates on an ambiguous grant; it does not itself state that any particular grant, including this one, is in fact ambiguous, and this clause does not evaluate whether this document's own terms are ambiguous. § 1069's text is not limited to easements — it states a general rule for interpreting a grant of any interest in real property — and this clause states its application to an easement grant specifically as an application of that general rule, not as a separate easement-specific statute. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's law on easements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, interpretation of a grant in favor of the grantee, except a reservation
citations.quote: A grant is to be interpreted in favor of the grantee, except that a reservation in any grant, and every grant by a public officer or body, as such, to a private party, is to be interpreted in favor of the grantor.

clauses.title: Recording an Easement: Constructive Notice and California's Race-Notice Rule
clauses.body: Once validly created, an express easement is effective as between {{grantorName}} and {{granteeName}} whether or not it is ever recorded; recording is not a condition of the easement's validity between the parties who created it. Recording matters for what it does against later claimants to the Servient Property at {{servientPropertyAddress}}. California law states that every conveyance of real property or an estate for years in it, once acknowledged, certified, and recorded as prescribed by law, serves from the time it is filed with the recorder as constructive notice of its contents to subsequent purchasers and mortgagees. California is a "race-notice" recording state: an earlier conveyance of the same property that is not recorded is void against a later purchaser or mortgagee of that property who takes it in good faith, for valuable consideration, and records first.
clauses.gap: §§ 1213 and 1214 are genuinely separate statutory sections within the same chapter and article (Civil Code, Effect of Recording, or the Want Thereof), treated here as two independent sources. California's race-notice recording rule is stated here as evidence of how one state resolves competing claims to the same property, not as a claim about which state's recording rule governs a particular property or easement — recording statutes vary by state, including "pure race" and "pure notice" states. This clause treats an easement as a "conveyance of real property" within §§ 1213 and 1214's own words; it does not independently verify, through case law, every circumstance in which an unrecorded express easement in fact binds or does not bind a later purchaser of the Servient Property. Separately, this clause addresses only an easement created by an express, written grant like this document. It does not state the elements of a prescriptive easement — an easement a court may recognize from a claimant's adverse use of another's land over time, without any written grant or recording at all. An attempt to verify those elements against a specific, well-known California appellate decision through CourtListener could not be completed in this research session because the CourtListener API returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429) on every attempt; rather than state those elements from unverified memory or invent a case citation, that gap is disclosed here. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's law on easements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, recording gives constructive notice
citations.quote: Every conveyance of real property or an estate for years therein acknowledged or proved and certified and recorded as prescribed by law from the time it is filed with the recorder for record is constructive notice of the contents thereof to subsequent purchasers and mortgagees; and a certified copy of such a recorded conveyance may be recorded in any other county and when so recorded the record thereof shall have the same force and effect as though it was of the original conveyance and where the original conveyance has been recorded in any county wherein the property therein mentioned is not situated a certified copy of the recorded conveyance may be recorded in the county where such property is situated with the same force and effect as if the original conveyance had been recorded in that county.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, race-notice recording rule
citations.quote: Every conveyance of real property or an estate for years therein, other than a lease for a term not exceeding one year, is void as against any subsequent purchaser or mortgagee of the same property, or any part thereof, in good faith and for a valuable consideration, whose conveyance is first duly recorded, and as against any judgment affecting the title, unless the conveyance shall have been duly recorded prior to the record of notice of action.

clauses.title: An Easement Attached to Land Passes Automatically on Transfer of That Land
clauses.body: California law states that a transfer of real property passes all easements attached to it. This means that if the easement this document creates benefits the real property at {{dominantPropertyAddress}} — an easement attached to that property rather than a right personal to {{granteeName}} alone — a later transfer of {{dominantPropertyAddress}} by {{granteeName}} to a new owner carries the benefit of this easement automatically, without a separate written assignment of the easement itself.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 1104); no additional independent statutory source was located for this rule. § 1104's text does not use the word "appurtenant"; it refers to "easements attached" to the transferred property, which this clause treats as the same attachment concept § 801 uses (see the separate clause on §§ 801 and 802) — that correspondence was checked directly against § 1104's own text rather than assumed. § 1104 also states a second, separate rule this clause does not address: that a transfer can itself create an easement over other land the transferor owned, based on how the transferred property was "obviously and permanently used" before the transfer — an implied-easement doctrine distinct from the express easement this document creates. This clause does not address whether or how an easement personal to the grantee (rather than attached to a Dominant Property) may be transferred. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's law on easements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, transfer of real property passes attached easements
citations.quote: A transfer of real property passes all easements attached thereto, and creates in favor thereof an easement to use other real property of the person whose estate is transferred in the same manner and to the same extent as such property was obviously and permanently used by the person whose estate is transferred, for the benefit thereof, at the time when the transfer was agreed upon or completed.

clauses.title: Two Statutory Bases for a Federal Trademark Application: Use, or Intent to Use
clauses.body: Federal trademark law provides two distinct statutory pathways for requesting registration on the principal register. Under one, the owner of a mark already used in commerce may apply, and the application must state the applicant's dates of first use of the mark and first use of the mark in commerce. Under the other, a person who has not yet used a mark, but who has a bona fide intention to use it in commerce, may also apply; that application does not require a first-use date because none yet exists. An application filed on the intent-to-use pathway does not mature into a registration merely because it was accepted for examination: after a notice of allowance issues, the statute requires the applicant to separately file a verified statement of use, specifying the date the mark was actually first used in commerce and the goods or services on which it is used, before a registration will issue. This information sheet's basis-for-filing fields, including {{firstUseDate}} where applicable, and its description of {{trademarkDescription}} and {{goodsServicesDescription}}, track the categories of information the statute requires an applicant to state.
clauses.gap: This is federal law (the Lanham Act, which applies nationwide), used as real evidence of the two statutory filing bases and of the additional statement-of-use step required for an intent-to-use application — not a claim about which basis applies to, or whether registration would be available for, the mark described on this sheet, which depends on facts (including actual use, if any) this clause does not resolve. This clause cites four subsections of the same statutory section (15 U.S.C. § 1051(a)(1), (a)(2), (b)(1), and (d)(1)); they are not independent sources and are cited together because they are the provisions of a single application-and-registration mechanism.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, application based on use in commerce
citations.quote: The owner of a trademark used in commerce may request registration of its trademark on the principal register hereby established by paying the prescribed fee and filing in the Patent and Trademark Office an application and a verified statement, in such form as may be prescribed by the Director, and such number of specimens or facsimiles of the mark as used as may be required by the Director.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, use-based application must state the applicant's first-use dates
citations.quote: The application shall include specification of the applicant’s domicile and citizenship, the date of the applicant’s first use of the mark, the date of the applicant’s first use of the mark in commerce, the goods in connection with which the mark is used, and a drawing of the mark.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, application based on bona fide intent to use
citations.quote: A person who has a bona fide intention, under circumstances showing the good faith of such person, to use a trademark in commerce may request registration of its trademark on the principal register hereby established by paying the prescribed fee and filing in the Patent and Trademark Office an application and a verified statement, in such form as may be prescribed by the Director.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, verified statement of use required before registration issues on an intent-to-use application
citations.quote: Within six months after the date on which the notice of allowance with respect to a mark is issued under section 1063(b)(2) of this title to an applicant under subsection (b) of this section, the applicant shall file in the Patent and Trademark Office, together with such number of specimens or facsimiles of the mark as used in commerce as may be required by the Director and payment of the prescribed fee, a verified statement that the mark is in use in commerce and specifying the date of the applicant’s first use of the mark in commerce and those goods or services specified in the notice of allowance on or in connection with which the mark is used in commerce. Subject to examination and acceptance of the statement of use, the mark shall be registered in the Patent and Trademark Office, a certificate of registration shall be issued for those goods or services recited in the statement of use for which the mark is entitled to registration, and notice of registration shall be published in the Official Gazette of the Patent and Trademark Office.

clauses.title: What Counts as "Use in Commerce" for Registration Purposes
clauses.body: Federal trademark law defines a specific standard for what qualifies as "use in commerce" of a mark. The statute requires bona fide use of the mark in the ordinary course of trade, and expressly states that use made merely to reserve a right in a mark does not satisfy the standard. The statute goes on to specify, separately for goods and for services, what that bona fide use must look like — for goods, the mark must be placed on the goods, their containers, displays, or associated tags or labels (or, where that is impracticable, on documents associated with the goods or their sale), and the goods must be sold or transported in commerce; for services, the mark must be used or displayed in the sale or advertising of the services, and the services must be rendered in commerce. This is the statutory backdrop against which any description of when and how {{trademarkDescription}} has been used, including on the {{goodsServicesDescription}} described on this sheet, is evaluated for registration purposes.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the statutory "use in commerce" standard — not a claim that any particular use described on this sheet does or does not meet that standard, which is a fact-specific determination this clause does not make. Older case law and pre-1988 practice sometimes used the phrase "token use" to describe use that would not qualify; the current statutory text (as amended by the Trademark Law Revision Act of 1988) does not use that phrase, and instead codifies the standard as bona fide use "not made merely to reserve a right in a mark" — this clause quotes the actual current statutory wording rather than the older "token use" terminology. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 1127); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, Lanham Act definitions — "use in commerce"
citations.quote: The term “use in commerce” means the bona fide use of a mark in the ordinary course of trade, and not made merely to reserve a right in a mark.

clauses.title: Statutory Grounds for Refusing Registration: Confusing Similarity, Descriptiveness, and Secondary Meaning
clauses.body: Federal trademark law states that a mark by which an applicant's goods can be distinguished from others' goods will not be refused registration on account of its nature, unless it falls within one of the statute's enumerated grounds. Among those grounds: a mark will be refused if it so resembles a mark already registered, or a mark or trade name already used in the United States and not abandoned, that it is likely to cause confusion, mistake, or deception; a mark will also be refused if, as used on the applicant's goods, it is merely descriptive or deceptively misdescriptive of them. The statute also provides that a mark otherwise merely descriptive is not barred from registration if it has become distinctive of the applicant's goods in commerce — commonly called "secondary meaning" — and it allows proof of substantially exclusive and continuous use of the mark for the five years before the claim of distinctiveness is made to serve as prima facie evidence of that distinctiveness. This statutory framework is the backdrop against which {{trademarkDescription}}, as used on {{goodsServicesDescription}}, would be examined if an application for it were filed.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of specific statutory refusal grounds — not a claim that the mark described on this sheet would or would not be refused registration under any of them, which depends on comparison against the existing federal trademark register and other facts this clause does not evaluate. This clause cites three provisions of the same statutory section (15 U.S.C. § 1052(d), (e)(1), and (f)); they are not independent sources and are cited together because they are part of the same enumerated-grounds structure. Separately: the statute's other refusal grounds not quoted here include immoral, deceptive, or scandalous matter, certain flags and insignia, and certain names or portraits of living individuals (§ 1052(a)-(c)); "genericness" is not itself listed as a lettered ground in this section — see the companion clause on incontestability for where genericness is actually addressed in the statutory text. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, refusal for likelihood of confusion with an existing mark
citations.quote: Consists of or comprises a mark which so resembles a mark registered in the Patent and Trademark Office, or a mark or trade name previously used in the United States by another and not abandoned, as to be likely, when used on or in connection with the goods of the applicant, to cause confusion, or to cause mistake, or to deceive

citations.cite: U.S. Code, refusal for a merely descriptive mark
citations.quote: Consists of a mark which (1) when used on or in connection with the goods of the applicant is merely descriptive or deceptively misdescriptive of them,

citations.cite: U.S. Code, registration of a mark that has become distinctive (secondary meaning)
citations.quote: Except as expressly excluded in subsections (a), (b), (c), (d), (e)(3), and (e)(5) of this section, nothing in this chapter shall prevent the registration of a mark used by the applicant which has become distinctive of the applicant’s goods in commerce. The Director may accept as prima facie evidence that the mark has become distinctive, as used on or in connection with the applicant’s goods in commerce, proof of substantially exclusive and continuous use thereof as a mark by the applicant in commerce for the five years before the date on which the claim of distinctiveness is made.

clauses.title: Trademark Rights Can Arise From Use Alone, Without Federal Registration
clauses.body: Federal registration is not the only source of trademark rights. Federal law itself creates a civil cause of action against a person who, in commerce, uses any word, term, name, symbol, or device likely to cause confusion as to the affiliation, connection, or origin of goods or services — a cause of action that, by its terms, does not require the mark at issue to be federally registered. This is the statutory basis for what is often called "unregistered" or "common-law" trademark protection: rights that can arise from a mark's actual use in commerce, independent of any application to, or grant of registration by, the USPTO. Separately, a federal registration certificate itself carries statutory weight: once issued, it is made prima facie evidence of the validity of the registered mark, of the registration, of the owner's ownership, and of the owner's exclusive right to use the mark in commerce on the goods or services in the certificate. This information sheet's fields describing {{applicantName}}, {{trademarkDescription}}, and {{goodsServicesDescription}} record facts relevant to rights that can exist prior to, and independent of, any registration, as well as to a registration application should one be filed.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that (a) an unregistered mark can receive federal protection under the cited unfair-competition provision, and (b) a registration certificate is made statutory prima facie evidence under a separate provision — not a claim about the scope or strength of any rights in the mark described on this sheet specifically, which depends on facts about actual use, distinctiveness, and the marketplace this clause does not resolve. The two citations in this clause are to different statutory sections (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a) and § 1057(b)) and are independent of each other. This clause does not address the further common-law doctrine, developed through case law rather than this federal statutory text, that unregistered rights are generally understood to be limited to the geographic area of actual use and reputation; that doctrine could not be independently verified with a citation in this research pass because case-law lookup was rate-limited at the time of drafting (see the companion note in the registration-benefits clause). This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, civil action for false designation of origin (protection independent of registration)
citations.quote: Any person who, on or in connection with any goods or services, or any container for goods, uses in commerce any word, term, name, symbol, or device, or any combination thereof, or any false designation of origin, false or misleading description of fact, or false or misleading representation of fact, which— (A) is likely to cause confusion, or to cause mistake, or to deceive as to the affiliation, connection, or association of such person with another person, or as to the origin, sponsorship, or approval of his or her goods, services, or commercial activities by another person,

citations.cite: U.S. Code, registration certificate as prima facie evidence
citations.quote: A certificate of registration of a mark upon the principal register provided by this chapter shall be prima facie evidence of the validity of the registered mark and of the registration of the mark, of the owner’s ownership of the mark, and of the owner’s exclusive right to use the registered mark in commerce on or in connection with the goods or services specified in the certificate, subject to any conditions or limitations stated in the certificate.

clauses.title: Nationwide Constructive Notice and Eligibility for Incontestable Status
clauses.body: Federal registration on the principal register adds statutory effects that use alone does not. Registration is made constructive notice of the registrant's claim of ownership of the mark nationwide — a legal effect distinct from, and in addition to, whatever actual reputation the mark has in any particular area. Separately, once a registered mark has been in continuous use in commerce for five consecutive years after registration, and certain other conditions are met (including that no final adverse decision or pending proceeding involves the mark, and that a timely affidavit is filed), the statute makes the owner's right to use the mark incontestable, subject to the specific exceptions the statute itself lists. The statute also expressly excludes one category from ever becoming incontestable: no incontestable right can be acquired in a mark that is the generic name for the goods or services, or a portion of them, for which it is registered. This clause describes statutory effects available upon registration; it does not evaluate whether {{trademarkDescription}} would qualify for registration or, later, for incontestable status.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the constructive-notice and incontestability provisions — not a claim that any registration of the mark described on this sheet has occurred, has reached five years, or would qualify for incontestable status, all of which are fact- and time-dependent and unresolved by this clause. Two of this clause's three citations are to the same statutory section (15 U.S.C. § 1065, both its opening paragraph and paragraph (4)); they are not independent of each other. The third citation (§ 1072) is to a separate, independent section. Note on a research-brief assumption: the generic-mark exclusion appears in § 1065(4) (the incontestability provision) and is referenced again in the abandonment definition at § 1127 and the cancellation-grounds provision at § 1064(3); it is not itself a lettered ground within § 1052's refusal list, which is why it is addressed here rather than in the refusal-grounds clause. This research pass could not locate independent case law (e.g., on how genericness is proven) because CourtListener case-law search was rate-limited (HTTP 429, "125/day" quota) at the time of drafting; no case citation is included here rather than fabricating one. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, registration as constructive notice of claim of ownership
citations.quote: Registration of a mark on the principal register provided by this chapter or under the Act of March 3, 1881, or the Act of February 20, 1905, shall be constructive notice of the registrant’s claim of ownership thereof.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, incontestability of the right to use a registered mark after five years
citations.quote: Except on a ground for which application to cancel may be filed at any time under paragraphs (3), (5), and (6) of section 1064 of this title, and except to the extent, if any, to which the use of a mark registered on the principal register infringes a valid right acquired under the law of any State or Territory by use of a mark or trade name continuing from a date prior to the date of registration under this chapter of such registered mark, the right of the owner to use such registered mark in commerce for the goods or services on or in connection with which such registered mark has been in continuous use for five consecutive years subsequent to the date of such registration and is still in use in commerce, shall be incontestable

citations.cite: U.S. Code, generic marks excluded from incontestable status
citations.quote: no incontestable right shall be acquired in a mark which is the generic name for the goods or services or a portion thereof, for which it is registered.

clauses.title: The ® Symbol Is Reserved by Statute for Registered Marks; the ™ Symbol Is Not Statutory
clauses.body: Federal trademark law codifies a specific way an owner may give notice that a mark is registered: displaying with the mark the words "Registered in U.S. Patent and Trademark Office," the abbreviation "Reg. U.S. Pat. & Tm. Off.," or the letter R enclosed within a circle (®). The statute ties this notice to a specific consequence — a registrant who sues for infringement without having given this notice cannot recover profits or damages unless the defendant had actual notice of the registration some other way. This ® symbol is accordingly reserved, as a matter of federal statute, for marks that have actually been registered. By contrast, the ™ symbol (and ℠ for services) is not mentioned in this statutory notice provision, or elsewhere in the reviewed sections of the Lanham Act; using ™ to claim rights in an unregistered mark is a matter of common practice rather than a specific federal statutory grant, though it operates alongside the unregistered-mark protections described in the companion clause on common-law rights.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that ® notice is tied by statute to a registered mark and to specific litigation consequences — not a claim about whether the mark described on this sheet is currently registered or eligible to use either symbol, which this clause does not resolve. On the ™ symbol specifically: this clause reports an absence, confirmed by reviewing the statutory notice provision (15 U.S.C. § 1111) and the Lanham Act's general definitions (15 U.S.C. § 1127) directly, rather than assuming it — neither provision defines, requires, or restricts use of ™, so no statutory citation is given for it and none should be inferred to exist. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 1111); no additional independent source was found for this. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, notice of registration; display with mark
citations.quote: Notwithstanding the provisions of section 1072 of this title, a registrant of a mark registered in the Patent and Trademark Office, may give notice that his mark is registered by displaying with the mark the words “Registered in U.S. Patent and Trademark Office” or “Reg. U.S. Pat. & Tm. Off.” or the letter R enclosed within a circle, thus ®

clauses.body: Applicant name: {{applicantName}}. Mark: {{trademarkDescription}}. Goods and/or services on or in connection with which the mark is used, or is intended to be used: {{goodsServicesDescription}}. This sheet records this information as stated by {{applicantName}} for reference in connection with a possible federal trademark application; it does not itself constitute a filing with the United States Patent and Trademark Office.

clauses.body: Basis for filing (use in commerce or intent to use), as applicable: [use in commerce / intent to use]. If the basis is use in commerce, date of first use of the mark anywhere: {{firstUseDate}}. If the basis is intent to use, no first-use date is stated, and a verified statement of use identifying the date of first use in commerce will be required after a notice of allowance issues and before registration can be granted on that basis.

clauses.title: Declaration and Scope of This Vacation Payout Statement
clauses.body:
This Statement of Accrued but Unused Vacation is prepared by {{employeeName}}, a former employee of {{companyName}}, whose employment ended on {{terminationDate}}. It identifies vacation or paid-time-off time that {{employeeName}} contends had already accrued and vested, under California law and the terms of {{companyName}}'s own written vacation or paid-time-off policy, before employment ended, and that remains unpaid as of the date of this statement.

This document deliberately goes deeper into California's vacation-payout rule than the brief, general, multistate clauses already found elsewhere in this project's forms. The Termination/Separation Letter document's accrued-vacation clause and the Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document's accrued-vacation-reference clause each note, in general terms, only that some states treat earned vacation as vested wages that cannot be forfeited while many other states do not require any such payout at all — without setting out California's own statutory text or case law on the subject in full. This document sets out that California-specific rule directly, including the statute itself, the case law interpreting it, and the state labor agency's own published guidance distinguishing a lawful accrual cap from an unlawful "use-it-or-lose-it" forfeiture.

clauses.title: Vacation Pay Vests as It Is Earned and Cannot Be Forfeited
clauses.body: Under California Labor Code section 227.3, whenever an employer's policy or an employment contract provides for paid vacation, an employee who is terminated without having used all of their vested vacation time must be paid, as wages, for all of that vested vacation at their final rate of pay — and neither an employment contract nor an employer policy may provide for forfeiture of vested vacation time upon termination. The California Supreme Court has held that this vesting happens gradually, as the labor is performed, rather than all at once on some later date a policy might specify: a proportionate, pro rata share of vacation pay vests with each day worked, so an employee who leaves before an arbitrary policy "anniversary date" still holds a vested, non-forfeitable right to the proportionate share already earned.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute and case law, used as real evidence of California's vacation-payout rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee; many other states do not require any vacation payout at termination at all. This clause does not address whether accrued but unused paid sick leave (as distinct from vacation) must also be paid out at termination; that distinction is addressed in a separate clause of this document. This session's CourtListener access was rate-limited (125 requests/day, exhausted before this document's case-law citation could be independently re-fetched and re-read this session, with the quota not resetting until roughly 14.5 hours later) — that limit is disclosed here rather than worked around. The Suastez quotation below was independently verified via CourtListener in this same project's corpus (the Termination/Separation Letter document's accrued-vacation clause, checked 2026-08-29) and is reused verbatim here rather than re-fetched; it is also independently corroborated by the California Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's own published FAQ on vacation (dir.ca.gov/dlse/FAQ_Vacation.htm, fetched and byte-compared twice with different User-Agent headers this session), which cites this same case for this same proposition and states that, unless otherwise provided by a collective-bargaining agreement, "upon termination of employment all earned and unused vacation must be paid to the employee at his or her final rate of pay," citing Labor Code section 227.3. The statutory text quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 227.3 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Unless otherwise provided by a collective-bargaining agreement, whenever a contract of employment or employer policy provides for paid vacations, and an employee is terminated without having taken off his vested vacation time, all vested vacation shall be paid to him as wages at his final rate in accordance with such contract of employment or employer policy respecting eligibility or time served; provided, however, that an employment contract or employer policy shall not provide for forfeiture of vested vacation time upon termination.

The right to a paid vacation, when offered in an employer's policy or contract of employment, constitutes deferred wages for services rendered. Case law from this state and others, as well as principles of equity and justice, compel the conclusion that a proportionate right to a paid vacation "vests" as the labor is rendered. Once vested, the right is protected from forfeiture, by section 227.3. On termination of employment, therefore, the statute requires that an employee be paid in wages for a pro rata share of his vacation pay.

clauses.title: A Reasonable Accrual Cap Is Permitted; "Use-It-or-Lose-It" Forfeiture Is Not
clauses.body: The text of Labor Code section 227.3 itself addresses only forfeiture of vacation time already vested — it does not, on its own face, say anything about whether an employer may cap how much vacation an employee accrues going forward, or about "use-it-or-lose-it" policies specifically. That distinction has instead been developed through case law and through the California Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's (DLSE) published interpretation of the statute. Under that guidance, a policy that simply stops further vacation from accruing once an employee's banked balance reaches a specified ceiling — a "cap" — is lawful, because it does not take away any vacation time already earned; it only pauses future accrual until the balance drops below the cap. A "use-it-or-lose-it" policy is treated differently, because it does take away vacation time the employee already earned if it is not used by some deadline, which section 227.3 does not permit.
clauses.gap: This is one state's case law and labor-agency guidance, used as real evidence of California's cap-versus-forfeiture distinction — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer's policy; many other states do not require any vacation payout at termination at all, and so have no occasion to draw this distinction the way California does. This session's CourtListener access was rate-limited (disclosed in full in this document's clause on vesting), so the Boothby opinion was not independently re-fetched and re-read this session; the quotation below is reused verbatim from this same project's own already-verified corpus (checked 2026-08-29) and is independently corroborated by the DLSE FAQ guidance quoted below, fetched fresh this session directly from dir.ca.gov and byte-compared across two fetches with different User-Agent headers. The DLSE FAQ is the state labor agency's own sub-regulatory interpretive guidance, not a statute or a binding judicial holding; it is cited here as real evidence of how the agency that enforces section 227.3 applies it, not as a claim that a court would necessarily reach the same result in every case.

citations.case: California DLSE, "Vacation" FAQ (California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.cite: DLSE FAQ - Vacation, Question 5
citations.quote: Unlike "use it or lose it" policies, a vacation policy that places a "cap" or "ceiling" on vacation pay accruals is permissible. Whereas a "use it or lose it" policy results in a forfeiture of accrued vacation pay, a "cap" simply places a limit on the amount of vacation that can accrue; that is, once a certain level or amount of accrued vacation is earned but not taken, no further vacation or vacation pay accrues until the balance falls below the cap.

clauses.title: Vacation Payout Follows the Same Final-Wage Deadlines, Not a Separate One
clauses.body: Labor Code section 227.3 does not itself set out any separate payment deadline for vested vacation — it requires only that vested vacation be paid "as wages at his final rate," without specifying a particular number of days after termination by which that payment must be made. The California Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's published guidance confirms that vacation payout is folded into the same final-paycheck requirement that governs other final wages, rather than treated as a separate category of pay with its own separate due date. Where California's vacation-payout rule applies, that payout is accordingly treated as part of the final wages covered by whichever statutory final-pay deadline and waiting-time-penalty framework already applies to {{employeeName}}'s separation from {{companyName}}.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute and labor-agency guidance, used as real evidence that accrued vacation payout is legally folded into the final-wage-payment deadlines, not given its own separate deadline — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular payout, and not a claim that any particular accrued balance is actually owed here. This clause deliberately does not re-derive the specific final-pay deadlines of Labor Code sections 201 and 202 or the waiting-time-penalty mechanics of section 203, because this project's Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document already contains dedicated, separately verified clauses covering those rules in full; this clause exists only to establish that vacation payout rides on those same deadlines rather than running on a timetable of its own. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 227.3, quoted in full in this document's clause on vesting and not re-quoted here) together with the DLSE guidance below, fetched fresh this session directly from dir.ca.gov and byte-compared across two fetches with different User-Agent headers; no case law was located, this session or in this project's existing corpus, addressing the payout-deadline question specifically (as opposed to the vesting and no-forfeiture questions the case law above addresses).

citations.quote: Because paid vacation benefits are considered wages, such pay must be included in the employee's final paycheck.

clauses.title: Vacation Is Distinct From Paid Sick Leave, Which California Law Does Not Require to Be Paid Out at Termination
clauses.body: California's statutory paid-sick-leave law is separate from the vacation-vesting rule described elsewhere in this document, and the two are not paid out the same way at termination. By its own text, the paid-sick-leave statute does not require an employer to compensate an employee for accrued, unused paid sick days upon termination, resignation, retirement, or other separation from employment. Where an employer instead combines vacation and sick leave into a single "paid time off" or "PTO" bank that an employee may use for any purpose, without the employer designating a portion of it as sick-leave-only, the state labor agency's published guidance treats the combined bank the same as vacation for payout purposes — meaning it is earned day by day, vested amounts cannot be forfeited, and any unused, accrued balance must be paid out at termination. Whether a specific benefit {{employeeName}} held at {{companyName}} was structured as vacation, as combined PTO, or as sick leave carved out separately under a compliant sick-leave policy depends on the terms of {{companyName}}'s own written policy.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute and labor-agency guidance, used as real evidence of California's vacation-versus-sick-leave distinction — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer's policy, and not a claim about how any particular policy at any particular employer is actually structured. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 246(g)(1)); the same statutory section also contains a related but separate rule, in § 246(g)(2), about reinstating accrued sick leave for an employee rehired within a year of separation, which this clause does not address because it concerns reinstatement on rehire rather than payout at termination. citations.quote: Where an employer replaces its separate arrangements for vacation and sick leave with a program whereby employees are granted a certain number of "paid days off" each year that can be used for any purpose, including vacation and sick leave, the employees have an absolute right to take these days off. Consequently, again applying the principles of equity and fairness, DLSE takes the position that such a program is subject to the same rules as other vacation policies. Thus, for example, the "paid time off" is earned on a day-by-day basis, vested paid time off days cannot be forfeited, the number of earned and accrued paid time off days can be capped, and if an employee has earned and accrued paid time off days that have not been used at the time the employment relationship ends, the employee must be paid for these days.

clauses.title: The Employer's Own Policy Sets the Accrual Rate, Cap, and Eligibility Terms
clauses.body: California's vacation-vesting rule does not itself dictate how fast vacation accrues, whether a cap applies, or who is eligible for it — Labor Code section 227.3 ties the payout obligation to "such contract of employment or employer policy respecting eligibility or time served." The specific accrual rate, any accrual cap, and the eligibility terms that applied to {{employeeName}}'s vacation or paid-time-off benefit at {{companyName}} are set by {{companyName}}'s own written policy, described here as: {{vacationPolicyTerms}}. Once vacation time vests under whatever formula that policy sets, California law requires it to be honored and prohibits the policy from providing for its forfeiture upon termination — but the formula itself, and any lawful cap on future accrual, is a function of the policy's own terms rather than a state-mandated rate.

clauses.title: Statement of the Accrued Vacation Balance and Signature
What a Provisional Application Must Contain
clauses.body: Federal patent law sets out what a provisional application for patent must include, and what it doesn't. Under 35 U.S.C. § 111(b)(1), a provisional application must include a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) — a written description of the invention — and a drawing as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. § 113, which requires a drawing only "where necessary for the understanding of the subject matter sought to be patented." The application must also be accompanied by the filing fee required by law, though the fee itself may be submitted after the filing date within a period the USPTO Director prescribes; failing to pay it within that period results in the application being regarded as abandoned. Unlike a nonprovisional application filed under 35 U.S.C. § 111(a), which must include one or more claims, 35 U.S.C. § 111(b)(2) is explicit that a claim "shall not be required in a provisional application." A provisional application describing {{inventionTitle}} — summarized in {{inventionDescription}} — would, as a factual matter, need a written specification and, where the subject matter admits of illustration, a drawing, but not a claim, to satisfy these statutory requirements.
clauses.gap: This clause cites three different paragraphs of the same statutory subsection, 35 U.S.C. § 111(b) — (b)(1), (b)(2), and (b)(3) — along with the related drawing requirement in 35 U.S.C. § 113, which § 111(b)(1)(B) itself incorporates by reference; these are different pieces of the same statutory scheme rather than independent corroborating sources for one another. Both statutes were checked directly against the U.S. Code text at Cornell's Legal Information Institute and re-fetched with a distinct User-Agent to confirm the returned text was byte-identical both times. This is federal law, used as real evidence of what a provisional application must and must not contain — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific invention or filing. This clause doesn't address the separate requirement that the application be made, or authorized to be made, by the inventor in writing to the Director, and doesn't address the oath-or-declaration requirement that applies to nonprovisional applications, since a provisional application has no oath-or-declaration requirement of its own under § 111(b)(1).

clauses.title: A Provisional Application Is Never Examined and Cannot Itself Become a Patent
clauses.body: Federal patent law treats a provisional application differently from a regular, nonprovisional application in a fundamental way: it is never examined on its merits, and no patent can issue directly from it. 35 U.S.C. § 111(b)(8) states that the provisions of Title 35 relating to applications for patent generally apply to provisional applications, "except that provisional applications for patent shall not be subject to sections 131 and 135" — the statute governing substantive examination of an application by the Patent and Trademark Office, and the statute governing derivation proceedings between competing applicants over priority of invention. Because a provisional application is never examined under § 131, a patent can issue only from a nonprovisional application — whether a new filing or one that later claims the benefit of an earlier-filed provisional application's filing date, as described in a separate clause of this document.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the mechanical relationship between a provisional application and eventual patent examination — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific invention or the outcome of any application. This clause confirms that § 111(b)(8) exempts provisional applications from § 131 (examination) and § 135 (derivation proceedings); it doesn't independently verify the full substantive content of those two sections beyond that exemption, since their own text wasn't separately fetched and checked for this research. Checked directly against the U.S. Code text at Cornell's Legal Information Institute and re-fetched with a distinct User-Agent to confirm the returned text was byte-identical both times.

clauses.title: The 12-Month Deadline Following a Provisional Application's Filing Date
clauses.body: Federal patent law fixes a firm deadline tied to a provisional application's own filing date. Under 35 U.S.C. § 111(b)(5), unless a timely request is made to treat the provisional application itself as a nonprovisional application under 35 U.S.C. § 111(a), "the provisional application shall be regarded as abandoned 12 months after the filing date of such application and shall not be subject to revival after such 12-month period." A corresponding nonprovisional application that claims the benefit of the provisional application's earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. § 119(e) must also be filed within that same 12-month window to obtain that benefit. Federal law provides one narrow, automatic adjustment to this calendar: under 35 U.S.C. § 119(e)(3), if the day that is 12 months after the provisional application's filing date falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or federal holiday in the District of Columbia, the period is extended to the next business day. For a provisional application with a filing date of {{filingDate}}, this 12-month period is measured from that date, subject to that narrow calendar adjustment.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the 12-month deadline that runs from a provisional application's own filing date — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific invention or filing decision. A related, separate provision, 35 U.S.C. § 119(e)(1), lets the Director prescribe regulations allowing the 12-month period referenced in that subsection to be extended by an additional 2 months where the delay in filing the later nonprovisional application was unintentional, subject to a fee; 35 U.S.C. § 111(b)(5)'s own cross-reference is limited to § 119(e)(3)'s weekend-or-holiday adjustment, and this clause doesn't resolve how, or whether, that separate unintentional-delay extension interacts with a provisional application's own abandonment under § 111(b)(5) — that procedural interaction wasn't independently verified in this research. Both statutes were checked directly against the U.S. Code text at Cornell's Legal Information Institute and re-fetched with a distinct User-Agent to confirm the returned text was byte-identical both times.

clauses.title: What Claiming the Benefit of a Provisional Application's Filing Date Actually Does
clauses.body: The concept of a "priority date" in patent law refers to a specific statutory mechanic, not a general notion of who thought of an invention first. Under 35 U.S.C. § 119(e)(1), a nonprovisional application "shall have the same effect, as to such invention, as though filed on the date of the provisional application filed under section 111(b), if the application for patent filed under section 111(a) or section 363 is filed not later than 12 months after the date on which the provisional application was filed" — and only for the invention actually disclosed in the provisional application in the manner 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) requires, and only if the nonprovisional application contains, or is amended to contain, a specific reference to the provisional application. The provisional application itself carries no independent right of priority: 35 U.S.C. § 111(b)(7) states that "a provisional application shall not be entitled to the right of priority of any other application under section 119" or to the benefit of an earlier filing date of its own — the benefit runs only in the direction of a later-filed nonprovisional application claiming back to the provisional, not the other way. And claiming that earlier filing date doesn't lengthen the eventual patent's term: 35 U.S.C. § 154(a)(3) states that "[p]riority under section 119...shall not be taken into account in determining the term of a patent," whose term instead runs from the nonprovisional application's own filing date.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of what claiming the benefit of a provisional application's filing date does and doesn't accomplish — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific invention or filing. This clause draws on three different sections of Title 35 — § 111(b)(7), § 119(e)(1), and § 154(a)(3) — each cited once; no two citations in this clause are to different subsections of the same section. It doesn't address what § 112(a)'s written-description and enablement requirements themselves demand of a provisional's disclosure for a later claim to actually receive the earlier date, a fact-specific inquiry that wasn't independently researched here, nor does it address the separate foreign-priority mechanic under § 119(a)–(d), which involves a different filing (a foreign application, not a U.S. provisional). All three statutes were checked directly against the U.S. Code text at Cornell's Legal Information Institute and re-fetched with a distinct User-Agent to confirm the returned text was byte-identical both times.

clauses.title: The Public-Disclosure Bar to Patentability, and the One-Year Grace Period for the Inventor's Own Disclosures
clauses.body: Federal patent law can bar an invention from being patentable based on disclosures that occurred before a patent application's effective filing date — including disclosures by the inventor. Under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1), a person is not entitled to a patent if "the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention." Filing a provisional application establishes an effective filing date for this purpose, for whatever subject matter the provisional actually discloses. Federal law also provides a limited exception for the inventor's own disclosures: under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1), "a disclosure made 1 year or less before the effective filing date of a claimed invention shall not be prior art to the claimed invention under subsection (a)(1)" if, among other conditions, "the disclosure was made by the inventor or joint inventor or by another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor." This one-year window runs backward from the effective filing date and applies only to the inventor's own qualifying disclosures (or those derived from the inventor) — it does not affect the separate, unconditional bar that can apply to a disclosure made by an unrelated third party who did not obtain the information from the inventor.
clauses.gap: This clause cites three different subsections of the same statutory section, 35 U.S.C. § 102 — (a)(1), (b)(1), and (b)(1)(A) — which describe interlocking parts of the same novelty and public-disclosure scheme rather than independent corroborating sources for one another. Checked directly against the U.S. Code text at Cornell's Legal Information Institute and re-fetched with a distinct User-Agent to confirm the returned text was byte-identical both times. This is federal law, used as real evidence of the novelty bar and the inventor's-own-disclosure grace period written into the Patent Act — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific disclosure or invention. This clause doesn't address 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(2) (the separate rule concerning an earlier-filed, later-published application by another inventor covering the same subject matter) or § 102(b)(2) (that section's own, differently structured exceptions), and it doesn't resolve the fact-specific question of whether any particular disclosure counts as "public use," "on sale," or "otherwise available to the public" under the case law interpreting those terms, which wasn't independently researched here.

clauses.title: What "Patent Pending" Does and Doesn't Mean
clauses.body: The phrase "patent pending" has a specific legal meaning under federal law, but that meaning is narrower than the phrase might suggest. Federal law makes it a fineable offense to mark or advertise an article with the words "patent applied for," "patent pending," or similar language "when no application for patent has been made, or if made, is not pending, for the purpose of deceiving the public" — confirming that the phrase, used honestly, indicates only that a patent application (provisional or nonprovisional) is currently on file and has not been abandoned, finally rejected, or already issued. It does not indicate that a patent will issue, and it does not itself confer any of the rights a patent confers. Under 35 U.S.C. § 154(a)(1), a patent grants its owner "a grant to the patentee, his heirs or assigns, of the right to exclude others from making, using, offering for sale, or selling the invention throughout the United States," and 35 U.S.C. § 154(a)(2) fixes the term of that grant as beginning "on the date on which the patent issues." Filing a provisional application places an application on file — and, described honestly, supports calling that status "patent pending" — but because a provisional application is never examined and cannot itself mature into a patent, patent-pending status arising from a provisional application alone does not, by itself, create any enforceable right to exclude anyone from doing anything with {{inventionTitle}}.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two different subsections of the same statutory section, 35 U.S.C. § 154(a)(1) and § 154(a)(2), alongside 35 U.S.C. § 292(a) for the meaning and misuse penalty tied to the phrase "patent pending" itself; the two § 154 citations describe related parts of the same grant-and-term provision rather than independent corroborating sources for one another. All three were checked directly against the U.S. Code text at Cornell's Legal Information Institute and re-fetched with a distinct User-Agent to confirm the returned text was byte-identical both times. Neither § 292 nor § 154 mentions provisional applications specifically; this clause connects them to the provisional-application context using the separately verified fact that a provisional application is never examined and cannot itself mature into a patent (35 U.S.C. § 111(b)(8), covered in a separate clause of this document) — that connection is this document's own inference from the statutes, not itself a quoted statutory statement. This clause also doesn't address whether marking something "patent pending" before any application has actually been filed, rather than after, independently violates § 292(a) — that fact-specific question wasn't researched here.
