clauses.title: How the Lien Is Actually Created and Its Priority
clauses.body: The debt described in Civil Code § 5650 becomes an actual, recorded lien on an owner's separate interest only when the association takes an additional statutory step. Civil Code § 5675(a) provides: "The amount of the assessment, plus any costs of collection, late charges, and interest assessed in accordance with subdivision (b) of Section 5650, shall be a lien on the owner's separate interest in the common interest development from and after the time the association causes to be recorded with the county recorder of the county in which the separate interest is located, a notice of delinquent assessment, which shall state the amount of the assessment and other sums imposed in accordance with subdivision (b) of Section 5650, a legal description of the owner's separate interest in the common interest development against which the assessment and other sums are levied, and the name of the record owner of the separate interest in the common interest development against which the lien is imposed." If the lien is to be enforced by nonjudicial foreclosure, Section 5675(c) further requires that "the notice of delinquent assessment shall state the name and address of the trustee authorized by the association to enforce the lien by sale." Once recorded, Civil Code § 5680 provides that the resulting lien "shall be prior to all other liens recorded subsequent to the notice of delinquent assessment, except that the declaration may provide for the subordination thereof to any other liens and encumbrances." If a notice of delinquent assessment affecting {{propertyAddress}} has been recorded, its recording date is stated as: {{lienRecordingDate}}.
clauses.gap: Civil Code § 5650 creates the underlying personal debt; it is Civil Code § 5675 — not § 5650 itself — that actually creates and perfects the recorded lien on the owner's separate interest, and only as of the recording of a notice of delinquent assessment meeting § 5675(a)'s content requirements. Two of the three citations in this clause, to § 5675(a) and § 5675(c), are to subsections of the same statutory section; they are quoted together because (c) states an additional content requirement that applies only when the lien is to be enforced nonjudicially. The third citation, to § 5680, is to a separate section addressing lien priority once recorded. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's HOA assessment lien and foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA or property; other states impose different or no comparable HOA lien/foreclosure limits. This document is informational: it does not itself create, record, or foreclose any lien, and does not determine whether a specific assessment or fine is validly owed.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 5675(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The amount of the assessment, plus any costs of collection, late charges, and interest assessed in accordance with subdivision (b) of Section 5650, shall be a lien on the owner’s separate interest in the common interest development from and after the time the association causes to be recorded with the county recorder of the county in which the separate interest is located, a notice of delinquent assessment, which shall state the amount of the assessment and other sums imposed in accordance with subdivision (b) of Section 5650, a legal description of the owner’s separate interest in the common interest development against which the assessment and other sums are levied, and the name of the record owner of the separate interest in the common interest development against which the lien is imposed.

citations.quote: In order for the lien to be enforced by nonjudicial foreclosure as provided in Sections 5700 to 5710, inclusive, the notice of delinquent assessment shall state the name and address of the trustee authorized by the association to enforce the lien by sale.

clauses.title: Fines and Penalties Cannot Be Enforced Through the Assessment Lien
clauses.body: California law limits an association's ability to use its lien and foreclosure remedies to collect fines and penalties, as distinct from assessments themselves. This limitation applies to any assessment lien {{hoaName}} may record or seek to foreclose against {{propertyAddress}}. Civil Code § 5725(a) permits one narrow exception: "A monetary charge imposed by the association as a means of reimbursing the association for costs incurred by the association in the repair of damage to common area and facilities caused by a member or the member's guest or tenant may become a lien against the member's separate interest enforceable by the sale of the interest under Sections 2924, 2924b, and 2924c, provided the authority to impose a lien is set forth in the governing documents." Outside that exception, Civil Code § 5725(b) is explicit: "A monetary penalty imposed by the association as a disciplinary measure for failure of a member to comply with the governing documents, except for the late payments, may not be characterized nor treated in the governing documents as an assessment that may become a lien against the member's separate interest enforceable by the sale of the interest under Sections 2924, 2924b, and 2924c." The statutory notice required in an association's annual policy statement, Civil Code § 5730, restates the same limitation for owners: "The association may not use nonjudicial foreclosure to collect fines or penalties, except for costs to repair common area damaged by a member or a member's guests, if the governing documents provide for this."
clauses.gap: The citations to § 5725(a) and § 5725(b) are to two subsections of the same statutory section, quoted together because (a) states the narrow common-area-damage-repair exception to the general rule stated in (b). The additional citation to § 5730 is to a separate section — the required content of an association's annual policy statement — that restates the same § 5725 limitation in summary form for owners. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's HOA assessment lien and foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA or property; other states impose different or no comparable HOA lien/foreclosure limits. This document is informational: it does not itself create, record, or foreclose any lien, and does not determine whether a specific assessment or fine is validly owed.

clauses.title: Minimum Dollar Amount and Delinquency Period Before Foreclosure
clauses.body: California law sets a minimum dollar amount and, alternatively, a minimum delinquency period before an association may use judicial or nonjudicial foreclosure to collect delinquent assessments. Civil Code § 5720(b) provides that an association seeking to collect "delinquent regular or special assessments of an amount less than one thousand eight hundred dollars ($1,800), not including any accelerated assessments, late charges, fees and costs of collection, attorney's fees, or interest, may not collect that debt through judicial or nonjudicial foreclosure," though it may still pursue small claims court, or record a lien it may not yet foreclose. Section 5720(b)(2) provides that an association that records a lien in this situation "may not foreclose until the amount of the delinquent assessments secured by the lien ... equals or exceeds one thousand eight hundred dollars ($1,800) or the assessments secured by the lien are more than 12 months delinquent." Section 5720(c) confirms that "[t]he limitation on foreclosure of assessment liens for amounts under the stated minimum in this section does not apply to" assessments "more than 12 months delinquent," assessments on time-share estates, or assessments owed by the developer. If a total delinquent-assessment amount for {{ownerName}}'s account with {{hoaName}} has been stated, it is stated as: {{amountDelinquent}}.
clauses.gap: The citations to § 5720(b), § 5720(b)(2), and § 5720(c) are to subsections of the same statutory section; they are quoted together because they define one threshold rule (the $1,800 floor) and its express exceptions (delinquency exceeding 12 months, time-share assessments, and developer-owed assessments). This document does not restate the procedural details of the small-claims-court alternative described in § 5720(b)(1). This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's HOA assessment lien and foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA or property; other states impose different or no comparable HOA lien/foreclosure limits. This document is informational: it does not itself create, record, or foreclose any lien, and does not determine whether a specific assessment or fine is validly owed.

citations.quote: An association that seeks to collect delinquent regular or special assessments of an amount less than one thousand eight hundred dollars ($1,800), not including any accelerated assessments, late charges, fees and costs of collection, attorney’s fees, or interest, may not collect that debt through judicial or nonjudicial foreclosure, but may attempt to collect or secure that debt in any of the following ways:

citations.quote: By recording a lien on the owner’s separate interest upon which the association may not foreclose until the amount of the delinquent assessments secured by the lien, exclusive of any accelerated assessments, late charges, fees and costs of collection, attorney’s fees, or interest, equals or exceeds one thousand eight hundred dollars ($1,800) or the assessments secured by the lien are more than 12 months delinquent.

clauses.title: Board Votes Required to Record a Lien and to Initiate Foreclosure
clauses.body: California law requires the association's board itself — not staff or an outside collection agent — to make two separate decisions in this process, each by a specified vote recorded in the board's minutes, and requires a further dispute-resolution offer before the second decision. These requirements apply to any decision by {{hoaName}}'s board to record a lien against, or foreclose upon, {{propertyAddress}}. First, before a lien for delinquent assessments is recorded, Civil Code § 5673 provides: "For liens recorded on or after January 1, 2006, the decision to record a lien for delinquent assessments shall be made only by the board and may not be delegated to an agent of the association. The board shall approve the decision by a majority vote of the directors in an open meeting. The board shall record the vote in the minutes of that meeting." Second, before the association initiates foreclosure of a lien that has already been validly recorded, Civil Code § 5705(b) requires the association to first offer dispute resolution: "the association shall offer the owner and, if so requested by the owner, participate in dispute resolution pursuant to the association's ‘meet and confer’ program ... or alternative dispute resolution ... The decision to pursue dispute resolution or a particular type of alternative dispute resolution shall be the choice of the owner, except that binding arbitration shall not be available if the association intends to initiate a judicial foreclosure." The decision to actually initiate foreclosure is then governed by § 5705(c): "The decision to initiate foreclosure of a lien for delinquent assessments that has been validly recorded shall be made only by the board and may not be delegated to an agent of the association. The board shall approve the decision by a majority vote of the directors in an executive session. The board shall record the vote in the minutes of the next meeting of the board open to all members. The board shall maintain the confidentiality of the owner or owners of the separate interest by identifying the matter in the minutes by the parcel number of the property, rather than the name of the owner or owners. A board vote to approve foreclosure of a lien shall take place at least 30 days prior to any public sale."
clauses.gap: This document's own research corrected an initial assumption that a single Civil Code section (variously anticipated as § 5673 or § 5710) governs the board-vote requirement for a decision to foreclose. As fetched, § 5673 governs a different, earlier decision — the vote to record the lien in the first place, taken by majority vote in an open meeting; the vote to initiate foreclosure of an already-recorded lien is instead governed by § 5705(c), taken by majority vote in an executive session, at least 30 days before any public sale. Civil Code § 5710, by contrast, governs how a trustee's sale is conducted once foreclosure has been decided (addressed in another clause of this document), not the board-vote requirement itself. The citations to § 5705(b) and § 5705(c) are to two subsections of the same statutory section, quoted together because (b) is a precondition to the board's exercise of the vote described in (c); the citation to § 5673 is to a separate section governing an earlier, different board decision. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's HOA assessment lien and foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA or property; other states impose different or no comparable HOA lien/foreclosure limits. This document is informational: it does not itself create, record, or foreclose any lien, and does not determine whether a specific assessment or fine is validly owed.

The board shall approve the decision by a majority vote of the directors in an open meeting. The board shall record the vote in the minutes of that meeting.

clauses.title: Waiting Period, Trustee's Sale Mechanics, and the Right of Redemption
clauses.body: Once a lien has been recorded and the association has completed the steps described above, California law sets further mechanics and timing for an actual sale of {{propertyAddress}}. Civil Code § 5700(a) provides that, subject to other provisions of the article, "after the expiration of 30 days following the recording of a lien created pursuant to Section 5675, the lien may be enforced in any manner permitted by law, including sale by the court, sale by the trustee designated in the notice of delinquent assessment, or sale by a trustee substituted pursuant to Section 2934a." If a trustee's sale is used, Civil Code § 5710(a) requires that it "be conducted in accordance with Sections 2924, 2924b, and 2924c applicable to the exercise of powers of sale in mortgages and deeds of trust" — the same statutory notice-of-default and notice-of-sale framework used for mortgage foreclosures. Section 5710(b) adds an association-specific requirement on top of that framework: "the association shall serve a notice of default on the person named as the owner of the separate interest in the association's records or, if that person has designated a legal representative ..., on that legal representative," served "in accordance with the manner of service of summons" under the Code of Civil Procedure. Unlike a mortgage lender's nonjudicial foreclosure sale, a completed HOA assessment-lien foreclosure sale carries a statutory right of redemption: Civil Code § 5715(b) provides that "[a] nonjudicial foreclosure by an association to collect upon a debt for delinquent assessments shall be subject to a right of redemption[, and t]he redemption period within which the separate interest may be redeemed from a foreclosure sale under this paragraph ends 90 days after the sale."
clauses.gap: The citations to § 5710(a) and § 5710(b) are to two subsections of the same statutory section, quoted together because (b) is an association-specific service requirement layered on top of the general mortgage-foreclosure sale framework incorporated by (a). The citations to § 5700(a) and § 5715(b) are to separate sections addressing, respectively, the 30-day wait after a lien is recorded and the post-sale right of redemption. The 90-day right of redemption under § 5715(b) is a feature specific to an association's foreclosure of an assessment lien; it does not describe redemption rights, if any, following a mortgage lender's nonjudicial foreclosure of a deed of trust, a separate topic addressed in a different document in this corpus. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's HOA assessment lien and foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA or property; other states impose different or no comparable HOA lien/foreclosure limits. This document is informational: it does not itself create, record, or foreclose any lien, and does not determine whether a specific assessment or fine is validly owed.
